Eleven ciphered letters from Pius V’s cardinal-nephew to the nuncio at Madrid (DECODE R93–R102, R115). George Lasry’s known key is polyphonic, every digit standing for two letters, so decryption is ambiguous; the letters were chosen by a search scored with a language model of 16th-century Italian, and all eleven decrypted end to end. Where Spagna 6/I and 6/II. DECODE has the transcriptions, 9,842 digits in 6/I, with a key but no plaintext; the catalogue here listed them as open. The cipher Polyphonic: each digit 1–9 stands for two letters, 0 is a null, and a small nomenclator uses four-digit groups with zeros in second and fourth place. How it was read Lasry’s 2020 key, with a search choosing between the two letters of each digit, scored by a model of 16th-century Italian. It gives continuous Italian on all eleven. What it says An approach to marry Philip II to a French princess, the Pope’s complaints about the King’s ministers, the Bolognese exiles, and Borromeo’s quarrel with the Milan senate. Still open A few dotted groups outside Lasry’s list, single-letter choices, and the comparison with Serrano’s 1914 print, which could not be reached. Credit George Lasry reconstructed the key in 2020.

Spagna 6/I is described by the archive as “Lettere orig. e cifre del cardinale Alessandrino dal 16 gennaio 1568”. DECODE has ten ciphertexts from it (items 1–10: ff. 6r, 42r, 55r, 81r, 88r–89v, 136r, 169r–v, 291r–v, 306r; item 8 has no folio on DECODE), 9,842 digits in all, and one from 6/II (item 13, f. 641r, 1569; 769 digits). None is dated on DECODE; the dossier’s folio order places 6/I in 1568, but R94’s covering letter (f. 44r, Rome 7 November 1567, “Con questa un poco di cifra”) dates that one to 1567, and R96’s covering letter is of 19 May 1568. The transcriptions were made for DECODE in 2016–2020 and are used here as they stand. Lasry’s key, attached to every record: Letters: 1 u|t · 2 i|m · 3 f|g · 4 a|l · 5 o|s · 6 e|n · 7 d|r · 8 b|c · 9 p|z · 0 null. There is no sign for h or q . Nomenclator: 1010 Nostro Signore · 1020, 4010, 9010 Sua Santità · 1050 Francia · 1090 V. S. · 2060 non · 2090 che · 3010 Re · 4030 S. M.tà · 4060 questo · 4090, 9030 Germania · 5020 per · 5090 qui · 6090 quel · 7090 quello · 8010 Re di Francia · 9020 quelle · 9060 questa; dotted 0̇0 comma, 3 0̇ 9 qua; and a few tentative (1040 Regina di Francia?, 3040 Fiandra?, 8090 sapere?). The contemporary decipherments correct and extend it: 9 also stands for con , dotted 0 for z , 0̇0 for et ; 1040 is lettere (not Regina di Francia), 8090 havere , 4010 Re di Francia (not Sua Santità), 2010 Imperatore , and 1020 esser , 3020 quando , 3060 -mente , 4020 come , 4040 Milano , 4080 et , 5070, 6050 and 7070 Imbasciatore , 6060 Inquisitione , 7030 Cardinale , 7040 galere , 8020 avviso , 8070 Ugonotti , 3050 and 6030 Italia , 9090 havendo , 6020 causa . The extended key is in key.md .

The first cipher (f. 6r), as deciphered from the figures and the contemporary decipherment on f. 8: N.S. è ricercato qui da alcuni amorevoli della corona di Francia a fare officio con Imperatore perché si contenti dare una delle sue figliole per moglie al Re di Francia; la qual pratica N.S. non ha voluta movere, non sapendo l'animo di Re in questa parte. Però V.S. potrà scoprirlo con quella maniera che le parerà più opportuna et conveniente, asecurandola che N.S. non è per farne parola mai se prima non saperà qual sia l'intentione sua espressamente; et saputa che […] l'habbia, mi ne darà avviso con la prima commodità. “His Holiness is asked here by some friends of the crown of France to use his good offices with the Emperor so that he be pleased to give one of his daughters as wife to the King of France; His Holiness has not wished to set this negotiation moving without knowing the King’s mind in this matter. Your Lordship will therefore find it out … assuring him that His Holiness will never say a word of it before he knows what his intention is …” The September decryption had taken the codes 2010 and 4010 with Lasry’s tentative values and made this a French bride for Philip II; the decipherment gives the Emperor and the King of France. Charles IX married the Emperor Maximilian II’s daughter Elisabeth of Austria in 1570. The fourth cipher (f. 81r, R96) is still waiting for an answer “sopra il particolare del matrimonio”, judging that it might bring “qualche bona unione o lega tra questi tre principi principali della Christianità”. f. 6r, the first five lines of the first cipher: unbroken digits, each standing for one of two letters, with 0 as a null and four-figure nomenclator codes among them. They open the passage on the French marriage quoted above. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 6/I f. 6r, via DECODE R93.

Each letter’s full Italian text and English translation are in the Full texts section below; the quotations are from those readings. 6/I/1, f. 6r (R93). The French marriage request, above. 6/I/2, f. 42r (R94), November 1567. Jurisdiction: the Pope “non intende di revocare i suoi privilegii antichi, ma sì bene di levare li abusi cresciuti in essi per colpa delli suoi ministri”; if the King strips the Holy See of its authority, the Pope will resist “non con forze temporali” but with spiritual ones, “usque ad effusionem sanguinis”. 6/I/3, f. 55r (R95). The French ambassador’s claim about raising troops in the state of Milan; the crusade alms and indulgence; the man who said “che il Re si saria alienato da questa santa Sede”; the Pope grieves more for the King’s soul than for any human respect. 6/I/4, f. 81r (R96). The marriage again; Scipione [?Cuttinardo], who aspires to be Regent of the Collateral, indicted by the Holy Office as a heretic; the order against the Hermits of St Jerome. 6/I/5, ff. 88r–89v (R97), four pages. The Duke of Ferrara, offended over exiles of the contado of Bologna, may complain to the King through Count Ercole Tassone; the Duke is the Holy See’s “feudatario”, bound to return its exiles. The French ambassador at Constantinople offers to join the Huguenots and the Protestants with the Turks, and at Adrianople urges Piali Pasha to come with a great fleet against Rome: “la povera Christianità”. 6/I/6, f. 136r (R98). The King’s orders to his ministers in Italy against a Huguenot move lose their effect while the ministers wait for new commissions; the nuncio is to ask for express orders. 6/I/7, f. 169r–v (R99). The Order of St Lazarus, its Grand Master and two galleys from Gian Andrea Doria; Don John of Austria’s opposition; in Milan the senate’s threats to the archbishop’s vicar before the Corpus Domini procession: the Pope “pensa di procedere in questa causa contra di loro con quelle armi spirituali che il signor Dio gli ha date”. The letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.7%, under the 95% bar. 6/I/8 (R100). The King’s ministers obstruct the Inquisition of Catalonia; the nuncio is to execute the brief. 6/I/9, f. 291r–v (R101). The chinea and the St Peter’s-day dues accepted under the fisc’s protest; devolution under the investitures of Julius II and Julius III; “un manifesto scisma in quello regno”, bishops’ notaries and executors imprisoned; “chi è disobediente a Dio et al suo vicario non sarà meraviglia se perderà la obedientia de' suoi sudditi”. 6/I/10, f. 306r (R102). Cardinal [Espinosa] fails in his office with the King in the service of the Holy See, and the Pope has judged him “indegno di quella dignità che tiene”; the nuncio may let him know, if amendment can be hoped for. 6/II/13, f. 641r (R115), 1569. The nomination of Don [?Francesco] de Reinoso to the see of Monreale, and the transfer to it of pensions on the archdeaconry of Toledo. It builds coherent sentences but reads at 88.5%, under the 95% bar.
alessandrino1568.html#method

Each digit 1–9 gives two letters and 0 nothing, but a group X0Y0 may be a nomenclator word or two letters with their nulls. The decoder ( targets/alessandrino1568/decrypt.py ) works through the page keeping the best few partial decryptions at each step; at each digit it tries both letters, the null, and any nomenclator group that starts there, and scores the resulting Italian with the repository’s shared five-gram model (it-cinquecento, spaces removed). The same code, with a different key table, decrypted the Morosini ciphers of 1588–89. Every page decodes at about −1.75 nats a letter, the level of ordinary text for this model, and ends in a few letters of clerk’s padding. That score did not make the text a reading. Divided into words, the beam output had corrupted runs (“liberagemptume”, “unmannifestsobismain”) and many single letters chosen by the model, and the reading audit of 22–23 October 2026 classed the letters decoded, not read until each was checked. The records’ DECODE “cleartext” images were then opened one by one: R94 (f. 45r), R95 (f. 58r) and R100 (under the cipher, f. 280r) on 22 October, and R93 (f. 8), R96 (f. 80), R97 (f. 90r–v), R98 (f. 139), R99 (a leaf after f. 169), R102 (f. 307) and R115 (a half-sheet with f. 641) on 23 October each hold the contemporary decipherment. Each was transcribed and aligned word by word with the figures ( reread_aless_align.py ); where the decipherer and the figures differ, the figures decide. R101 has no decipherment; it was decoded again with the extended key and deciphered word by word on the figures.

Translation R94_en.md # R94 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio, cipher of [7 November 1567]) Taking a good occasion, and invited also by the talk His Majesty sometimes has with Your Lordship on these matters of jurisdiction, His Holiness wishes you to tell him freely that His Holiness does not intend to revoke his ancient privileges, but rather to remove the abuses that have grown up in them through the fault of his ministers, who, for their own private interest more than for anything else, have tried to enlarge them and to use them to the detriment of that authority which granted His Majesty's predecessors the graces and privileges they allege. But this will have to be said at a suitable moment, as I tell you, […] His Majesty begins […] freely, and is out of the trouble of the funerals; adding further that, should His Majesty be resolved, through his ministers, to strip this Holy See in fact of its authority in some cases, His Holiness — not with temporal forces but with those the Lord God has granted him — will put up every strong and lively resistance, even to the shedding of blood. Translation R95_en.md # R95 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio, cipher of early 1568) Answering your letters of last month more particularly, I tell you that, were what the French Ambassador has said not true — about being able to raise troops in the State of Milan in case it were attacked from here — it would give the King just cause to give up his protection and even to become indignant with that Ambassador, who spreads such falsehoods. Now as to the [08.: the Crusade?], His Holiness did not say it […] so that those who gave the alms should not gain the indulgence, but so that Christian discipline should not slacken in Spain, as has happened elsewhere; but His Holiness is content to grant him a new concession of it in such manner as his conscience allows, at the great instance made [an] by […], who in the office he [?performed] on this matter did not fail to say that the King would become estranged from this Holy See; but that, if that happened, His Holiness would grieve more for the loss the King would make of his soul than for any other human consideration. And in this same sense Your Lordship is to speak whenever you hear the subject raised. His Holiness waits to hear some answer from Your Lordship on the particular of the marriage between the Emperor and the King of France, about which I wrote to you in the last few days so that you might learn the Emperor's view of it, His Holiness judging that if by chance it were concluded, one could easily hope for some good union or league among these three chief princes of Christendom. You will let the King know as soon as possible that in this Holy Office Scipione [?Cuttinardo] has been charged as a heretic, who, it is understood here, aspires to be Regent of the Collateral [Council of Naples]; and as the news is of great importance, as you see, do not fail to tell it to the King at once in His Holiness's name. If in the execution of that order against the Hermits of St Jerome there should be opposition or any difficulty, once Your Lordship has made the proper inquiries you must [give] me notice of everything, so that from here provision can be made for [?whatever] will be needed in this matter. R97 (ASV, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 6/I, item 5, f. 088r-089v (DECODE R97), unknown) The Duke of Ferrara, displeased over the Bolognese exiles (Cavaliere Gualengo), may complain to the King through Count Ercole Tassone; the Pope's case under the investiture. The French ambassador in Constantinople offers to join Huguenots and Protestants with the Turks; in Adrianople he urged Piali Pasha to bring the fleet against Rome; his removal is to be sought. Translation R97_en.md # R97 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio, cipher, Rome 1568) Same holes as R97_reading.md. Modern spelling; codes as names. It is known for certain that the Duke of Ferrara, out of the dissatisfaction he has perhaps felt with His Holiness in a matter of the exiles of the county of Bologna, dealt with here in his name by the Cavaliere Gualengo, intends to make some complaint of it to the King; and if Count Ercole Tassone comes to your court he will probably have a particular commission to speak to him on this matter. That office ought not to be done by this ambassador, considering the fatherly affection His Holiness bears him and the little respect shown on his side to this Holy See, of which he is a feudatary, not observing the terms of his investiture, and in particular one that obliges him to hand over the exiles of this state whenever they are asked of him. […] I wanted Your Lordship to know, so that if you hear it spoken of you can tell the King to be pleased to keep an ear for His Holiness, who will justify himself in such a way that he does not doubt he can satisfy all the princes, if it comes to hearing their reasons; but if you do not hear it spoken of, there is no need to take any step, and you will be […] watchful while the said man stays at court, and keep me informed of what happens from time to time. It would be well to see, through His Holiness, that that bad ambassador who is there in the name of the King of France be removed, who does so many ill offices for Christendom that if he is tolerated he puts it in great danger, as he offers to unite the Huguenots with the Protestants in a league with the Turks to attack […] and besiege poor Christendom from every side; and to establish that league he affirms that ambassadors of the Prince of Condé and of the Protestants will soon be in Constantinople, promising that after everything has been ruined and destroyed they will all unite and be all of one faith with the Turks. This talk, which at another time would have been laughable, is now much to be feared for afflicted Christendom; so that by removing so bad an instrument from there, besides the King of France showing that these offices are not done with his consent, no small benefit would be done to the affairs of Christendom. And by another route it is likewise understood that in Adrianople the ambassador [of] the King of France has done many ill offices with Piali Pasha, general of the sea, against His Holiness, against the Emperor and against Italy, urging him to procure from the Sultan to come with a very great fleet to seize Rome and His Holiness; and he has done this not only as ambassador [of] France but also on commission from the Protestant princes, promising that ambassadors on their part will soon be there […], and offering that in Italy countless Huguenots would easily and quickly be sent to corrupt the minds of the Italians. R98 (ASV, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 6/I, item 6, f. 136r (DECODE R98), unknown) The King's orders to his ministers in Italy against a Huguenot move into Italy are good, but ministers delay waiting for new commissions; the nuncio is to press for express orders now, so that the Pope can call on them in time for the security of Italy. Translation R101_en.md # R101 — English (Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio, cipher of summer 1569) For Your Lordship's instruction, [you will know?] that His Holiness [recently?] accepted the hackney and the customary moneys paid on St Peter's day, but with a protest by the fisc, to which His Holiness adheres — that is, that he has not accepted it as a census but as the fruits of that kingdom, a direct fief of this Holy See — and claims the devolution [of the kingdom] on many heads of the investiture of Julius II and Julius III, of holy memory. The King or his ministers having by his order stirred up a manifest schism in that kingdom, as anyone free of passion can make out, taking away obedience to the Apostolic See, so that neither the bishops nor their vicars can have notaries to serve them, nor executors who, for the most part, in doing their office are not imprisoned by the royal ministers; and […] from this […] a doctor from [?Sora], of decrepit age, was left to die in prison. If such is His Majesty's mind, as his ministers say, His Holiness will have patience and will pray the Lord God to free His holy Church from such tribulation; but let the King beware of the judgement of God, who is indeed wont to permit His Church to be troubled, but in the end whoever troubles it will not go unpunished; and whoever is disobedient to God and to His vicar, it will be no wonder if he loses the obedience of his own subjects. Therefore, if the King does not resolve to remedy it soon, His Holiness will be obliged to take some measure there [6020]. For Your Lordship's information. Each letter comes from a target's profile.json , the record kept for every cipher on this site. It is placed at the city where it was written and the city it was sent to, as the notes state them. A court or a person is placed where they were at that date. Letters whose sender or recipient cannot be located from the evidence are left off rather than guessed. So are the cryptograms with no route at all, such as Voynich, Scorpion and the gold bars. A line stands for one route in one direction, and it gets thicker with each letter sent along it. Moving dots show the direction of travel on the busiest routes on screen. A route's colour is the commonest outcome among the letters showing: key recovered here, an existing key applied , an existing decipherment , or not solved . The glossary gives the exact categories. Hollow rings are letters from the catalogue with no known decipherment, at the one place the catalogue names, where that place can be located. English excerpts appear only where a reader has passed the reading, and never for texts withheld at their owner's request; each write-up has the complete text. The coastlines are modern (Natural Earth). The map draws no frontiers, because they moved too often over five centuries.

Clear Italian with fifteen runs of cipher and nine Latin code words. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, no. 4; DECODE R4793, catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. Senatore (2009) cites it. The cipher Capitals, digits and signs, one sign per letter as far as read, with Latin code words ( Calor = duca, storps = Lucca, cras = pace, pedesi = Iacopino). How it was deciphered None of the six keys of the 1450s filed in the same bundle fits. Below the text, torn on the left, an alphabet is written over its cipher signs; with the recipient’s glosses it gives the key. What it says Tentatively: Borghesi pressed King Alfonso over the promises made when Lucca was besieged; the Duke is said to be well disposed to Lucca and to peace; the peace with Iacopo Piccinino, the Florentine clergy, the Pope and the cardinals, and “contra lo Turcho” follow between holes. Credit Francesco Senatore identified the letter (2009). Still open The second half of the letter, which does not yet build sentences; the rapid clear hand of lines 18–23 on the only image; 19 rare signs; the code words toffe and vapor beyond their glosses. This letter was filed on this site until 14 October 2026 with the rest of the Sienese bundle of cipher letters, in which each letter has its own key. The other letters whose keys were found are different ciphers, each with its own page: no. 25 , no. 18 , no. 14 and nos. 6 and 24 (deciphered by George Lasry); the unread pieces and the filed keys are on the bundle’s page .

A letter in clear Italian with fifteen runs of cipher (144 signs) and nine Latin code words, from the jurist Galgano Borghesi, on embassy to King Alfonso, to his colleague Leonardo Benvoglienti; Senatore (2009) cites it as “una lettera in cifra di Borghesi a Benvoglienti … da Napoli, 12 maggio”. The recipient glossed some runs between the lines (“duca”, “papa”, “per parte del duca”, “al re”): this is the partial decipherment behind the 1952 inventory’s “solo parzialmente decifrate”. None of the six 1450s keys of the bundle fits, though one of them (R4750, the Milan ambassadors’ key of 1454) shares the code word storps . Below the text, torn away on the left, an alphabet is written out over its cipher signs , i to u ; with the glosses it gives the key. 114 of the 144 signs read securely, 11 more from context, 19 remain unread. No. 4, the alphabet fragment below the text: l m n o over the cipher signs ∫ 2 a T. Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 4, via DECODE R4793.

The reading audit of 22 October 2026 classed the letter decoded, not read: the first cipher runs complete their clear sentences, but the second paragraph is cipher runs, code words and unread signs between doubtful clear words. On 23 October the glosses and lines 17–24 were re-read on the DECODE image. The code word pedesi is glossed “Iacopino” (Iacopo Piccinino, whose war on Siena was settled in 1456 under King Alfonso’s arbitration), cras is glossed “a pace” and “pace” (not “parte”), and toffe “al papa”. A partial reading of the whole letter was built ( transcripts/no04_reading.md ). The first paragraph of news holds: Apresso. La Maestà del re ebbe a le strette gli adversarij e […] per mia instigatione volse includere de le […] Et tandem hec fuit […] che dicevamo che quando Lucha era assediata da Fiorentini, che le […] promesse al capitano […] se no[…]. E con questo […] stavamo […] e di mandato per [?papa] de le scritture disse erano rimasti a Milano, e che non le potemmo mostrare. Tunc rex parvi fecisse […] est, e chosì rimasero quasi beffati; tutto però buono per mettere aqua al mulino nostro. “His Majesty the King had his adversaries in a tight corner and […] at my instigation wished to include some of the […] that we said that when Lucca was besieged by the Florentines, the […] promises to the captain […] the writings, he said they had been left at Milan and that we could not show them. Then the King made light of it, and so they were left almost mocked; all of it good, though, to bring water to our mill.” The second paragraph builds only its first sentence, “Antonio d'Arezzo qua era detto el duca essere bene disposto et a Lucca et a pace” (the Duke well disposed towards Lucca and towards peace); after it come the peace with Iacopino, the Florentine clergy, “ne al papa ne a cardinali” and “contra lo Turcho”, between holes. The rapid clear hand of lines 20–23 does not resolve at two or three times on the only image, so the letter stays decoded, not read.

The letter is not read to the bar (second paragraph fragmentary). ## Translation Worshipful and magnificent sir, honoured as a father, after commendation etc. Since you left us here we have had no news from you, which is not without some surprise. We do not think there is in you […] any negligence, which is not your way, but rather some difficulty that we think [?has arisen]. Which, besides surprising us, also displeases and troubles us, and in [?frequent] […] that we sometimes use your term, and we say that someone, and by the road too, […] does not get here. So we ask you to let [?this] be advised quickly, and whether it is a thing to be said […] and to my instruction well etc. If there is anything else, if need be use the cipher and say we do it, and we here will keep this [?order] […]. Next. His Majesty the King had his adversaries in a tight corner and […] at my instigation wished to include some of the […] And in the end this was […] that we said that when Lucca was besieged by the Florentines, the […] promises to the captain […]. And with this […] we stayed […] and being sent for [?the Pope?] the writings, he said they had been left at Milan and that we could not show them. Then the King made light of it […], and so they were left almost mocked; all of it good, though, to bring water to our mill. But let us know about […] troops. Antonio d'Arezzo here was saying that the Duke was well disposed both towards Lucca and towards peace. And that he had satisfied [the] Pope that, for the peace with Iacopino [Piccinino], he should take some of the […] ready […] of the clergy of the Florentines […] who had not yet allowed either the Pope or the cardinals to take any […] one day in another way […]. […] and then, as needed, against the Turk […]. This same, if it is true, you must have likewise […]. […] and so [?he said?] all of it, on behalf of the Duke, to [?report] to the King […]. At Siena we think the same, by the letter left with this one […] that we do not know whether it is true, to inform them of everything, and that we have news of us […] when it happens there is need of another expense to send it […] to Siena […] could do more, that we have been kept without a penny […] so that we have news of you […] Nothing else […] greet. Given at Naples, 12 May. Key: no04_key.txt

The 21 maximal runs of four or more alphabet groups (106 letters) were scored with a 4-gram model built from 2.7 million characters of seventeenth- to nineteenth-century English. The null hypothesis permutes the 24 letter identities over the same periodic structure. score Pitt’s row −217.5 20,000 random rows: mean / sd / best −333.7 / 12.1 / −271.1 z; rows scoring at least as well 9.6; 0 of 20,000 A free period scan (annealing a 24-letter row for periods 20–32) is not decisive and is recorded as such: at 106 letters the annealer over-fits, and periods 27–32 reach higher scores than the true key. The argument for period 24 is structural (the odd/even construction, the 24-apart homophones, the alphabetical supplementary blocks), and the decryptions that match the cleartext (“A C · · knowledge”, “[835] D E R stand”, “Y O U R E [C] R E D E N T I A L S” beside Simpson’s “Our Re-credentials”) are the confirmation.

boswell.html#context

The King’s letter is addressed to the envoy. It answers the envoy’s letter of 6 October, calls the Duke “your Master” three times, sends “your re-credentials”, and wishes him a safe return to his master. Simpson’s Civil War Papers (Scottish History Society Miscellany I, 1893) prints the King’s letter to Duke James of Courland of the same day, calling itself “these Our Re-credentials”, and the envoy’s later memorial: the passage was unsafe and “the ministers of their Majesties at the Hague” dissuaded him from crossing and took his letters. Nicholas tells Boswell that the King’s two letters are “put into your character” and that Boswell is to “decifer & interpret them”. Hence the catalogue’s “Charles I to Boswell”. “Monsieur F I R X S S appeares not here.” Simpson names Major Georg von Firks as the Duke’s agent. A man expected at Oxford who has not come is the envoy’s own account of himself. The arms. Muskets, match and powder to Weymouth, Dartmouth, Exeter, Falmouth or a fifth port: the Duke’s memorial says he was told their Majesties needed munitions rather than men, and Nicholas wrote to Roe in December 1643 that “arms and powder are arrived at Dartmouth for his Majesty” (CSPD). The funerals of Duke Friedrich (d. 1642) and his brother Wilhelm (d. 1640), held together in February 1643: “the Late Dukes his Father & Unkle”. Nicholas’s instruction to hinder “the coming ouer of the [181]s from the [726]”, people “understood here not to affect Monarchy”, fits the States General’s embassy of mediation resolved on in late 1643 and received at Oxford early in 1644, which the King did not want: 181+S = Ambassadors, 726 = States. These two values rest on the history; the cipher alone does not fix them.

Two cipher letters and two troop returns after the capture of Dominica, marked not decrypted in the ANOM inventory. Brice Dudout read them with a key rebuilt from the pencil glosses on the same governor’s 1779 letters (0.894 of words on a held-out letter); 455 of 458 words are read. 250.266.5.361.587.694.381.303 … l’ et at de la situation des troupes … Martinique → Versailles · numerical nomenclator of about 850 numbers · Sept–Dec 1778 · read with known key Bouillé to the minister of the Navy, 1778 Go to the full text ↓ Two cipher letters and two troop returns after the capture of Dominica, marked “not decrypted” in the archive inventory, read with a key rebuilt from the same governor’s glossed letters of 1779. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 2 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letters The marquis de Bouillé, governor general of the Windward Islands, to Antoine de Sartine, Secretary of State for the Navy: no. 238 of 17 September 1778 (a duplicate) and no. 259 of 5 December 1778, with ciphered returns of 9 December. Where Archives nationales d’outre-mer, COL C8 A 77, fol. 88 (image FRANOM23_C8A_077_0141) and fol. 101 (images 0162–0164). The inventory says “Lettre chiffrée non décryptée”. The cipher Bouillé’s cipher of 1778–1782: a numerical, syllabic nomenclator of about 850 numbers with homophones (361 = de , 250 = l’ , 607 = le , 817 = s ) and code names (267 Martinique, 428 Guadeloupe, 138 Dominica). How it was deciphered The key (K6, 490 values) was rebuilt only from the pencil glosses on five of Bouillé’s 1779 letters and frozen. It read a held-out letter against its modern translation at 0.894 of words and 0.897 of characters, against at most 0.182 and 0.174 for 200 permuted keys. What it says Ten days after taking Dominica from the British, Bouillé says he is 817 men short and cannot garrison other islands. In December he sends the Dominica garrison (1,072 men) and the state of the Martinique army (4,057 present, 1,031 short). Still open Three words are unresolved, all in a heading and a note of the second return. The period key in Marine B4 195, which an archivist’s note points to, has not been consulted. The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout rebuilt the key, read the letters and checked the returns, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The same cipher reads the Damas letter of 1787 , which has its own page.
bouille1778.html#the-letters

Bouillé took Dominica on 7 September 1778. On 17 September he explains why he went no further: he was 817 men short, and every island taken needed a garrison. On 5 December he sends the new garrison of Dominica as a ciphered return, and the state of the whole army in Martinique as a second one. The inventory records both letters as not decrypted, and no decipherment sits on the images or the neighbouring leaves.
bouille1778.html#the-key

The key was built only from the pencil glosses between the lines of Bouillé’s 1779 letters (C8 A 78: fol. 3 nos. 173 and 175, fol. 31 no. 281, fol. 144 no. 372 and fol. 123 no. 363; 4,991 groups) and frozen as K6 with its SHA-256 recorded. Numbers 163, 586 and 257 are nulls, because they always fall where the sense is complete without them. An archivist’s pencil note on C8 A 78 fol. 3 says the 1779 letters were deciphered with the key at the beginning of the register Marine B4 195, a period table not yet consulted. Translation translation.md # English translation Letter of 17 September: I have the honour to send you the return of the troops as of the 1st of this month. I await the recruits announced to me by the Minister of War all the more impatiently because the shortfall of 817 men does not yet allow me to undertake anything against other English islands: I could not put a garrison there without stripping Martinique, where, after deducting the hospitals and the garrison of Dominica, only 3,300 effective men remain. I shall send you […] the return of the garrison of that last island, which is supplied half by Martinique and half by Guadeloupe, both regular troops and militia. Letter of 5 December: I have the honour to send you the return of the troops of Martinique as of the 1st of this month and that of the garrison of Dominica. The works for the security of that colony are nearing their end, and it is now in a state of defence. Return: garrison of Dominica on 1 December 1778 — Armagnac 104; Auxerrois 4; Viennois 280; Martinique […] 197; Guadeloupe 145; Bouillé’s Volunteers 81; […] 39 (26 from Martinique, 13 from Guadeloupe); Guadeloupe militia 10; free men of colour 222 (64 from Martinique, 81 from Guadeloupe, 67 from Dominica). Total: 1,072 men. Second return: troops in Martinique on 1 December 1778 (present; short of establishment; losses of the previous month) — Auxerrois 1,210 present (131 in hospital, 4 in Dominica), 370 short, 16 lost; Viennois 1,169 (106 in hospital, 280 in Dominica), 411 short, 9 dead; Martinique regiment 1,292 (93 in hospital, 197 in Dominica), 180 short, 23 lost; French artillery 210, 46 short, 3 dead; Martinique artillery 176, 24 short, 1 dead. Total: 4,057 present (360 in hospital, 507 in Dominica), 1,031 short, 2 discharged, 5 deserters, 45 dead. Note: one […] in the artillery and one gentleman sent home. Bouillé to the minister, 5 Dec 1778 (no. 259) and its two returns (Dominica garrison; troops in Martinique), 9 Dec 1778 Works at Dominica nearly finished; Dominica garrison 1,072 men; troops in Martinique 4,057 present, 1,031 short. J’attends avec d’autant plus d’{impatience} les recrues que le [ministre] de la guerre m’a annoncées, que le {vuide} de huit cent dix-sept hommes ne me permet pas d’entreprendre encore sur quelques isles angloises, ne pouvant y mettre une garnison [sans] dégarnir la Martinique, où il ne reste, en déduisant les hôpitaux et la garnison de la Dominique, que trois mille trois cent hommes {effectifs}. Translation translation.md # English translation Letter of 17 September: I have the honour to send you the return of the troops as of the 1st of this month. I await the recruits announced to me by the Minister of War all the more impatiently because the shortfall of 817 men does not yet allow me to undertake anything against other English islands: I could not put a garrison there without stripping Martinique, where, after deducting the hospitals and the garrison of Dominica, only 3,300 effective men remain. I shall send you […] the return of the garrison of that last island, which is supplied half by Martinique and half by Guadeloupe, both regular troops and militia. Letter of 5 December: I have the honour to send you the return of the troops of Martinique as of the 1st of this month and that of the garrison of Dominica. The works for the security of that colony are nearing their end, and it is now in a state of defence. Return: garrison of Dominica on 1 December 1778 — Armagnac 104; Auxerrois 4; Viennois 280; Martinique […] 197; Guadeloupe 145; Bouillé’s Volunteers 81; […] 39 (26 from Martinique, 13 from Guadeloupe); Guadeloupe militia 10; free men of colour 222 (64 from Martinique, 81 from Guadeloupe, 67 from Dominica). Total: 1,072 men. Second return: troops in Martinique on 1 December 1778 (present; short of establishment; losses of the previous month) — Auxerrois 1,210 present (131 in hospital, 4 in Dominica), 370 short, 16 lost; Viennois 1,169 (106 in hospital, 280 in Dominica), 411 short, 9 dead; Martinique regiment 1,292 (93 in hospital, 197 in Dominica), 180 short, 23 lost; French artillery 210, 46 short, 3 dead; Martinique artillery 176, 24 short, 1 dead. Total: 4,057 present (360 in hospital, 507 in Dominica), 1,031 short, 2 discharged, 5 deserters, 45 dead. Note: one […] in the artillery and one gentleman sent home. Key: key.tsv

brulart1615.html

Two royal letters to the French ambassador in Venice (BnF fr. 18043 f. 83 and fr. 18044 f. 109, DECODE R2785 and R2786), partly in the Brûlart de Léon cipher of 1615–18. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed its key and read both letters in 2021; the 1615 letter also carries a contemporary decipherment between the lines. Nothing was deciphered here; a few symbols Tomokiyo left open are probably nulls. 2́ amytie · 20́ de · 97́ pour · 5̄ pre · 7̄ que · 18̄ roi · 37̄ vous ö duc de Savoye · ä duc de Mantoue (Tomokiyo’s key) Poitiers and Paris → Venice · homophonic signs with numbered words and syllables · 1615, 1617 · existing decipherment Louis XIII to Brûlart de Léon, 1615 and 1617 from Louis XIII Go to the full text ↓ Two royal letters to the French ambassador in Venice, partly in cipher; Satoshi Tomokiyo rebuilt the key in 2021; both letters were taken here from the decipherments written between their lines, checked against his key. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (earlier solution) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (100% of the cipher) The letters Louis XIII, countersigned by Brûlart de Sillery, to Léon Brûlart, his ambassador in Venice: one of 16 September 1615 (Poitiers) and one of 25 July 1617 (Paris). French, with passages in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 18043 f. 83–84 and fr. 18044 f. 109–110. DECODE R2785 and R2786, both “partially decrypted”. The cipher Letter-like signs with two or three forms for most letters; numbers with a stroke for words and syllables; dotted vowels for the dukes of Savoy and Mantua; signs to cancel or repeat. How it was deciphered Both letters have a decipherment of the time written above most cipher runs. On 22 October 2026 the clear text and the glosses were transcribed from the DECODE images and every run checked against Tomokiyo’s key (2021); two unglossed runs were decoded with it. What it says 1615: Mantua’s harshness to his rebels, the fear that Savoy will renew the quarrel, Marini withdrawn to Genoa. 1617: Venice and Savoy urged to end the war; the Grisons and the Venetian secretary’s expulsion. Still open Lines of spaced signs with no gloss that give no French under the key (probably nulls, as Tomokiyo thought), parts of four rows of the 1617 letter, and three cramped glosses of 1615. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo (key and reading); the contemporary interlinear decipherment. Until 14 October 2026 these letters shared an entry with Louis XIII’s letter of 1631 to Melchior de Sabran in Genoa, because DECODE lists all three under the King’s name. That letter is in a different cipher, solved by George Lasry, with its own page .
brulart1615.html#letters

Léon Brûlart was French ambassador in Venice from 1611 to 1620. BnF fr. 18043 holds many letters of 1615–16 sent to him partly in cipher by Louis XIII, Marie de Médicis and Puysieux; fr. 18044 holds more of 1617–18. The royal letters are countersigned “Brulart”, by Brûlart de Sillery. DECODE has two of them: R2785 , fr. 18043 f. 83–84, 16 September 1615 (catalogued as the 15th). DECODE gives the place as “Poictyers[?]”, and the date line reads “Escript a Poictiers le xvi jour de Septembre 1615”. In the clear the King says he is still held in the town by the illness of his eldest sister (“ma soeur aisnee”), the court on its way to the Spanish marriages. brulart1615.html#cipher

Tomokiyo’s key, “Brulart de Leon’s Cipher (1615–1618)”, is attached to both DECODE records and printed on Cryptiana. It has: an alphabet of letter-like signs, with two or three different signs for most letters; numbers with a small stroke (a virgule) for words: 2 amytie , 20 de , 35 en , 70 je , 97 pour …; numbers with a bar over them for syllables and short words: 5 pre , 7 que , 18 roi , 37 vous , 30 tion …; vowels with dots for princes: ö the Duke of Savoy, ä the Duke of Mantua; a sign that cancels what comes next and a sign that repeats. Tomokiyo notes that the cipher is not much different from other French ciphers of the time, although Brûlart de Léon left a treatise on ciphers.
brulart1615.html#reading

Both letters carry a contemporary decipherment written above most of the cipher runs, probably made in the embassy. Tomokiyo recorded on DECODE what he could not read: in 1615 “some passages”, which “may be partially or totally nulls”; in 1617 “some symbols”, at least some of them cancelled. Until 22 October 2026 nothing of either letter was transcribed here, and the reading audit of that day classed both decoded, not read. The same day all four page images of each record were fetched from DECODE, the clear text and the interlinear decipherments transcribed, and every cipher run aligned with its gloss and checked against Tomokiyo’s key ( texts/R2785_align.tsv , texts/R2786_align.tsv ). The sign θ, not in his table, is a null. In 1617 the decipherer’s “incommoditez” is “inconvenients” in the figures, and one unglossed run, “en mesme temps”, was decoded with the key. 16 September 1615 (R2785). The King disapproves of the Duke of Mantua’s harshness to his rebel subjects, fears the Duke of Savoy will use it to renew the quarrel, and suspends his good offices: Partant je commande au sieur Marini de se retirer a Gennes soubz couleur de ses affaires domestiques, pour ne donner aucun ombrage, faisant estat d'envoyer bientost quelque autre, peust estre [?Manjeaux] qui est a Rome, pour aller resider pres led. duc de Savoye et continuer a me tenir adverty de toutes occurrences “Therefore I am ordering Sieur Marini to withdraw to Genoa under colour of his private affairs, so as to give no umbrage, and I mean soon to send someone else, perhaps [?Manjeaux], who is in Rome, to go and reside with the said Duke of Savoy and to keep me informed of all occurrences.” He is held at Poitiers by his eldest sister’s illness; the letter is dated “Escript a Poictiers le xvi jour de Septembre 1615”, the 16th, not the 15th as catalogued. 25 July 1617 (R2786). Venice should take the openings offered to end the war; the Duke of Savoy should use the French forces sent to help him “pour conclurre et asseurer un bon accord que pour faire durer la [?guerre]”; the Grisons have expelled the Venetian secretary [?Padavin], and Gueffier has reported on the Leagues.

Ceste rigueur et ressentiment trop vif qu'il demonstre offence plus les princes ses amis et alliez qui se sont entremis de la composition de ce differend qu'il ne sert au bien et advancement de ses interestz. Et si sur ceste occasion mon oncle le duc de Savoye prenoit conseil d'user de revanche, et se prevaloir de ce pretexte pour renouveller la querelle, Je ne scay [?autre] quelles raisons nous en pourrions divertir la Republique, qui a subiect d'en estre offensee aussy bien que nous tous qui nous en [?scaurions] [?presser]. Elle faict, comme j'apprendz de vostre derniere du xxv Aoust, bien de rendre encores en son endroict quelque office pour obvier aux inconvenientz de la continuation de ce mal entendu, qui serviront tousiours pour tesmoignage de sa bonne volonte. Quand a moy, j'ay delibere, recognoissant tant d'accroches du coste du duc de Mantoue [et] de celuy du gouverneur de Milan, qui faict quelque difficulte de se joindre aux remonstrances que j'avois ordonne estre faictes aud. Mantoue, et ne scachant encores ce qui pourra sur cela arriver de la part de mon oncle le duc de Savoye, de surseoir la continuation de mes exhortations et offices envers les partys, tant par crainte et prevoyance qu'ilz soyent infructueux, ### f. 83v qui pour ne juger a propos en [?ceste] conioncture de m'y embarasser davantage apres avoir si bien reussy en la premiere negociation. Partant je commande au sieur Marini de se retirer a Gennes soubz couleur de ses affaires domestiques, pour ne donner aucun ombrage, faisant estat d'envoyer bientost quelque autre, peust estre Manseau qui est a Rome, pour aller resider pres led. duc de Savoye et continuer a me tenir adverty de toutes occurrences, qui [?m'est possible] [...] sur celles qui se passent en [?l'Equidray], estant tousiours suspect que Marin prenne par ses dictz mouvemens, qui ont este [...] fomentez par [...] soubz [...] d'en profitter. Je suis encores arreste en ceste ville de l'indisposition de ma soeur aisnee, mais laquelle au dire des medecins me pourra permettre de partir a la fin de ceste sepmayne et continuer mon voyage avec le bonheur que je l'ay commance, cependant que le Mareschal de Boisdaufin pourvoyera de son coste avec les troupes que je luy ay laissees aux affaires qui se presentent du coste de Soissons, ### f. 84r esperant que mon auctorite sera en fin recognue de ces princes par amour ou par force. Je prie Dieu, Mons. de Leon, qu'il vous tienne en sa saincte et digne garde. Escript a Poictiers le xvi jour de Septembre 1615. Louis. This rigour and over-keen resentment that he shows offends the princes his friends and allies who took part in settling this quarrel more than it serves his own good and interests. And if, on this occasion, my uncle the Duke of Savoy should decide to take revenge and use this pretext to renew the quarrel, I do not know [?any other] reasons by which we could turn the Republic away from it, which has cause to be offended by it as much as all of us who [?could press] it. Same holes; modern spelling. --> # R2786, Louis XIII to Léon Brûlart, ambassador in Venice, Paris, 25 July 1617 ## Translation ### f. 109r Monsieur de Léon, I made my intentions known to you so clearly in my previous letters, carried to you by express courier, that I have little to add on receiving yours of the [?11th] of this month, except that I was very glad to learn of the satisfaction and gratitude these Lords [of Venice] showed you for my declaration, so prompt and favourable to the good of the cause they uphold, and that you were able to confirm to them what they wished: that I meant to settle this [?single] quarrel as a whole and leave none of the parties behind or [?in the right] on so important an occasion. I hope they will know how to make use of the advantage offered them to end this contention as soon as possible by means that are to their honour and safety, in the judgement of those who have their good, and the public good, at heart in this matter. But they will commit a signal fault against both if they neglect the said openings, fit to draw them out of a passage to which they must have regard, [...] so far committed. That is why, by at least yielding to reason, they will gain advantages of great weight: to make the general voice well-disposed and favourable to them, to oblige their friends and those who have taken up the defence of their cause to help and protect them with the good offices and means they have in hand, and to [?load] their adversaries with shame and blame, if they are capable of such salutary counsel, ### f. 109v to which you must invite and encourage them; and [?this] greatly justifies the right of their cause and the candour of their intentions. For prolonging the war [?increases] the public misery and calamity, and their own certain loss, and there is no doubt that they [?would] gain from a prompt settlement, if they consider what they have spent on it so far in money, men and reputation, [...] troubles [16] [21] [...] which will grow on every side as the war goes on, and at the same time they lose in consequence what [...] obtain through the agreement we are pursuing. I do not yet know what counsel the Duke of Savoy will have taken on the said proposals, but if he refuses to accept a reasonable settlement he will do great harm to his affairs, as I am having him told, so that he uses the forces I am sending to his help to conclude and secure a good agreement rather than to prolong the [?war] at this juncture. The one may be [...] the intention [...] in any way [...]. I assure you [...] to me [...] quite different. I [...] and you [...] ### f. 110r leave [...] towards him. As for the matter of the Grisons, if those Lords had deferred to the advice of their true friends and had not let themselves be misled by the persuasions of the ministers they employed, they would not have come to this pass, nor have seen their secretary Padavino withdraw from the country before the indignation of those peoples. Sieur Gueffier arrived two days ago and has set out to me the state of the said Leagues, which are beginning to recognise and perceive how harmful the multiplicity of alliances is to them, without my having opposed the Republic's suits. Good offices are being made towards the said Grisons, about which the Republic had just cause for complaint. Praying God, Monsieur de Léon, to keep you always in His holy and worthy care. Written at Paris, 25 July 1617. Louis. Brûlart.

DECODE R9970, AGS Estado leg. 1563 fol. 572, catalogued after Galende Díaz as Andrea del Burgo’s ciphered letter to Gattinara from Ferrara, 26 October 1527, holds no cipher. It is two drafts of a clear Spanish minute “al príncipe”: the Emperor tells Prince Philip of an exchange of 110,770 ducats with Anton Fugger, written 1543–1554. The Burgo letter is not on the record. al príncipe · demás de los cambios que hasta aquí se an hecho por n[uest]ro mandado con Antonio Fucar CX U DCC LXX d[ucad]os de a LXV gruesos = 110,770 ducats Emperor → Prince Philip · clear minute, no cipher · 1543–1554 (catalogued 26 Oct 1527) “Andrea del Burgo to Gattinara, 1527” is Charles V to Prince Philip on a Fugger loan from Charles V → to Philip II Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1563 fol. 572 (DECODE R9970), catalogued as a four-page ciphered letter of Andrea del Burgo, imperial envoy at Ferrara, to Chancellor Gattinara, 26 October 1527, not deciphered. The scans hold no cipher. They are two corrected drafts of a Spanish minute headed “al príncipe”, in which the Emperor tells his son of an exchange contract with Anton Fugger. The minute is at least sixteen years later than the date DECODE gives it. It is not Andrea del Burgo’s letter to Gattinara of 26 October 1527 that the catalogue gave. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1563 fol. 572; DECODE R9970, taken from Galénde Díaz’s 1994 list (p. 163) of Simancas ciphers. The cipher None. Every line is ordinary Spanish in an untidy secretary hand; the Roman numerals and the U thousands sign explain DECODE’s “numerical, graphic signs” tags. How it was checked The four images were put in archive order from the scan banners and pencil numbers: two heavily corrected drafts headed al príncipe , then a blank page. Dating Philip was born in May 1527 and governed Spain as prince in 1543–1548 and 1551–1554, so the minute belongs to those years, not to 1527. Still open The Burgo letter was not found on DECODE, on PARES, in the Calendar of State Papers or in Tomokiyo; its real location is open.

Openings of the two drafts, with abbreviations expanded in brackets and deleted words left out. This is a reading of the key passages, not a full edition. Both drafts are heavily corrected, and several abbreviations and later lines are not securely read. Draft 1. demás de los cambios que hasta aquí se an hecho por n[uest]ro mandado con Antonio Fucar, de que os hab[em]os avisado con los correos pasados, a convenido, por estar en lo que estamos, hazer este cambio de CX U DCC LXX d[ucad]os de a LXV gruesos … Draft 2. demás de los cambios que hasta aquí se an hecho, a convenido hazer otro de CX U DCC LXX d[ucad]os de a LXV gruesos … Archive page 2 (DECODE image 3): the second draft, headed “al príncipe”, repeating the opening and the amount. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1563 fol. 572, scan 0002, via DECODE R9970. In English: “besides the exchanges made so far by our order with Anton Fugger, of which we advised you by the last posts, it has been necessary, as things stand, to make this exchange of 110,770 ducats at 65 groats …”. Further on, the second draft asks that the money be repaid “el principal con intereses a los plazos” (principal with interest at the terms), and that the cédulas be “cumplidas, guardadas y observadas”. A payment date “a los vj de …” is given, without a year. Sender and recipient. “Por nuestro mandado” and “os habemos avisado” are the royal first person plural, and “al príncipe” is Prince Philip, who ran the government in Spain while his father was away. This is a minute of Charles V (or his secretaries) for a letter to his son. Antonio Fucar is Anton Fugger (1493–1560), head of the Augsburg firm, always written Antonio Fúcar in Spanish documents. The sum. CX U DCC LXX is 110 × 1,000 + 770 = 110,770. The U-shaped sign is the usual Spanish sign for thousands ( calderón ). “De a LXV gruesos” reckons the ducat in Flemish groats. The reading of the unit is tentative, but it points to a loan raised north of the Alps and repaid in Spain.
burgo1527.html#the-date

Philip was born at Valladolid on 21 May 1527, five months before the date DECODE gives. The Emperor’s letters to “el príncipe” about asientos with the Fuggers belong to Philip’s regencies of 1543–1548 and 1551–1554. He stopped being “the Prince” in July 1554, when he became King of Naples on his marriage to Mary Tudor. The drafts give neither year nor place, and the loan has not been matched to a particular Fugger asiento. Ramón Carande’s Carlos V y sus banqueros , which lists them, was not consulted. The scans carry the cited shelfmark in the archive’s own banner, so this is not a mix-up of images on DECODE. Galende Díaz’s list, drawn partly from Carmona’s Tratado de criptografía (1894), gives this reference for the Burgo letter. Either the reference is wrong, or it uses an older numbering of the legajo.

Two sheets of numbers filed as pages of Burr’s 1804 letter to Alston (Gilder Lehrman GLC01523) are three letters to his daughter from Baltimore, 31 January to 18 February 1808, in a six-place Vigenère over the numbers 1–26. The key was recovered here from the cipher alone; 969 of 973 numbers read. Hiding “incog.”, Burr plans a secret visit to The Oaks and waits for money for “the long voyage” to Europe. 19,17 · 8,8,17,2 · 18,23,16,1,3,26 · 3,19,15 … my last letter was … · key 6 18 22 7 24 8, period 6 Baltimore → Theodosia Burr Alston, The Oaks, South Carolina · Vigenère, period 6 · January–February 1808 Aaron Burr to Theodosia, Baltimore, 1808 from Aaron Burr → to Theodosia Burr Alston Go to the full text ↓ Two sheets of numbers filed with Burr’s 1804 letter turn out to be three letters to his daughter from the winter of 1808, hiding at Baltimore before he left for Europe; the key was recovered here. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letters Aaron Burr to his daughter Theodosia Burr Alston: a cover note of 10 February, a copy of his letter of 31 January, and a short letter of 18 February, all from Baltimore. The year is not written in the cipher; a docket on one sheet reads “Balt.” and “1808”. Where Gilder Lehrman Collection, GLC01523, where the two sheets are counted as pages two and three of Burr’s July 1804 letter to Joseph Alston; one is pencilled “1523A”. That letter has its own short cipher and its own page . The cipher A Vigenère over the alphabet numbered a = 1 to z = 26, with a six-place key (shifts 6, 18, 22, 7, 24, 8) that runs on through the letters and starts again at each section. The numbers of a word are joined by commas; words are kept apart. How it was read The key was recovered from the numbers alone: the index of coincidence rises at period six, and fitting each of the six columns to English letter frequencies gives the shifts. A control text of the same length, enciphered with 20 random keys, is broken by the same method every time. What it says Burr, “at Baltimore incog.”, still means to visit her secretly at The Oaks (“let it be believed, except by mari, that I am in Philadelphia”) and waits “hourly” for “money for the long voyage”. Still open One group of four numbers on the 18 February sheet, rubbed on a fold.
burr1808.html#the-sheets

Gilder Lehrman’s catalogue describes GLC01523, Burr’s letter to Joseph Alston of July 1804, as three pages of which “the second and third pages are in cypher”, and the Institute’s Hamilton Education Program shows the cipher as part of that letter, “not yet decoded”. The July letter does carry a cipher, ten lines of figures and stroke signs on its clear page, read on its own page . The two sheets of numbers are something else. The larger sheet (pencilled “1523A” at the foot) is written full in three sections divided by ruled lines. The first section begins “Below the black line is copy of my last” and is dated in the text “the tenth February”; the second is that copy, the letter of “this blessed thirty first day of January”; the third, below the second line, is the end of it. The smaller sheet has three lines at its head, the letter of 18 February, and a docket in another hand: “Balt.” and “1808”. The note of 10 February, above the first ruled line: “Below the black line is copy of my last, by the schooner Wolf …” Image: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, GLC01523 (sheet pencilled 1523A), via the Hamilton Education Program. The year fits nothing but 1808. After his acquittal at Richmond in September 1807 Burr went east, was hanged in effigy by a crowd at Baltimore in November, and spent the winter out of public view while he raised money to go to Europe; he sailed from New York for England on 7 June 1808. Theodosia, often ill, was with her husband in South Carolina. The letters are to her, not to Alston: “the hope of seeing me keeps you at the Oaks at the hazard of your life”, “except by mari” (French, her husband), the pet name at the end of the copy. “Gamp” is Burr himself, as in the journal he later kept for her in Europe.
burr1808.html#the-reading

Burr writes no punctuation in the cipher; it is added here. Spelling as enciphered. [?] marks a word read against one number that disagrees with the key; [s] a letter Burr left out. Baltimore, 10 February [1808] Below the black line is copy of my last, by the schooner Wolf, Capt. Jones, to sail about the eighteenth. You will hear again. Keep up your spirits. My plans are not changed. Yet at Baltimore incog., the tenth February. Business now detains me. We must submit, submit, submit to ten days more of suspense. The promise in[?] my last was rashly made. Affairs begin to look up. J’y travaille. What would Gamp not give to know that you are all well. Copy of the letter of 31 January [1808] My last letter was written eight days ago. Poor Gamp is still at Baltimore on this blessed thirty-first day of January, still hoping and still persisting in all the plans so often written to you. It distresses me to think that the hope of seeing me keeps you at the Oaks at the hazard of your life. Indeed my be[s]t endeavors are used and shall be used to get to you. If after ten days further delay it be found impracticable, a person shall be sent express to you, and for you just four hours work, huzzey. No person must suspect that I mean to visit you in S.C. Let it be believed, except by mari, that I am in Philadelphia. Baltimore, 18 February [1808] The letter of 18 February, with the docket “Balt.” and “1808” above it. Image: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History, GLC01523 (sheet docketed Balt. 1808), via the Hamilton Education Program. Baltimore, eighteenth Feb. Nothing new. The same hopes and intentions continue. Have[?] patience. [four numbers rubbed] hourly expectation of money for the long voyage, and nothing else detains[?] me. “J’y travaille” is French, “I am working at it”. The plan of the copy is a secret journey south: Burr would come to The Oaks himself, or, if that proved impossible after ten more days, send an express. By 18 February the journey is not mentioned; only the money for “the long voyage” keeps him.
burr1808.html#the-cipher

Each letter is numbered a = 1 to z = 26 and shifted by one of six amounts in turn: key place 1 2 3 4 5 6 shift 6 18 22 7 24 8 a is written 7 19 23 8 25 9 Cipher number = letter number + shift, counted round from 26 to 1. The key moves on with every letter, not with every word, and starts again at the head of each section; the same word therefore looks different in different places, except when it falls at the same key place, as submit (26,19,10,19,1,16) does three times running. No keyword lies behind the six shifts (as letters, a = 0: G S W H Y I).
burr1808.html#method

The note of 10 February (80 words, 341 numbers) was transcribed first. All 26 values occur and the commonest has only 8.5% of the text: not a simple substitution. Some words could not be English under one alphabet (a doubled number in 21,11,23,23 ; 3,22 and 23,12 as two-letter words). The index of coincidence is 0.0435 for the whole and 0.0618 for every sixth number: a six-place key. For each of the six columns, the shift that best fits English letter frequencies (chi-square) was taken. The note read at once: “below the black line is copy of my last by the schooner wolf”. The rest was transcribed and reads with the same key. Two places fell out of step. A pass over the words scored with an English language model found them: Burr wrote 10,11,16 for best , leaving out the s but moving the key on; and on the 18 February sheet the rubbed group stands before a fall-back of one key place. Control: Burr’s own letter of 18 July 1804 (Davis’s text), cut to 341 letters and enciphered with 20 random six-place keys, is broken by the same method 20 times out of 20. A statistical check ( docs/_validate.py , tokens tagged by key place): −2.21 per letter against −7.47 for 200 random keys and −4.18 for keys refitted to shuffled text: a pass.
burr1808.html#open

18 Feb, before “hourly” : four numbers, the second rubbed on a fold (read 2?, 11?, 1, 23). No word fits at any key place; “in” would need 17, 20. Open, blocked by the image. in[?] (10 Feb, 15,16 ): gives “ix”; the key needs 15, 6. Burr’s slip or a misreading. Grade C. have[?] and detains[?] (18 Feb): one number each disagrees with the key (11 for 14, 13 for 18), easy confusions in this hand. Grade C. impracticable and for (31 Jan): the last digit of one number in each is torn away at the edge; the key needs 25 and 24, and the visible 2 fits both. Grade H. huzzey and mari are read as written. Grade C for the gloss. Kline and Ryan’s edition of Burr’s papers (1983) prints no letter of January or February 1808; its editorial note “The Road to Exile” (vol. 2, p. 1040) was not read and may refer to these letters.

Two League letters to Rome in Tomokiyo’s polyphonic cipher, each sign two letters, written three days before Henri IV went to Mass. desportes1593.html#letters

On 22 July 1593 the League in Paris sent a packet to Rome. Henri of Navarre had announced his conversion, the conference of Suresnes was ending in a truce, and the Spanish party was pressing the Estates to elect a king. Four letters of that day, all written by Mayenne’s agent in the same hand and the same cipher, were intercepted and are now bound together in BnF fr. 3984. They went to Pope Clement VIII (f. 176–176v and f. 179r), to the bishop of Lisieux (f. 188), to the Pope’s nephew Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini (f. 186) and to Girolamo Frachetta, a political writer in the papal service (f. 189). The royal office deciphered the first two; its decipherments are bound beside them (f. 177–178 and f. 184–185). It never did the other two. Its register of 1593 says of the letter to Aldobrandini that “l’on n’a eu loisir encores de deschiffrer”, and the letter to Frachetta “n’a non plus encore esté deschiffrée” (BnF fr. 3983 f. 141v, entries 13 and 14). The backs of both letters say the same. Tomokiyo’s page on the cipher lists f. 186 as “enciphered passages are undeciphered” and f. 189 as “undeciphered”. The office signed its decipherments “Baudouyn Desportes”, and the BnF names the writer Baudouin-Desportes. Whether he is Mayenne’s secretary Baudouin or Thibault Desportes, sieur de Bévilliers, Mayenne’s envoy to Rome, is still open. Rosson’s prior_art/scholarship.md sets out the evidence. F. 189, the letter to Frachetta, upper half. The only clear line, the eleventh, reads celuy qui est loing en parle comme ung aveugle des couleurs ; the rest is cipher. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3984 f. 189 (Gallica btv1b9060633d view 353), reduced copy from P. Rosson’s repository.
desportes1593.html#cipher

Tomokiyo reconstructed the League’s cipher of 1592–93 from deciphered letters. Each of eleven signs stands for two letters of the alphabet split in half: a/n, b/o, c/p, d/q, e/r, f/s, g/t, h/u, i/x, l/y, m/z. Further signs stand for que , qui , pour and et , and a handful of signs stand for persons: the Pope, Mayenne, the King of Navarre, the King of Spain, the Legate, Guise, the Infanta. So the key was never the problem. The reader has to name each sign, and then choose one of its two letters from the context. The two letters hold about 6,700 signs, drawn small and fast. A sign named wrongly spoils the words around it, because each sign carries two letters. This project tried on 17 September 2026. It aligned the cipher of f. 188v with its decipherment, about 1,100 labelled signs, and trained classifiers on them. They named only 73–79% of held-out signs correctly; at that rate the decoder recovered 30–40% of the letters of a known text. The folder was closed with a note on what would reopen it: a larger labelled set from f. 176 and its decipherment f. 177.
desportes1593.html#method

Paolo Rosson, working with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, took that route. He transcribed the office’s decipherment of the letter to the Pope (f. 177–178, 74 lines) and aligned it, with f. 188v and its decipherment, sign by sign. That gave 112 lines and 6,794 labelled signs in the same hand. He corrected the reference texts to the cipher’s own spelling (“espagnolz”, “fist”). A line recogniser trained on these lines names the signs, and a decoder with a model of period French and a lexicon of 77,004 word forms chooses one letter of each pair. Then the model checked every line against the page image. His measurements, from rosson/accuracy.md : On held-out lines (f. 188v ll. 7–10, f. 176r ll. 20–23; 482 signs, 505 letters, labelled by eye before any model was trained): 98.5% of signs and 95.6% of letters correct. On a blind test, a third cipher page of the letter to the Pope (f. 179r, 21 lines) found after the models were trained and scored against the office’s decipherment on f. 178r: 99.7% of signs (4 errors in 1,301) and 98.3% of letters. On the unread pages, nine models disagree on 1.0% of signs (f. 189), 1.3% (f. 186r) and 2.0% (f. 186v). The key is Tomokiyo’s, applied unchanged. No key was recovered, so the method is “read with known key”. Here the hard part was transcription, not cryptanalysis.

Nostre volonté estoit bonne, la puissance asses grande pour la faire reussir; mais a savoir si en la continue nous eussions peu subsister, c’est ce qui nous a fait demeurer cois. Et en ces entrefaites nos amis ne se sont pas seulement montrés neutres, mais ennemis formelz, et fait ce qu’ilz ont peu pour tendre a la ruine de l’amy(?) de l’homme du colege et le vostre, sans l’avoir rien espargné, oposans tantost un sujet tantost un autre, secondés par nostre docteur Gratian, qui a mieulx joué le personnage que nul des autres, jusques a y coucher de l’autorité de son {M[aist]re}, voir[e] l’avoir mis en compromis et fait beaucoup de prejudice. Si nostre oncle eust voulu parler suivant la promesse qu’il en avoit faite a celuy qui l’ala trouver, et que l’homme de la chesne eust donné d’autres asseurances que des paroles, la teste baissee on y eust entré. Mais croies qu’il n’y a peu a penser {celuy qui est loing en parle comme ung aveugle des couleurs. Or(?)} tout ce qui se pouvoit de mieulx estoit la protection et gaigner le temps. Il ne s’est pas fait; il faloit la trefve. L’imprudence du monarque et des siens ai[a]nt esté telle qu’il n’avoit fait nul preparatif, ou du moins si petit[e] que le moindre gentilhomme en une querelle en eust fait davantage. Et pour vostre costé, ç’a esté un autre bel acte que le licentiement que feist vostre auditeur(?). Je veulx(?) croire ce que vous m’escrivez, qu’il n’y a nul changement; toutesfois c’est un fait estrange que nostre Poquinteste ne nous ait rien raporté de {part[iculi]er}, et que l’on nous aie dit ce que l’on a voulu; et ce n’a esté que des paroles, les plus extravagantes que j’eusse pensé. Perdre tout, voire estre privé de paradis, j’eusse passé bien plus avant: se travailler, se ruiner, faire ce [qui] se peut, tant que sans nostre prudence on ne dureroit pas une heure; et pour recompense bastir une ruine. Or je ne serois pas si charitable, je le confesse. Si nostre ami du colege en vouloit parler a l’homme de la chesne, il obligeroit infinyment nostre amy, qui est tout sien. Et a ce qui regarde vostre pension, cela ne se peult, car nul ne l’asiste que le prelat a qui la piece est affectee, et il n’est pas temps de luy rien lever. Ç’a esté vostre malheur et le mien. Courage, il se presentera d’autres occasions. Je tien que l’on aura la trefve dans peu de jours. Le voiage de [sign not identified] a esté le plus pernicieulx que chose du monde: il a fait changer de religion au [roy de Navarre] et offre [.5c?] mil escus. Leur party estoit ruiné sans se changement. Nostre legat a fait ce qu’il a peu pour couvrir l’Espagnol; il a embrassé leur affaire avec tant d’ardeur qu’il a negligé ce qui estoit du service de son {M[aist]re}, jusques a n’avoir fait tenir un seul de nos brefz(?), qui eussent infiniment profité; mais ce n’estoit pas ce qu’il desiroit(?), au contraire, de haster le desmembrement de nostre estat. Par la lettre de [Sa Sainteté(?)] vous saurés au vray l’estat general de nos affaires. {Je vous baise les mains … A Paris ce xxij e Juillet 1593.} Translation (Rosson’s, shortened): Our will was good and our power great enough … Our friends showed themselves not only neutral but open enemies … seconded by our Doctor Gratian, who played the part better than any of the others … If our uncle had been willing to speak as he promised the man who went to see him, and if the man of the chain had given other assurances than words, we would have gone in head down … The best that could be done was protection and to gain time; the truce was necessary … I hold that we shall have the truce in a few days. The journey of […] was the most pernicious thing in the world: it made the King of Navarre change his religion … Our legate did what he could to cover the Spaniard; he neglected his master’s service, so far as not to deliver even one of our briefs … to hasten the dismemberment of our state. This is the only letter of the four written in cover names: “nostre oncle”, “l’homme de la chesne”, “l’homme du colege”, “nostre docteur Gratian”. The name in line 17 is written in clear in the letter to Lisieux (“par le retour de poquinteste”, f. 188r, copied on f. 184r), so it is a person’s name, not a misreading.

A clear opening of eleven lines (“Si je n’ay escrit a Sa Sainteté et a V re Seigneurie Ill me aussi souvent que le devoir me le commande …”) runs into 41 lines of cipher on the recto, with short clear phrases between, and 33 on the verso. The full reading and translation are in rosson/f186_reading.txt . Some passages: F. 186r ll. 21–23: …ns a l’election d’un roy, lors que l’ennemy commence a gagner les voix de beaucoup qui luy estoient ennemis, par l’aparance qu’il fait de se vouloir faire catolique, et doit dimanche aller a la messe. N’avoir rien pour luy resister sinon des promesses, ou l’on a tant… The 2 in the third line is the sign for pour . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3984 f. 186r ll. 21–23 (Gallica btv1b9060633d view 347), reduced copy from P. Rosson’s repository. The papal commissaries (r11–17): from “M r Mateouci” on, “eulx seulx ont plus aporté de ruine aux affaires que les ennemis”. He has sent the Pope a discours on Matteucci’s conduct, and Malvasia and Mayenne have fallen out. Spain (r17–20): “l’armee du [roy d’Espagne] n’a rien fait sinon de demeurer sur la frontiere … et qui s’est retiree seulement sur un bruit que [le roy de Navarre] l’aloit chercher”. The Mass (r20–27): the Legate wants an election “lors que l’ennemy commence a gagner les voix … et doit dimanche aller a la messe”, and everyone is “las de servir de fable a toute la crestienté”. Henri IV abjured and heard Mass at Saint-Denis on Sunday 25 July. His mission in Rome (r32–42): he asked for “un de la maison de Bourbon”, then for “le mariage de [l’Infante] avec un de nos princes”, and was refused both and sent back to the Legate and the Duke of Feria. He rejected a candidate “qui me fust proposé de [Sa Sainteté], que a la verité eust esté le meilleur”. Mayenne and Guise (v17–21): if Aldobrandini knew how “M r [le Legat] s’est monstré leur partisan pour deschirer nostre pauvre estat”, he would wonder at “la patience de [M. du Maine], qui s’est porté jusques a vouloir accepter M r [de Guise] pour roy, pourveu que l’on y feist voir le moien de le pouvoir deffendre”. Rosson’s comparison.md sets the two letters against the two that the office read. The forecast of the Mass was not news to the office: the letter to Lisieux says “Il se doibt faire cath. dimanche” (f. 184r). Seven passages are in the unread letters only, among them the attack on Matteucci and Malvasia, the two refused requests, the Pope’s own candidate, Mayenne’s readiness to accept Guise, and the Legate holding back briefs. Three passages occur in both a read and an unread letter. The facts agree and the words differ, which is an independent check of the reading.

On 20 October 2026 Rosson’s repository ( pangoleen/desportes-1593 , commit 33c854a) was read as data. Its code was not run; the checks below used scripts written here. The decode follows the key. His raw output gives every word with the string of sign classes the recogniser gave. Of 1,533 letter words, 1,524 spell exactly under Tomokiyo’s pairs. The other 9 use the recogniser’s second-choice class, which the output gives beside the first. The output holds 2,088 signs on f. 189, 2,565 on f. 186r and 2,046 on f. 186v. Our labels agree with his. The 100 signs of f. 188v ll. 3–4 that this project labelled by hand in September all have the same class in his gold transcripts. The images. F. 186r ll. 21–23 (above) and the opening words of f. 189 (“Nostre volonté estoit bonne, la …”) were checked again sign by sign on the Gallica image with this project’s reference sheet of the hand. Every sign has the class his output gives. The clear insertions of f. 189 fall where his reading puts them. An independent reading. Brett Burford, also with Claude Opus 5.5, made a second reading by another method before opening Rosson’s text: Claude named the signs against a reference sheet in three passes, and the passes were voted ( BravoBravoIX/desportes-1593-rereading , 18 October 2026). It agrees with Rosson’s on 95.9% of signs (f. 189), 93.1% (f. 186r) and 93.8% (f. 186v). Burford reports that wherever the two differ, Rosson’s is the better reading. Extent. His output holds 1,790 cipher words. Five are left unread and 21 carry a question mark. Not counting either, 1,764 (98.5%) read as sense, over the bar of 95% of the cipher giving sense.
desportes1593.html#priority

No reading earlier than Rosson’s is known. The office in 1593 did not decipher the letters, and Tomokiyo’s page (last changed in 2023) lists them with no decipherment. This project’s attempt of September 2026 did not get there. Rosson published his reading, version 0.2, on 1 October 2026. Tomokiyo’s article “An Intercepted Report of Henry IV’s Upcoming Attendance at Mass in a Polyphonic Cipher” (first posted 3 October 2026) presents it as the first full decipherment, with a partial check of his own and three corrections to the clear text, which Rosson adopted. Burford’s re-reading followed on 18 October. Maxim Egorov has also published an analysis of the letters, not read here. Brice Dudout drew this project’s attention to the result on 19 October. Rosson also deciphered a slip in a variant of the same cipher, BnF fr. 4715 f. 61 (Gallica btv1b52509819x view 137), where Tomokiyo had read five short spans. His reading is copied to rosson/fr4715_f61_reading.txt ; it was not checked here.
desportes1593.html#open

F. 189 l. 26: the sign for the traveller whose journey “a fait changer de religion au [roy de Navarre]”. It occurs once and in no sister letter. F. 189 l. 32 and f. 186r l. 30: two single person or title signs read from context (“Sa Sainteté(?)”, “pape(?)” before “Gregoire”). F. 186v ll. 1–3: three short groups (about nine signs) where the binding hides one or two signs of each line on the microfilm. They are not read. The cover names of f. 189 are read as words, but no key or sister letter says who they are. Rosson’s guesses: “nostre oncle” the Pope, “l’homme de la chesne” Spain or its ambassador, “l’homme du colege” a cardinal, “docteur Gratian” the Legate or a man of his legation. 21 words carry a question mark in his files (7 on f. 189, 14 on f. 186). Each comes with his note on the sign classes. No palaeographer has yet checked the whole of either reading. An intended recipient may have read a first copy in Rome; the letter to the Pope is marked “Duplicata”. Copies Frachetta gave the Spanish ambassador in September 1593 (Simancas, Estado leg. 961–963) have not been checked.
