Et de soy mesme elle peut considerer que l'armee du [roy d'Espagne] n'a rien fait sinon de demeurer sur la frontiere, servant d'oprobre a un si grand monarque, et qui s'est retiree seulement sur un bruit que [le roy de Navarre] l'aloit chercher. Et outre, M[onsieu]r [le Legat], sans consideration quelconque, veult que nous en venions a l'election d'un roy, lors que l'ennemy commence a gagner les voix de beaucoup qui luy estoient ennemis, par l'aparance qu'il fait de se vouloir faire catolique, et doit dimanche aller a la messe. N'avoir rien pour luy resister sinon des promesses, ou l'on a tant esté trompé! Il faudroit beaucoup [?d'effecz] avant que de nous faire rejecter l'aparence d'une paix; et ne sera peu fait si nous la moderons par une trefve, un chacun estant las de servir de fable a toute la crestienté et de se voir abandonnez, pour enfin rendre les abois. Car pour des promesses, nos ennemis n'en sont pas despourveus, et offrent de monstrer l'estres de ⟨V.S.Ill.me⟩ pour, en cas qu'il se face catolique, d'estre receu. Le S[ain]t Siege, lassé de continuer sa despence, que l'on peut dire avoir esté quelque chose durant le pontificat du [?pape] Gregoire; mais depuis il luy eust mieulx esté que de tout point on nous eust desnié toute esperance de secours, affin de nous faire prendre une certaine resolution. Et mais que ⟨V.S.I.⟩ se souvienne avec quelle instance j'ay demandé un de la maison de Bourbon, et le refus qui m'en fust fait; apres, le mariage de [l'Infante] avec un de nos princes: de tout point on m'en fist refus, s'en remettant a M[onsieu]r [le Legat] et au duc de Feria, ou je pense avoir asses fait cognoistre que jamais n'asarderion[s] nostre religion, honneurs et vies sans estre autrement asseurés; et que [Sa Sainteté] ne parlast plus [?clair] (par d'autres asseurances que d'elle nous n'en voulons point, en estant la plus interessee), que l'on ne seroit pas pour faire mieulx a l'advenir que par le passé; et eusse esté bien imprudent d'en user autrement, moy qui cognoist les Espagnols. Qui me feist rejecter ce sujet qui me fust proposé de [Sa Sainteté], que a la verité eust esté le meilleur; mais il y faloit voir une lumiere [?asseuree]. Aussi, ores que mon ⟨M[aist]re⟩ s'i fust voulu laisse[r] aller, il n'y en a point qui luy eust plus fait de resistance que moy. Et ou en seroit il maintena[n]t? Les ennemis offrant encores de faire voir une lettre de [Sa Sainteté] adressante a M[onsieu]r [le Legat], par laquelle il luy mande de ne rien faire au prejudice de la maiso[n] de Bourbon, contre les lois fondamentales du roiaume, ny contre les catoliques qui assistent [le roy de Navarre]: chose bien contraire a tant de protestations que l'on m'a faites. Je l'ay dit et le diray jusques a la mort, que s'il en arrive mal, que l'on l'a voulu ainsi; car on n'a pas manqué de remonstrer tout ce qui se peut, sans avoir eu autre passion que la religion. Mais entre ces incertitudes on demeure; et si les autres se servent de l'occasion, ne font ilz bien? Encores pour recompense de toutes nos peines j'en atten[s] un monde de reproches, toutes tombantes sur [M. du Maine], qui fait plus qu'il ne devroit, sans aucune aprehention; car l'honneur vault mieulx que toutes [?ces] aparances recherchees par la pluspart des hommes; joint que la fin coronnera l'oeuvre. Car au temps que […] […] est bandé pour deschirer nostre estat, qui ameneroit en apres la ruine de la chrestie[n]té, habandonné de tout le monde, neglige tous ses [?advertissemens], et sur iceulx […] […] de personnes [qui], hormis leur qualité d'estre ministres d'un grand prince, ne seroien[t] pas hors de ranc ny de trop bonne maison pour tenir lieu de serviteurs, prent coeur c[o]ntre toutes sortes de tempestes, pour [?faire] le souverain et seul remede que sa presence, affi[n] d'empescher d'une prochaine cheute l'estat et la religion. Il ne faut point douter qu'il n'y en ait qui ne veuillent, selon leur coustume, couvrir leurs malices par un monde de [?faucetés]; mais si on a seu rendre leur dessein vain, il ne manque pas de personnes pour po[uv]oir escrire de bonnes apologies, et feront retomber la honte que l'on voudroit [?gecter] sur la face de ceulx sur lesquelz il n'i a que marque d'honneur et de magnanimité. Et pleut a Dieu que [Sa Sainteté] seust comme moy la façon dont ont usé ses ministres, leur interest, et de ceul[uy] qui monstre a n'estre que religieu[x], au lieu qu'il n'i a que pure ambition trop descouverte, nonobstant un nombre de protestations au contraire; et ou il n'y avoit nul moien de pouvoir respondre, si M[onsieu]r [le Legat] ne s'i fust point entremis, ou l'honneur de [Sa Sainteté] [l']a esté grandement interessé. Je parle de ses affaires a ⟨V.S.I.⟩ avec beaucoup de langage; aussi, si je ne c[r]aignois de l'importuner, ⟨il y auroit pour en remplir une rame de papier. Et pour n'estre trop ennuyeulx je luy diray que⟩ si elle savoit comme moy l'artifice de nos amis, ce qu'ilz ont [et] [?font], leur foiblesse, comme M[onsieu]r [le Legat] s'est monstré leur partisa[n] pour deschire[r] nostre pauvre estat, au prejudice de l'honneur du S[ain]t Siege, et un monde d'autres choses, elle s'estonneroit mil et mil fois de la patience de [M. du Maine], qui s'est porté jusques a vouloir accepter M[onsieu]r [de Guise] pour roy, pourveu que l'on y feist voir le moien de le pouvoir deffendre. Mais on veut que l'on croie en paroles, co[m]me s'il y avoit aparance de plus adjouster foy a des gens qui ne nous firent jamais paroistre en avoir, et qui ont pour maxime de nous vouloir tromper. Par avanture mesme trouverés vous estrange que je vous ay remarqué les deux poins que font [se] [?courir] les ennemis, tant de la lettre de [Sa Sainteté] que de celle de ⟨V.S.I.⟩ en ⟨part[iculi]er; mais il m'a semblé qu'il est bon qu'elle soit advertie du tout pour y pourvoir. Il est vray, et l'ay assez protesté [mil?] fois, que s'il plaist a⟩ [Sa Sainteté] de me faire part de ses intentions, a [M. du Maine], sans l'interposer [a?] M[onsieu]r [le Legat], il [n]e prendra pour luy que ses commandemens. Et puis les choses en sont entre eulx en telz termes que, sans le respect de [Sa Sainteté], il ne sejour[ne]roit plus si longtemps a ses despens ny de la ruine de tous ceulx de sa maison. Mesmes il a esté si peu respectueux qu'il luy a donné une aprehention de [?Sa Sainteté] d'estre en sa mauvaise grace; que neaumoins un chacun pense estre artifice pour parvenir a ses desseins, affin d'obliger l'Espagnol, qui a esté tousjours sa principalle fin. ⟨Illustrissimo Monseigneur, je suplie treshumblement le Createur donner a V're S'rie Ill.me tresheureuse et treslongue vye. A Paris ce xxije Juillet 1593. D. V. S. (uncertain events, unsafe roads); "... In short, unless God sets His hand to it, I see the security of the Catholic religion in this kingdom in a bad way, for several reasons I could tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship ..."; what the ministers "here for the Holy See" report has nothing to do with the truth, "which will now be found such as I have always told it, at the"⟩ cost of my head. Beginning with Monsieur Matteucci, down to the one who remains here, they alone have brought more ruin to our affairs than the enemy, so full have they been of I know not what that does not suit us, or of small knowledge of our humours and passions. And if I put anything forward in the discourse I am giving to His Holiness on the conduct of the said Matteucci, the least letter that anyone could write me about it will always let me show it, wherever one wishes, to make it good. As for Monsieur de Malvasia, I was not there when he and Monsieur du Maine fell out; yet the nephew of the Legate complained to me of it; and it is hard to contradict a rumour […]. And of yourself you can consider that the army of the King of Spain did nothing but stay on the frontier, a reproach to so great a monarch, and withdrew on a mere rumour that the King of Navarre was coming to seek it. Moreover the Legate, with no consideration at all, wants us to proceed to the election of a king just when the enemy is beginning to win the voices of many who were his enemies, by the show he makes of wishing to become Catholic; and he is to go to mass on Sunday. To have nothing to resist him with but promises, by which we have been so often deceived! It would take many [?deeds] before we could be made to reject the appearance of a peace; and it will be no small thing if we temper it by a truce, everyone being tired of being the talk of all Christendom and of seeing ourselves abandoned, only to be brought to bay in the end. For as to promises, our enemies do not lack them, and they offer to show letters of Your Most Illustrious Lordship [saying] that, if he becomes Catholic, he will be received. The Holy See is tired of continuing its expense, which may be said to have been something during the pontificate of [?Pope] Gregory; but since then it would have been better for it if we had been denied all hope of help outright, so as to make us take a firm resolution. And let Your Lordship remember how urgently I asked for one of the house of Bourbon, and the refusal I was given; then the marriage of the Infanta with one of our princes: I was refused outright, and referred to the Legate and the Duke of Feria, to whom I think I made it plain enough that we would never hazard our religion, honours and lives without other assurance; and that unless His Holiness spoke more [?clearly] (for we want no assurances but his, he being the most concerned), no one would do better in future than in the past; and I would have been most imprudent to act otherwise, I who know the Spaniards. That is what made me reject the candidate His Holiness proposed to me, who in truth would have been the best; but one needed to see a [?sure] light in it. And even if my master had been willing to let himself go that way, no one would have resisted him more than I. And where would he be now? The enemies offer, further, to show a letter of His Holiness addressed to the Legate, by which he orders him to do nothing to the prejudice of the house of Bourbon, against the fundamental laws of the kingdom, nor against the Catholics who assist the King of Navarre: a thing quite contrary to so many protestations made to me. I have said it and will say it until death: if harm comes of it, it was willed so; for we did not fail to remonstrate everything that could be said, with no passion but religion. But amid these uncertainties we remain; and if the others use the occasion, do they not do well? And for reward of all our pains I expect a world of reproaches, all falling on Monsieur du Maine, who does more than he should, without any fear; for honour is worth more than all [?these] appearances sought by most men; and besides, the end will crown the work. For at the time when […] is bent on tearing our state apart, which would bring after it the ruin of Christendom, abandoned by everyone, he neglects all their [?warnings], and on them […] of persons who, but for their quality of ministers of a great prince, would be neither out of rank nor of too good a house to serve as servants, he takes heart against every kind of storm, to [?make] the sovereign and only remedy, his presence, so as to keep the state and religion from an imminent fall. There is no doubt that there will be some who, as is their custom, will cover their malice with a world of [?falsehoods]; but if their design has been made vain, there is no lack of persons able to write good apologies, and they will turn back the shame that one would [?cast] on the face of those on whom there is only the mark of honour and magnanimity. Would to God His Holiness knew as I do how his ministers have behaved, their interest, and [that] of the one who makes a show of being nothing but religious, whereas there is nothing but pure ambition, too plainly uncovered, in spite of a number of protestations to the contrary; and to which there was no means of replying if the Legate had not put himself in the matter, in which the honour of His Holiness has been greatly engaged. I speak of his affairs to Your Most Illustrious Lordship at great length; and if I did not fear to weary you, there would be enough to fill a ream of paper. And not to be too tedious, I will tell you that if you knew as I do the artifice of our friends, what they have [and] [?do], their weakness, how the Legate has shown himself their partisan to tear our poor state apart, to the prejudice of the honour of the Holy See, and a world of other things, you would wonder a thousand and a thousand times at the patience of Monsieur du Maine, who went so far as to be willing to accept Monsieur de Guise as king, provided he was shown the means of being able to defend him. But they want us to believe in words, as if there were any reason to trust further people who never showed us that they had any, and whose maxim is to deceive us. Perhaps you will even find it strange that I have pointed out to you the two points that the enemies [?put about], both from the letter of His Holiness and from that of Your Most Illustrious Lordship in particular; but it seemed good to me that you should be told everything, to provide for it. It is true, and I have protested it a [?thousand] times, that if it pleases His Holiness to let me know his intentions, for Monsieur du Maine, without putting the Legate between them, he will take nothing for his rule but His commands. And besides, things between those two are on such terms that, but for respect for His Holiness, he would no longer stay so long at his own cost and at the ruin of all those of his house. He has even been so disrespectful as to make him fear that he is in the disfavour of [?His Holiness]; which everyone nonetheless thinks a device to reach his own ends, so as to oblige the Spaniard, which has always been his principal aim. ⟨Most Illustrious Monseigneur, I most humbly pray the Creator to give Your Most Illustrious Lordship a most happy and most long life. Paris, 22 July 1593. Your Most Illustrious Lordship's most humble and most obedient servant, Desportes.⟩ f. 189 (no. 90), to Girolamo Frachetta, July 1593 A letter in cover names ("nostre oncle", "l'homme de la chesne", "l'homme du colege", "nostre docteur Gratian"): the truce is expected "dans peu de jours", an envoy's journey "a fait changer de religion au [roy de Navarre]", and the Legate held back "nos brefz". TRANSLATION Our will was good, and our power great enough to make it succeed; but whether we could have held out in the long run, that is what made us keep still. Meanwhile our friends showed themselves not only neutral but open enemies, and did what they could to ruin the friend(?) of the man of the College, and yours, sparing nothing, putting up now one candidate, now another. Our Doctor Gratian seconded them; he played the part better than any of the others, so far as to stake his master's authority on it, indeed to compromise it and do it much harm. If our uncle had been willing to speak as he promised the man who went to see him, and if the man of the chain had given other assurances than words, we would have gone in head down. But believe me, a man who is far away could not think of this: he speaks of it as a blind man speaks of colours. The best that could be done was protection, and to gain time. That was not done; the truce was necessary. The imprudence of the monarch and his people was such that he had made no preparation, or so small a one that the least gentleman in a quarrel would have done more. On your side, the disbanding that your auditor carried out was another fine deed. I want to believe what you write, that nothing has changed; yet it is strange that our Poquinteste brought us back nothing in particular, and that they told us what they pleased; and it was only words, the most extravagant I could have imagined. To lose everything, even to be shut out of paradise: I would have gone much further; to toil, to ruin oneself, to do all that can be done, so that without our prudence we would not last an hour; and for reward, to build a ruin. I would not be so charitable, I confess. If our friend of the College would speak of it to the man of the chain, he would greatly oblige our friend, who is wholly his. As to your pension, it cannot be done, for no one supports it but the prelate to whom the benefice is assigned, and this is not the time to take anything from him. That was your bad luck and mine. Courage; other occasions will come. I hold that we shall have the truce in a few days. The journey of [sign] was the most pernicious thing in the world: it made [the King of Navarre] change his religion, and it offers [500?] thousand ecus. Their party was ruined without this change. Our legate did what he could to cover the Spaniard; he took up their cause with such ardour that he neglected his master's service, so far as not to deliver even one of our briefs, which would have done great good. But that was not what he wanted; on the contrary, [he wanted] to hasten the dismemberment of our state. From the letter to [His Holiness?] you will know the true general state of our affairs. I kiss your hands ... Paris, 22 July 1593. Letters from Dole, besieged by Condé, to the relief army of the Marquis of Conflans, June–July 1636, with one number per letter set between clear words. Brice Dudout learnt the key from the period gloss in the margin of one folio, tested it on a held-out block (0.907 of letters against at most 0.229 for shuffled keys) and read the unglossed letters: 124 of 128 words. The clear text was already printed by Longin in 1912. 11.25.1.11.44.40.42.5.40.42 … le plus tost … que vous pourez venir sera le meilleur Dole → the relief army · one number per letter, set between points · June–July 1636 · key from adjacent plaintext The siege of Dole, 1636: the “points” cipher from Antoine Brun Go to the full text ↓ Letters smuggled out of Dole while Condé besieged it, in a cipher the Parlement had already warned was broken, read with a key taken from a decipherment written in the margin at the time. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 4 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (earlier solution) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letters Four letters from Dole, besieged by the Prince of Condé from 27 May to 15 August 1636, to the Marquis of Conflans and Jean Girardot de Beauchemin, who were raising a relief army: the Parlement and the Archbishop (7 June and 22 July), the commis au gouvernement (25 June) and the procureur général Antoine Brun ([1 July]). Where Besançon, Bibliothèque municipale, Ms 1594 (Ms 1591–1595 vol. IV, papers of Jean Girardot de Nozeroy), fols. 127, 181, 183, 191 and 200; clear copy fol. 182. Not on DECODE and not in the project’s catalogue. The cipher A simple substitution of one number (1–54) per letter, the numbers separated by points and set inside clear text. 23 distinct numbers; c has two (20 and 29). How it was deciphered The key was learnt from block 1 of fol. 200, whose 177 numbers line up one to one with the marginal gloss, and frozen. One measurement on block 2 of the same folio (341 numbers) gave 0.907 of letters against at most 0.229 for 200 shuffled keys. The unglossed letters were then read with the frozen key. What it says Come as soon as you can with the cavalry relief; bring rations and tools to reap; burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler and Mirebeau and destroy the forge of Drambon where the bombs thrown on Dole are made. Still open Four words: a struck-out group, a word under a blot, ?atlons and o… . No number for k was seen. Fol. 106 (12 August) is in another cipher, not broken. Credit Brice Dudout transcribed the numbers, recovered and tested the key and read the letters, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The clear text of the letters was already printed by É. Longin (1912), a fact found after the reading.

Dole, capital of the Franche-Comté, was besieged by the Prince of Condé from 27 May to 15 August 1636. The Parlement and the governor wrote to the relief army of the Marquis of Conflans and of Jean Girardot de Beauchemin, and the letters that reached it are kept among Girardot’s papers at Besançon. Only the words that mattered were enciphered. The rest is clear French, with the cipher passages set in it as strings of numbers. The cipher did not stay secret. Antoine Rossignol deciphered the intercepted dispatches in Paris, and in July Richelieu sent him to Condé’s camp with “the decipherment of the letters that those of Dole were writing to the Marquis of Conflans” (Longin, no. CCLXXVIII). In late July and early August the court warned Conflans three times that “the enemy has found the key of the cipher”, and the letter of 12 August (fol. 106) changes to another cipher.
dole1636.html#the-key

The numbers run in two stretches: p = 1, then o 5, n 7, m 9, l 11 going up by two; a = 35, b 31 going down; q = 36, r 38, s 40, t 42, u 44 going up. Fol. 200 carries two blocks of cipher, each glossed in the margin at the time. Block 1 gave the key: 177 numbers aligned with 177 letters of the gloss, the majority letter per number, frozen before anything else was decrypted. Letters Numbers p o n m l 1 5 7 9 11 i (and j) h g 15 17 19 c f e d c 20 21 25 27 29 b a 31 35 q r s t u (and v) 36 38 40 42 44 x y z 50 52 54 Block 2 (341 numbers) was the test, with the protocol written and hashed before the measurement: letter agreement with its gloss 0.9072, against a best of 0.229 and a mean of 0.131 for 200 shuffled keys. The thresholds (0.85, and the best control plus 0.30) were fixed in advance and the key passed. Three numbers had no value in training (17, 21, 50) and were given h, f and x by the gloss afterwards. The value 20 = c comes from sense ( cavalerie ), 54 = z from the clear copy fol. 182 ( douze ).
dole1636.html#the-reading

Fol. 191 (Brun, [1 July]) and fol. 127v (7 June) carry no gloss. The frozen key gives French from the first line: le plus tost que vous pourez venir sera le meilleur … le secours de cavalerie envoyé par son altesse … a vous aller joindre a Salins Brun asks the army to come at once with the cavalry relief, not to go to Salins to join it, and warns that four or five days lost would be a great risk. He recalls the diversions, the signals and the recognition marks, and the cutting of the enemy’s communications; an attack by day would be more honourable and more useful than one by night. They are to bring flour and corn and tools to reap, the garrison of Gray is to burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler and Mirebeau, and above all to destroy the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown on Dole are made. Of 128 cipher words on fols. 191 and 127v, 113 are certain, 11 probable and 4 unresolved (96.9%). Fol. 127v reads “c’est[oit] un piège pour l’ennemi”. Fol. 183 (25 June) read with the key matches the period clear copy fol. 182 apart from vous / nous and ou / a : the commis describe the French quarters, with a separate attack by the bridge of three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot, and elsewhere one of twelve hundred men. Fol. 200 (22 July) is the glossed folio itself: the Parlement praises the relief army’s resolution to come without delay and says it is better to risk something than to lose everything. The reading was made from the numbers alone. Only afterwards was the clear text found, printed by É. Longin in Le siège de Dole par le prince de Condé (1912, nos. LIV, CXXXII, CLXXVIII and CCLXXXVII) from Brun’s drafts, the words to be enciphered in brackets. Letter agreement of the mechanical decryption with Longin’s text is 0.967 (584 of 589 letters on fols. 191 and 127v). Longin used the drafts, not the letters received, and gives no key; his text differs in “par S. A.” for par son altesse and “à plein” for à plain .

Four unresolved words on fols. 191 and 127v: a struck-out group, a word under a blot, ?atlons (Longin: rations ) and o… (Longin: c’estoit ). Longin brackets “de Mercy et de Forgats” and “accueillir” in the 1 July letter; they were not read on fol. 191 and have not been checked against the image. Translation f200_translation.md # English translation of fol. 200r (22 July 1636) ## Block 1 We praise God for the good and courageous resolution you have taken to come to us without delay, to which we invite you again as far as we can, because every consideration presses. ## Block 2 Although we see some slight danger in your arrival, having been put off too long, it is nevertheless not possible to delay it any further, and it is better to risk something than to lose everything; but we hope that, acting in good order, boldly and courageously as you know how to do, and we on our side making the rest of our efforts to second you, all will go to our glory and to the confusion of our enemies. A. Brun, [1 July 1636] (fol. 191) and the Parlement, 7 June 1636 (fol. 127v) On 1 July (fol. 191) Brun writes that they must come as soon as possible with the cavalry relief sent by “His Most Serene Highness” (not identified here), without going to join it at Salins; that letting four or five days pass is a great risk; he recalls the diversions, the signals and recognition marks, the cutting of the enemy’s communications; an attack by day would be more honourable and more useful than by night. They are to bring rations, flour and corn, with tools to reap; the Gray garrison is to burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler and Mirebeau, and above all destroy the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown on Dole are made; raids are to go into the Duchy, Bassigny and Bresse. Brun, [Dole, 1 July 1636] - P1: the sooner you can come, the better - P2: the cavalry relief sent by His Most Serene Highness - P3: to go and join you at Salins - P4: to delay as little as you can, and to expect no new help other than that relief - P5: [that it is] a great risk to let four or five days go by without your coming to our gates - P6: the diversions - P7: the signals, the liveries (recognition marks) - P8: the communications of that enemy - P9: both more honourable and more useful by daylight than at night - P10: [rations], flour and corn - P11: with tools to reap the harvest there - P12: that they burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler, Mirebeau - P13: that they destroy outright the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown at us are made - P14: [raids] into the Duchy [of Burgundy] as well as Bassigny and Bresse ## fol. 127v (view 226), Archbishop and Parlement, Dole, 7 June 1636 - R1: it was a trap for the enemy ## fols. 181r (view 316) and 183 (view 319), commis au gouvernement, 25 June 1636; clear copy fol. 182 (view 318) - Q1: which suits you only [for] - Q2: [giv]ing a separate attack - Q3: [three] or [four] hundred horse and six [hundred] - Q4: foot soldiers - Q5: for an attack of tw[elve hundred] - Q6: men - V1: which suits you only for making a separate attack with three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot - V2: for an attack of twelve hundred men ## Summary On 7 June (fol. 127) the Archbishop and the court urge Conflans to attack quickly; a letter they had addressed to him “was a trap for the enemy”. On 25 June (fols. 181, 183; clear on fol. 182) the commis describe the French quarters: on the side of the bridge, a separate attack with three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot; elsewhere, an attack of twelve hundred men. On 1 July (fol. 191) Brun writes that they must come as soon as possible with the cavalry relief sent by “His Most Serene Highness” (not identified here), without going to join it at Salins; that letting four or five days pass is a great risk; he recalls the diversions, the signals and recognition marks, the cutting of the enemy’s communications; an attack by day would be more honourable and more useful than by night. They are to bring rations, flour and corn, with tools to reap; the Gray garrison is to burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler and Mirebeau, and above all destroy the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown on Dole are made; raids are to go into the Duchy, Bassigny and Bresse. The cipher was broken at the time. Antoine Rossignol deciphered the intercepted dispatches in Paris; in July Richelieu sent him to Condé’s camp with “the decipherment of the letters that those of Dole were writing to the Marquis of Conflans” (Longin, no. CCLXXVIII). In late July and early August the court warned Conflans three times that “the enemy has found the key of the cipher”; the letter of 12 August (fol. 106) says so again and changes to another cipher, which we have not broken. Commis au gouvernement, 25 June 1636 (fols. 181 and 183; clear copy fol. 182) On 25 June (fols. 181, 183; clear on fol. 182) the commis describe the French quarters: on the side of the bridge, a separate attack with three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot; elsewhere, an attack of twelve hundred men. Translation translation.md # English translation of the ciphered passages (each passage is a phrase inside a letter written in clear) ## fol. 191r-v (views 332-333), A. Brun, [Dole, 1 July 1636] - P1: the sooner you can come, the better - P2: the cavalry relief sent by His Most Serene Highness - P3: to go and join you at Salins - P4: to delay as little as you can, and to expect no new help other than that relief - P5: [that it is] a great risk to let four or five days go by without your coming to our gates - P6: the diversions - P7: the signals, the liveries (recognition marks) - P8: the communications of that enemy - P9: both more honourable and more useful by daylight than at night - P10: [rations], flour and corn - P11: with tools to reap the harvest there - P12: that they burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler, Mirebeau - P13: that they destroy outright the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown at us are made - P14: [raids] into the Duchy [of Burgundy] as well as Bassigny and Bresse ## fol. 127v (view 226), Archbishop and Parlement, Dole, 7 June 1636 - R1: it was a trap for the enemy ## fols. 181r (view 316) and 183 (view 319), commis au gouvernement, 25 June 1636; clear copy fol. 182 (view 318) - Q1: which suits you only [for] - Q2: [giv]ing a separate attack - Q3: [three] or [four] hundred horse and six [hundred] - Q4: foot soldiers - Q5: for an attack of tw[elve hundred] - Q6: men - V1: which suits you only for making a separate attack with three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot - V2: for an attack of twelve hundred men ## Summary On 7 June (fol. 127) the Archbishop and the court urge Conflans to attack quickly; a letter they had addressed to him “was a trap for the enemy”. On 25 June (fols. 181, 183; clear on fol. 182) the commis describe the French quarters: on the side of the bridge, a separate attack with three or four hundred horse and six hundred foot; elsewhere, an attack of twelve hundred men. On 1 July (fol. 191) Brun writes that they must come as soon as possible with the cavalry relief sent by “His Most Serene Highness” (not identified here), without going to join it at Salins; that letting four or five days pass is a great risk; he recalls the diversions, the signals and recognition marks, the cutting of the enemy’s communications; an attack by day would be more honourable and more useful than by night. They are to bring rations, flour and corn, with tools to reap; the Gray garrison is to burn Rigny, Talmay, Pontailler and Mirebeau, and above all destroy the forge of Drambon and the others where the bombs thrown on Dole are made; raids are to go into the Duchy, Bassigny and Bresse. The cipher was broken at the time. Antoine Rossignol deciphered the intercepted dispatches in Paris; in July Richelieu sent him to Condé’s camp with “the decipherment of the letters that those of Dole were writing to the Marquis of Conflans” (Longin, no. CCLXXVIII). In late July and early August the court warned Conflans three times that “the enemy has found the key of the cipher”; the letter of 12 August (fol. 106) says so again and changes to another cipher, which we have not broken. A sheet of 139 number groups docketed ‘Cypher from Mr Eichel 1758 / Prussia’ carries no message. A key in the same volume, R596, found by scoring the SP 106 keys, declares its own nulls: under its rules 117 groups are nulls and 21 of the other 22 fall on cells the key leaves blank. 2512 · 405 · 207 · 1480 · 3037 · 2167 · 2897 blank · null · null · (écus?) · null · null · null R596: any number with a 7, 1–503, 1115–1198, 1483–1999, 2600–2802 = nonvaleurs Mr Eichel (Prussia) → unknown · numerical nomenclator · 1758 Mr Eichel's cipher sheet of 1758, written in nulls and blank cells TNA State Papers 106/7 (DECODE R595) is one page of number groups, listed as a ciphered letter from “Mr Eichel” with no decipherment, whose code “may be found” in the next record. That key does not fit. A second key in the same volume, R596, does. Applying its own null rules leaves no message: every group but one is a null or an empty cell of the table. DECODE listed it as a ciphered letter of 1 January 1758 from Mr Eichel, “probably from Russia”, a misreading of the docket. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/7, image 0020 (DECODE R595). The key DECODE proposed (R594) gives nonsense. The cipher The right key is R596 in the same volume (1,696 French values between 504 and 3293). Its heading declares as nulls every number containing a 7 and the ranges 1–503, 1115–1198, 1483–1999 and 2600–2802. How it was checked Under those rules 117 of the 139 groups are nulls, and 21 of the other 22 are numbers the key leaves blank. Blank cells are only 7% of its live numbers, so the writer chose them on purpose. What it is No message: a specimen, a test or a blind written wholly in non-values of the R596 cipher. Still open R596 is undated and nothing here proves it was Eichel’s own key. The key’s blank cells were not each checked on the key images.
eichel1758.html#the-record

DECODE R595 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0020)”) has a single image: a bifolium opened out. The upper half is blank apart from three dockets, “Cypher from Mr Eichel 1758”, “Prussia 1758” in pencil, and “Mr Eichel”. The lower half holds eighteen lines of numbers separated by points, 139 groups in all, with no decipherment above or beside them. The DECODE date, 1 January to 31 December 1758, comes from the docket. The catalogue's “1 Jan 1758” is the first day of that span. SP 106/7, image 0020: the first fifteen lines of the sheet, turned upright. Many groups end in 7, and the lower lines run through the 1900s and 2600s–2800s. These are the key's null ranges. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/7, image 0020, via DECODE R595.
eichel1758.html#finding-the-key

R594, which the DECODE note proposes, is a French nomenclator from the same box, “Russia 1758” on DECODE. It covers only 39% of the letter's groups, and what it covers decrypts to province, de Prusse, Bavière, ob-, blo, des … , which is nonsense. The transcriptions of the other key records in SP 106 boxes 6–8, and of the Prussian keys on DECODE, were each scored by coverage. Coverage alone does not decide: the large 3,000-value codes of 1750 cover almost every group and give nonsense. What decides it is a rule written on the key itself. R596 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0013-0017)”, five images, undated) opens with this heading: Tous les nro où je trouve un ou plusieurs 7 sont les nonvaleurs dans le présent chiffre, de même que les nro depuis 1 jusqu'à 503 inclusivement et depuis 1115 jusqu'à 1198, tout comme aussi depuis 1483 jusqu'à 1999, depuis 2600 jusqu'à 2802. The table follows the rule: no value in it contains a 7, and the values begin at 504 ( un ). The letter fits it closely. Its groups end in 7 far more often than chance allows (2167, 3037, 2897, 3117, 3007 …). Its closing lines run through 1901–1984 and 2603–2802, exactly the reserved ranges.
eichel1758.html#what-is-left-after-the-nulls

With R596's rules applied, 117 of the 139 groups are nulls. A random choice of numbers from 1 to 3299 would make only about 55% of them nulls. These 22 remain: 2512 1480 1413 2492 1434 3026 2093 3143 853 3150 3161 966 1291 1253 1311 1413 861 2853 2264 2264 863 911 Twenty-one of them are numbers that R596 lists but gives no value: 2511 montrer , 2512 — , 2513 mont ; 852 armement , 853 — , 854 arranger ; 2263 informer , 2264 — , 2265 inopinément . The key has 107 such blanks among its 1,527 live numbers, 7%. Twenty-one blanks out of twenty-two draws would happen by chance about once in 10 23 tries. The only group left with a value is 1480, écus , and the transcriber marked two of its digits as doubtful. An alternative reading of one figure does not change this. The DECODE transcriber read a looped figure as “8?”. In this hand it is more likely a 0: compare 2001 and 2002 on the last lines. With that reading, 27 groups survive. Twenty are blanks, and the others are isolated values that make no sentence: deu, Ci, difficile, chose, françois, Clo, difficile .
eichel1758.html#what-it-is-and-what-remains-uncertain

No message. The sheet is written wholly in non-values of the R596 cipher, nulls by its own rule plus blank cells of its table. It needs a writer who held the key and avoided every live number. Most likely it is a specimen or trial of the cipher, or a blind meant to occupy an interceptor. It is not a despatch. Eichel and R596. The docket names Eichel and Prussia. R596 carries no name or date on DECODE, though its vocabulary includes Moravie, Mecklenbourg, Saxe and Hollande. That the Deciphering Branch had this key, and that the sheet uses its non-values so precisely, links the two. Whether R596 was Eichel's own cipher or a copy the Branch reconstructed is not settled here. Transcription. The analysis uses the DECODE transcription of the letter, checked against the image, and of the key. The key's blank cells were not each checked on the key images. The 21-in-22 coincidence does not depend on that check. DECODE. The note's “probably from Russia” is a misreading of the docket “Prussia”, and the key it names, R594, is the wrong one.

George W. Erving, chargé at Madrid, wrote privately to Madison on 24 March 1807 (No. 21) “In the Cypher of the Legation”, the code Charles Pinckney had used in Spain. He reports a secret conversation between the Prince of the Peace (Godoy) and the Prussian chargé Henry: Bonaparte has offered the Prince the Electorate of Hanover for himself, and the Prince hopes by holding Hanover to make a separate peace with England and exchange it for Gibraltar. The Madison editors (PJM-SS 13:529–31) print the letter from Madison’s interlinear decode on the first received copy and state that the key has not been found (Weber, pp. 152–53). The decode has holes: “Haweder”, “Ha——er”, “Giblartar [sic]”, “see the he was more so”, “sp[eak]”, and at note 8 “to the […]” where Madison wrote “se al e”. Three sources were used: the first received copy with Madison’s decode (NARA RG 59, Despatches from Spain vol. 10, microfilm M31 reel 12, frames 0283–0286); the “Duplicate” in the Madison Papers at the Library of Congress (mjm014714), coded throughout and not decoded; and Pinckney’s own despatches in the same code (M31 reel 7 frames 0346–0352, 22 February 1803, one copy decoded by Jacob Wagner on frame 0348; reel 8 frames 0083–0084, January 1804). Pinckney’s pages confirm the common values: 1651 the , 133 of , 1343 and , 244 to , 1578 that , 69 in (Wagner: “the In-tend-ant” = 1651.69.1586.103), 1515 late . M31 reel 12, frame 0285 (detail): “he thinks having Ha—er to be able to make a separate peace with England & to exchange Hanover for Giblartar ”. The same three groups 724. 529. 934 that Madison decoded “Hanover” on the fourth line he left as “Ha — er” on the second. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, M31 reel 12, frame 0285, via the National Archives Catalog (NAID 188605361).

Sender and recipient are not named; the Duke of Bavaria is asked for help. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 f. 129; DECODE R9325, part of catalogue entry 161, listed with no decipherment. The cipher One sign per letter, signs for doubled letters (bb, cc, ss …), six signs that mean nothing, and a nomenclator of the affair: the Pope, the nuncio, the abbot, chapter and dean of Fulda, the Emperor’s councillors, the Duke of Bavaria. How it was deciphered Key R9324 on ff. 124–127 of the same volume has exactly the same set of null signs, which is how the two were matched; applied unchanged, it gives Latin in every word. What it says The abbot protests that he accepted the papal inhibition under compulsion; the Pope should declare it against the canons; failing that the Emperor’s councillors will judge; the Duke of Bavaria and the nuncio are to help. Still open Nothing in the text. Who wrote the note and to whom is not stated. Until 15 October 2026 this note was filed on one page with thirteen other ciphertexts of the same key volume. They are different ciphers, each with its own page; the largest group is System A′ of the dukes’ agents in Hungary.

Protestatus [est] abbas secreto coactum [se] ad litem acceptare Pontificis inhibitionem. Rogatus Pontifex ut contradicendo se interponat, declaret sive sponte sive vi contra canones esse. Si id fiat, Abbas agere cessat et cum Pontifice litigabit; ad [quod] cum non possit, Consiliarii Caesaris iudicabunt, aut Pontifex tum facit quod iam voluit. Rogatus Dux Bavariae auxilio sit; Nuncius suadeat Pontifici ita ad protectionem via[m]. “The abbot has protested that he was secretly forced to accept the Pope’s inhibition for the lawsuit. The Pope is asked to intervene by contradicting it and to declare whether it was willing or forced, against the canons. If that is done, the abbot stops proceedings and will plead before the Pope; if he cannot, the Emperor’s councillors will judge, or the Pope then does what he already wished. The Duke of Bavaria is asked to help; the nuncio should persuade the Pope towards protection in this way.” The writer slipped three times: secreto is written without its second e, auxilio begins with the i-sign, and voluit ends with the d-sign.
fulda1576.html#key

The key sheet (ff. 124–127) gives a letter alphabet (a = x-shape, b = t-shape, c = o, d = a barred p, e = a small 2 … s = Λ, t = a long-tailed Z, u = w), signs for doubled letters and for sch, st, sp and ch, six nulls (g, a ringed o, a stemmed square, a boxed bar, a W-like sign and an underlined 8), and a nomenclator that names the Fulda affair of 1576: Pontifex, the Cardinals of Como and Matutius(?), the Apostolic Nuncio, the ecclesiastical electors, the Bishop, Chapter and Dean of Würzburg, the Abbot, Chapter and Dean of Fulda, the Emperor, the Archdukes Matthias and Ernst, the Landsberg league, the Duke of Bavaria, Landgrave Wilhelm, the Elector of Saxony and the princes of the Augsburg Confession. The six nulls are the same set as on the note, which is how the key was found. A re-run of the key over the transcription (15 October 2026) matches the reading in 252 of 270 signs; the rest are the writer’s slips, the o/c look-alike written as o in the transcription, and one line where the transcription keeps a first pass. The reading was made on the image.

A cipher letter of the Spanish ambassador at Genoa about a marquis who was stalling on money for munitions. Brice Dudout rebuilt the numerical cipher on neighbouring letters that survive with a contemporary clear copy, tested it on a held-out pair (0.896 of characters), and read this letter, which has no clear copy. 8 86 51 250 an v 48 d 16 yo hi ot an 45 x 16 37 ß 36 46 … que el marqués de Leganés pa b lo … Genoa → Madrid · numerical cipher of the Genoa embassy · 19 May 1638 · key from external plaintext Siruela to Philip IV, 19 May 1638 Go to the full text ↓ A Spanish ambassador at Genoa tells the king in cipher that a marquis is delaying money for munitions, read with a key rebuilt on neighbouring letters that survive with clear copies. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 2 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on plaintext from external sources · Extent: complete · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) external text At a glance Key from external plaintext · complete The letter Juan de Velasco y la Cueva, Count of Siruela, Spanish ambassador at Genoa, to Philip IV, 19 May 1638, a signed original. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, legajo 3594, no. 156 (PARES 3586918). It is one of 20 cipher letters of catalogue entry 755. The cipher The numerical cipher of the Genoa embassy in 1638: vowels 16–20, syllables in series of five numbers (25 ba, 30 ca, 35 sa, 40 da, 45 la), disguised syllables, single letters and code signs such as 85/86 = que . How it was deciphered Other 1638 letters of the same bundle survive with a contemporary clear copy next to them. The key was rebuilt on three of those pairs, frozen, and tested on a held-out pair (3594,160 against 159): 0.896 of characters and 0.784 of words, against a 99th percentile of 0.343 and 0.204 for 200 permuted keys. What it says The king had ordered the Marquis Pablo Jerónimo Pallavicino to advance the money for munitions. The marquis was stalling, and Velasco warns that if he fails his suppliers they will fail him in turn. Still open One code sign (197, probably a name) is unresolved, and 205 is restored as haciendo . The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout rebuilt the key, ran the held-out tests and read the letter, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

In the spring of 1638 the Spanish ambassador at Genoa had to buy munitions on the spot. The king had ordered the Marquis Pallavicino (“Palavesín”) to advance the money, and the marquis was stalling. The bundle keeps, as nos. 154 and 155, a letter of Pallavicino to Velasco dated 25 May 1638, presumably the sequel. Most of Velasco’s other 1638 cipher letters in the bundle have their clear copy beside them (143/142, 146/145, 147/144, 158/157, 160/159, 169/168). No. 156 has none among items 110–242, so it is the reading added here. The letters of 1643–1651 in entry 755 are in other ciphers and were not attempted.
genes1638.html#the-key

Key K3f was built step by step on the pairs 146/145, 143/142 and 169/168 and frozen with its SHA-256 before each test. The earlier held-out tests (169 later pages and 158/157) gave 0.75–0.84 of characters, below the criterion fixed in advance (0.85 of characters and 0.75 of words). The causes were code words still missing from the key and confusion of two signs of the second hand (a tall long-s for s , a small loop for a ). The final pre-registered test used 3594,160, whose transcription was frozen before its clear copy was opened: 0.896 of characters and 0.784 of words, so the criterion was met. Applied unchanged to 3594,147, the previous key version recovered its clear copy at 0.923 of characters and 0.850 of words.

Of the 94 words of the cipher part, 89 are certain, three are probable ( marqués , me , faltando ), one is restored from the sense and one is unresolved: 93 of 94, or 98.9%, read as sense. Code sign 250 stands for “marqués de Leganés” in an April letter of the same bundle, but the singular verbs here point to Pallavicino, so we read “el marqués” and mark it probable. A Milanese agent’s report from Charles V’s court to Francesco II Sforza (Cotton MS Vespasian C IV ff. 214–218, DECODE R8572), listed on DECODE as not decrypted. Nine pages in Italian, clear passages alternating with cipher. Where British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV ff. 214–218 (DECODE R8572, catalogued as not decrypted, place given as “Daredos”). The cipher Barred letters with two-digit numbers for syllables in ordered rows (B.31–50 ba – gu ), plus letters with several signs each, a few words and titles, and nulls. How it was done A scan of the Sforza key sheets on DECODE found the matching one, R5258, filed under another agent, the Cavaliere Bilia. George Lasry had already rebuilt the key from the letter itself with Italian cribs; the two keys agree on 101 of the 106 numbered signs both editions name. What it says Gattinara out of favour, Bourbon dead, Genoa lost, Milan to go to the Infante. Still open 9 signs and about 45 doubtful words in the R5258 reading; five tentative values in George Lasry’s key. Credit George Lasry: independent key reconstruction, transcription and full Italian reading (with Codex assistance), contributed 14 October 2026. Key sheet: Archivio di Stato di Milano, via DECODE.

Gilino’s letter, ff. 214–218 of Cotton Vespasian C IV, is nine pages in Italian, clear passages alternating with cipher. The address leaf reads “Ill mo et Ex mo D no D no Mediolani Duci … Cremone”, and it is signed “Servo el Gilino”. How it came among Wolsey’s papers is not recorded. The volume also holds Ghinucci’s letters to Wolsey, whose cipher also writes digits above the signs; the two are unrelated ( Ghinucci to Wolsey, 1527 ). The key is DECODE R5258 , a sheet in the Milan archive (ASMi Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1591 no. 24) docketed “Cum equite Bilie / extracta ex cifris”: the key of the Cavaliere Bilia, another Sforza agent, which Gilino also used.
gilino1527.html#r8572

Folio 214r: the end of the clear opening (“alla fine di questo alla corte cesarea”) and the first cipher lines. With the key R5258 they read mi è affirmato da molti che sua signoria si trova in poca bona gratia del Imperatore : Gattinara is out of favour. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV f. 214r, via DECODE R8572. The cipher has barred base signs (G written like a 6, B, D, d, o, H, A, P, R) with numbers from 20 to 80, about forty unnumbered signs, and nulls. A one-sign-one-letter solver run on it gave no Italian, as expected for a syllabary. DECODE holds about 377 Sforza key records from the Milan archive. Their contact sheets were scanned for Gilino’s rows. R5256 is of the same family but its syllables differ. R5258 fits: B.31–50 ba … gu , B.51–54 fa … fo (B.55 and B.56 are title codes in this letter), D.51–65 la … nu , 6.56–80 pa … tu , o.33–47 va … zu , H.27 che , R.23 con , D.40 i in this letter. Applied with a few values added from context, it gives Italian throughout (Italian 4-gram score −1.52 per letter, in the range of real text). The folios run 214r, 214v, 215r, 215v, 216r, 216v, 217r, 217v, 218r; DECODE’s image order mixes them. What the cipher says, in summary: Gattinara, just landed at Barcelona, is in poor favour with the Emperor over two intercepted letters to the Viceroy of Naples: send the Naples galleys to relieve Genoa, and let Lope de Soria spend what is left of the 100,000 ducats of the exchange on the city. The Emperor’s confessor and the secretary Lalemand are his enemies. Since Bourbon’s death the Duke has only Gattinara to rely on, and should have “the Bilia” keep on good terms with him. The new Portuguese ambassador brought a letter in the Pope’s own hand to the nuncio, and two briefs asking the Emperor to take the Church under his protection. The Abbatino returns to Italy with all he asked for; the Pope had also been negotiating through Gregorio Casale; Paolo Luzzasco is to go over to the Emperor with 300 light horse. The French ambassadors swear that Francis I insists the Duke keep Milan; the nuncio has gone to Palencia to watch them. On the news from Lombardy the Emperor is said to be revoking the Pope’s liberation. The Ferrarese ambassadors and the Colonna agents call the Pope a traitor and a false pope. Andrea da Burgo writes to the Emperor pro opprimenda Italia . The investiture of Milan has been sent to the Infante with 100,000 ducats, for him to come down and defend it. Measured: 3,111 cipher signs, 122 of them nulls; of the 2,989 that carry text, 9 are not deciphered and about 108 fall in 45 doubtful words, leaving 2,872 (96.1%) that give sense. Measured on the words of the running reading ( r8572_reading.md ), the letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.6%, under the 95% bar; George Lasry’s edition, measured the same way, reads at 94.2%. No decipherment of this letter, on the manuscript or in print, was found.

The DECODE images were fetched at full size with the project’s login (the record carries no transcription). The letter was transcribed by a sub-agent working from crops and corrected in 24 places against the key. A one-sign-one-letter homophonic solver gave no Italian, as expected for a syllabary. A second sub-agent scanned the contact sheets of the Sforza key records on DECODE (ASMi Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1591, R5235–R5309) and found R5258. decode_r8572.py applies it with the context values in key_extra.tsv . The reading was checked against an Italian letter model of the period: it scores far above readings from random keys and from keys fitted to shuffled text ( validation.tsv ). The neighbouring DECODE records were opened; none is in this key.

[?His] detractors, who openly are the confessor and [?the German] secretary, will have it that Lautrec, on such information, sent part of the troops [?…] to the siege of Genoa which were destined for another place, and that for this the said city [?…] was no longer defended, [?for] the great need that I see His Majesty has of him. I cannot think but that he will keep himself in the Emperor's good favour, and for this I shall not cease to urge «Your Excellency» to order the Bilia by your letters to keep on good terms with him. Now we cannot hope for anything but good offi[c]es from His Lordship, above all with the death of Bourbon. I have resolved to go to meet him as far as three days' journey, and I know that for this I shall not be held suspect by the confederate ambassadors. The ambassador of the King of Portugal, newly come in the Pope's name, is not sent principally by His Holiness, [?…], as the Datary writes to the Lord Nuncio; but as he was about to go on to [?his] King, he begged Our Lord that it might please him [to honour him] with the honour of a brief in [?his] [?…] person to the Emperor, with authority to negotiate his settlement, promising to have him released at once and restore him to his former friendship with His Majesty and to the ancient state of the Church; which has not come about for him as he had promised, and [as] said not only in [?Italy] but also in Spain. Here he has been known for a light man; and with this good opinion of himself he leaves the Imperial court tomorrow for Portugal. This ambassador has brought a letter in the [?Pope]'s own hand to the Nuncio, as credence for [?Saporito], chamberlain of His Holiness, [?who] died in Genoa, «so wisely and prudently written that hardly anything more could be wished», exhorting him not to fail in his due service; likewise two briefs to the Emperor, full of many fine sentences, and with fine reasons it persuades His Majesty to take up the patronage of the Church and not to oppress it, above all sub fide, although unlearnedly written. The Abbatino returns despatched as he desires; the Emperor has granted him all he knew how to desire and ask. It is true that on many heads, since His Majesty does not know of what moment they are, he writes to the Viceroy of Naples, as better informed of the affairs of Italy, that he should satisfy the [?aforesaid] Marquis, as far as he can, for such is his mind. «No particular have I been able to learn beyond what is already written; [?…] at the first opportunity I shall advise Your Excellency of it; hold this for certain» that the settlement has followed with this Majesty, although he had come to terms with [?…] [?…], as we have news here that he was negotiating it through[h] [?…] the Cavalier Casale. The Emperor has given his mind to this settlement through the reminders of the Duke of Ferrara and the work of the Nuncio. I believe, however, that the Marquis, being obliged to the Florentines, will not show himself wholly in favour of the Emperor, but will see to it that Pagolo Luzzasco with three hundred light horse passes into the service of His Majesty, as [?yesterday] the aforesaid Abbatino, where [?…] to leave for your parts in all haste, and by him I have written to Your Excellency under cover of the Lady Marchioness of Mantua. Both have also sworn to me that the Most Christian [King] lately writes to them that he absolutely wants Your Excellency to remain in the state of Milan in the settlement, which does not agree with what he wrote to them lately; none[the]less [?I] leave it to the truth. The Lord Venetian ambassador and I alone, the day before yesterday, were with the Lord A[po]stolic Nuncio at [?Usiglios], and begged him to be willing to go to Palencia and stay there while the Fre[n]ch ambassadors stay, and to use diligence to learn the truth of what they will negotiate, and above all concerning that matter. He promised us to do it willingly, and so we understand that His Lordship has gone there; and I am almost certain that he will serve us, both out of respect for Your Excellency, and for what he owes to Italy [?…], and for the friendship he holds with the said Venetian ambassador. I understand also that the Emperor, as soon as he heard of the surrender of Genoa, sent a [?new] despatch to Monseigneur de [?Miliao] [?…], who until that time had not embarked for Rome; and it is hinted to me that His Majesty is revoking the liberation of the Pope because of the new events in Lombardy. What leads [?me] to believe this are the bad offices which the Ferrarese ambassadors and the agents of the Colonna publicly do against His Holiness with the Emperor; of whom, when they speak of him, they cannot name him except as traitor, false pope, bastard, maker [?of] poisons, and with a thousand other insults which it would be long to write. With him, I am told, they will despatch Troilo Negrono, and that His Majesty [?…] now says he wants to grant many favours to the Lords Colonna; and this is the present difficulty of the affairs of Lombardy, and has caused it; therefore they fear that after the one ruin the other, of the kingdom of Naples, may follow. C IV ff. 214r-218r: "el Gilino" to Francesco II Sforza, Paredes, 15 Sept 1527: English translation of George Lasry's edition Translation (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026) of George Lasry's Italian working reading, `lasry/plaintext_reading.txt` (7 Oct 2026, contributed 14 Oct 2026): the whole letter, clear passages and deciphered passages, in its restored physical order (P1 214r, P2 214v, P7 215r, P3 215v, P5 216r, P4 216v, P6 217r, P8 217v, P9 218r). His marks are kept: `[word?]` a conjecture (translated as `[?word]`), `[…]` unread; *Emperor?* and *His Majesty?* translate word codes whose expansion he leaves unproved. His notes on unresolved signs are kept in brackets. ## Translation ### f. 214r *Clear.* Most Illustrious and Most Excellent, my only Lord, my ever most honoured Lord. I kiss the hands of Your Excellency. After visiting these places around Valladolid I came to Paredes on the 9th of this month, where I have in part been given knowledge of what I write to you below, of which Your Excellency will be able to judge with the prudence that is natural to you. The Lord Grand Chancellor, by his letters of the 27th of last month, arrived in Barcelona with Messer Giovanni Bartolomeo di Gattinara, Martino Centurio[?ne], [?general in the making] of Monseigneur de Bourbon, and a few of his household. Most stayed in Genoa for lack of ships. His Lordship had a very contrary voyage, both from storms at sea and from having been followed by some galleys of the French fleet. He is expected at the Imperial court at the end of this month. *Cipher.* I am assured by many that His Lordship stands in little favour with the [?Emperor] for one single [?thing] that is imputed to him: namely that, by two letters of his intercepted to the Viceroy, [he asked] that he send the galleys of Naples to the relief of Genoa, and order Lope de Soria to use the rest of the [?hundred] thousand ducats of the exchange for the benefit of that city, both for providing infantry and victuals. ### f. 214v *Cipher.* Otherwise the whole would be lost. His detractors, who are openly the confessor and the German secretary, will have it that Lautrec, on such information, sent [?part] of [?his] troops to the siege of Genoa, which had been destined for another place, and that for this reason the said city was no longer defended. I, for the great need that I see His Majesty? has of him, cannot think but that he will keep himself in the Emperor?'s good favour; and for this reason I shall not cease to urge Your Excellency to order the Bilia by your letters to keep on good terms with him. Now we cannot hope for anything but good offices from His Lordship?, above all with the death of Bourbon. I have resolved to go to meet him as far as three days' journey, and I know that for this I shall not be held suspect by the ambassadors of the confederates. ### f. 215r *Clear.* Monseigneur de Tarbes has given me a copy of the aforesaid intercepted letters, which I would have sent to Your Excellency if the present bearer had not shown himself so difficult. *Cipher.* The ambassador of the King of Portugal, newly come in the Pope's name, is not sent principally by His Holiness. So [uncertain passage] the Datary writes to the Lord Nuncio. But as he was about to go on to his king, he begged Our Lord that he would [?do] him the honour of a brief, in his person, to the [?Emperor], with authority to negotiate his settlement, promising to have him released at once and restored to his former friendship with [?His Majesty] and to the ancient state of the Church. Which has not come about for him, and he had promised, [as] said, not only in [?Italy] but also in Spain. Here he has been known for a light man, and with this good opinion of himself he leaves the Imperial court tomorrow for Portugal. This ambassador has brought ### f. 215v *Cipher.* a letter in the Pope's [?own] hand to the Nuncio, as credence for Saporito, chamberlain of His Holiness, who died in Genoa, which [was] *Clear.* written so wisely and prudently that hardly anything more could be wished, *Cipher.* exhorting him not to fail in his due service. Likewise two briefs to the [?Emperor], full of many fine sentences, and with fine reasons it persuades [?His Majesty] to take up the patronage of the Church and not to oppress it, above all sub fide, which [?unlearnedly: uncertain passage] written. The Abbatino returns despatched and desires […], and the [?Emperor] has granted him all he knew how to desire and ask. It is true that on many heads, since [?His Majesty] does not know of what moment they are, he writes to the Viceroy of Naples, and better informed of the affairs of Italy, that he should satisfy the [?aforesaid] Marquis as far as he can, for such is his mind. [to to qu gu: unresolved sequence.] *Clear.* [?No] particular have I been able to learn beyond what is already written; on learning of any [… a word in the right margin not read with certainty], at the first opportunity I shall advise Your Excellency of it. Hold this for certain: *Cipher.* that the settlement has followed with this Majesty; that he had come to terms with France, and here we have news that he was nego- ### f. 216r *Cipher.* -tiating it through the Cavalier Casale. The Emperor? has given his mind to this settlement through the reminders of the Duke of Ferrara and the work of the Nuncio. I believe, however, that the Marquis, being obliged to the Florentines, will not show himself wholly in favour of the Emperor?, but that he will see to it that Pagolo Luzasco, with three hundred light horse, passes into the service of His Majesty?. And yesterday the aforesaid Abbatino was to leave for your parts in all haste, and by him I have written to Your Excellency under cover [?of] the Lady Marchioness of Mantua. [Su: unresolved final fragment.] *Clear.* The Magnificent Lords the French ambassadors hold letters from the Most Christian King of the 29th of August, by which they are informed of the [?defeat] at Portofino, the surrender of Genoa, and the hope of soon obtaining Alessandria. Together they tell me they have a commission from their King that the negotiation of the peace be conducted on the content of the articles made at [?Madrid], a thing to which up to now the aforesaid Most Christian [King] had not been willing to assent, and that for this reason they have almost certain hope that an agreement [?will come to] follow [an interlinear correction not wholly resolved]. They, with the Lords the English ambassadors, have been at Palencia [?and are staying there] to discuss what their King can or cannot swear of the above-written articles. ### f. 216v *Cipher.* Both have sworn to me that the Most Christian [King] lately writes to them that he absolutely wants Your Excellency to remain in the state of Milan in the settlement, which does not agree with what he wrote to them lately. Nonetheless I leave it to the truth. The Lord Venetian ambassador and I alone, the day before yesterday, were with the Lord Apostolic Nuncio at Usiglios, and begged him to be willing to go to Palencia and stay there while the French ambassadors are there, and to use diligence to learn the truth of what they will negotiate, and above all concerning that matter. He promised us to do it willingly, and so we understand that His Lordship has gone there. I am almost certain that he will serve us, both out of respect for Your Excellency, for what he owes to all Italy, and for the friendship he holds with the said ### f. 217r *Cipher.* Venetian ambassador. I understand that the [?Emperor], as soon as he heard of the surrender of Genoa, sent a new despatch to Monseigneur de Miliao, who [?until] that time had not embarked for Rome. And it is hinted to me that [?His Majesty] is revoking the liberation of the Pope because of the new events in Lombardy. What leads [?me] to believe this are the bad offices that the Ferrarese ambassadors and the agents of the Colonna publicly do against His [?Holiness] with the [?Emperor]; [?of] whom, [?as often as] they speak of him, they cannot name him except as traitor, false pope, bastard, maker of poisons, and a thousand other [?insults] which it would be long to write. [Three signs left in the cipher block, o29 vp b+, literally v-v-u, function unresolved.] *Clear.* Today the Magnificent Messer Ludovico Catto, doctor of laws, the old ambassador of the Most Illustrious Lord Duke of Ferrara, has gone to Valladolid to take leave of His Imperial Majesty [a word struck out] to return to his country. I have always found him much inclined to the benefit of Your Excellency, and therefore you [?are] under an obligation to him. *Cipher.* With him, I am told, they will despatch Troilo Negrono; [and] that [?His Majesty] now [?says] that he wants to grant many favours to the Lords Colonna. If this is so, the present difficulty of the affairs of Lombardy has caused it; they fear that after the one ruin the other, of the kingdom of Naples, may follow. There are here letters of Messer Andrea Borgo ### f. 217v *Cipher.* [?to] the [?Emperor] and to Valdesio, formerly his servant, full of counsels pro opprimenda Italia [for crushing Italy] and long discourses for keeping the state of Milan in the devotion of [?His Majesty]. At the end they conclude that the Infante is the one who can hold it and defend it from any violence that might descend to occupy it. Since the taking of Genoa it is said that the [?Emperor] has sent word to have the Infante come down and to give all Italy as a prey to the Germans; that [?His Majesty] shows greater heart than ever, and that it has come out from the confessor that the loss of Genoa has been a strong spur to the [?Emperor], [that] he should show himself wholly bent on [?war], and [?how] powerful their [?forces] are. [The final groups LU-V-I follow, unresolved.] *Clear.* It is also said that His Imperial Majesty has sold the state of the Count of Caiazzo in the Kingdom for twenty-eight [thousand] ducats to the son of the Count of Monteleone, Viceroy of Sicily. In the Lord Marco Pio I see every day his goodwill towards Your Excellency growing, and his desire to do you service; which has caused in me a certain uncommon regard for His Lordship, which obliges me to be with him many times and to honour him greatly. ### f. 218r *Cipher.* Written thus far, I have been advised by several safe ways that the [?Emperor] has sent by three couriers the investiture of the state of Milan to the Infante [abbassi: word not yet resolved in context] to the defence of that state, and that at present he is providing him with a hundred thousand ducats. The loss of Genoa has been confirmed by way of the Lord of Monaco, whom [?His Majesty] is providing with money so that he may keep himself in his devotion. [Final sign overwritten or corrected, not resolved.] *Clear.* I would not know what more to write to you for now, except that I commend myself to your good grace as humbly as I can, praying Our Lord God to give you that happiness which you desire for yourself. From Paredes, the 15th of September 1527. Of Your Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Lordship the most humble and perpetual servant, el Gilino Key: key_r8572.tsv , key_R5258.md , key.txt , key.json

Reference · outcome methods · terms Glossary Every write-up states two things about its outcome. The method says how the key or the text was obtained. The extent says how much of the text was obtained: complete or partial. The methods follow the categories proposed by George Lasry, with one addition for items that already had a full decipherment. glossary.html#methods

The first three are cryptanalysis: the key was recovered here. The next three applied a key or decipherment that already existed; the work was transcription and decipherment. Whether someone had solved an item before, and when that was found, is stated on each write-up. ciphertext-only break Key recovered from ciphertext-only The key was rebuilt from the ciphertext alone: frequencies, solvers, pattern words, the order of the key. No plaintext and no existing key was used. If someone had solved the same text earlier and it was found only afterwards, the write-up says so: an independent re-solution. 90 write-ups → key from external plaintext Key recovered based on plaintext from external sources The key was rebuilt by matching the ciphertext against a plaintext found elsewhere: a printed edition, a calendar of state papers, a copy of the same letter in another archive. 19 write-ups → key from adjacent plaintext Key recovered based on adjacent plaintext The key was rebuilt from plaintext next to the ciphertext: a partial decipherment written between the lines or in the margin, clear passages in the same letter, a deciphered copy in the same file. 98 write-ups → external key matched Read after matching with key from external sources An existing key that had not been connected with this document (a key for another correspondent or series, a key sheet filed elsewhere) was found to fit, and applied. 37 write-ups → known key applied Read with known key The key was already identified for this document or its correspondence (on its archive or DECODE record, published for it, filed with it) and was applied. glossary.html#extent-complete-or-partial

Complete : at least 95% of the cipher symbols give sense, every document is covered, and what stays open is scattered code groups or pieces blocked from outside. Partial : anything less; the write-up lists what is open and why.
glossary.html#terms

Cipher and code A cipher replaces letters or syllables with symbols. A code replaces whole words or names with groups taken from a list (a codebook). Most early-modern diplomatic keys mix the two. Nomenclator The usual early-modern key: a cipher alphabet, often homophonic, plus a list of code groups for names, titles and common words, and sometimes nulls. Simple substitution Each plaintext letter always becomes the same one symbol. Homophonic A plaintext letter can be written with any of several symbols (its homophones), to flatten the letter frequencies. Decryption is still unambiguous. Polyphonic One symbol stands for more than one plaintext letter. Decryption is ambiguous: the reader chooses the value that makes sense, so applying even a known key takes judgement. Variable-length Cipher units of different lengths (for example one- and two-digit numbers) are written without separators, so the text has to be divided into units before it can be decrypted, and several divisions may be possible. Null A symbol that means nothing, added to disturb frequency analysis. Key The table that gives the plaintext value of every cipher symbol and code group. Plaintext, ciphertext, cleartext Plaintext is the message the cipher hides; ciphertext is the enciphered form. Cleartext is the part of a document that was written openly, not enciphered, often around the ciphered passages. Decipherment Plaintext obtained from ciphertext. A contemporary decipherment was made at the time, by the recipient's clerk, and is often written between the lines (interlinear) or on a separate sheet. Cryptanalysis (a break) Recovering an unknown key from the material. The three routes used here are ciphertext-only, from adjacent plaintext and from external plaintext (see the methods above). Crib A guessed or known piece of plaintext placed against the ciphertext to recover part of the key. Transcription Copying the cipher symbols from the image into text a program can read. Symbols that are not letters or digits have to be given labels first; misreadings here look like errors in the key. Extent: complete or partial Complete means at least 95% of the cipher symbols give sense, every document is covered, and what stays open is scattered code groups or pieces blocked from outside (illegible, too short). Anything less is partial. Prior solution Whether a decipherment or key existed anywhere before this project worked on the item, and when it was found. It is recorded for every target because a model may have seen it. DECODE The online database of historical cipher documents and keys (Megyesi et al.); record numbers are cited as R1234.

Where Printed in 1840 by Christoph von Rommel from the Marburg originals, with the ciphered passages as two-digit figures he could not decipher. The cipher Two-digit figures. Rommel had the key six years later from Groen van Prinsterer and van der Kemp and printed it in a German journal with one sample letter, going no further. On 20 May 1606 he warns that the Spaniards mean to have a King of the Romans elected at their devotion. hesse1603.html#documents

Maurice of Hesse-Kassel (1572–1632) was the most learned and the most francophile of the Calvinist princes of the Empire, and Henri IV’s regular correspondent on German affairs from the Bongars mission of 1599 to the Jülich crisis of 1610. Rommel, the Hessian archivist and historian, printed 118 pieces of the exchange from the Marburg archive in 1840 (Paris, Renouard). The Landgrave’s letters are in clear; several of the King’s carry passages in figures, which Rommel set as he found them, and some of the King’s letters he printed from a contemporary decipherment with the figures omitted. The list below is what the volume prints in figures from the King’s side; nothing else on it was ciphered by him. Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310, the middle of the King’s letter of 20 May 1606: the Spanish design on the election of a King of the Romans and the call to “prendre conseil ensemble”. Image: Rommel (ed.), Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310, via the Internet Archive (correspondancein00henr, leaf 352). Henri IV to the Landgrave Rommel pp. In figures Read before 22 November 1602 84 13 lines no 12 January 1603 99 12 lines no; Lettres missives vi p. 12 prints the figures 3 April 1604 170–175 5 pages yes, Rommel 1846 (used here as control) 27 December 1604 211–214 3 pages no 28 April 1605 230 11 lines no; Rommel’s footnote regrets it 22 December 1605 269–272 3 pages no 20 May 1606 307–314 6 pages no 24 January 1609 391 1 line no The catalogue entry that set this target (“12 Jan 1603, 28 Dec 1603, 27 Dec 1604, pp. 12, 148–189, 388–393”) came from Tomokiyo’s page and was wrong about the pages: p. 12 is the Lettres missives reference, the 28 December 1603 letter is printed from a decipherment with no figures at all, and pp. 388–393 hold a single line. The passages of 1602, 1605 and 1606 were on no list.

The letter table is on p. 402. Image: Rommel, Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Geschichte V (1846), p. 403, via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_Zpc1AAAAMAAJ). The cipher is the one Tomokiyo found as an original sheet in BnF Clairambault 360 f. 168, dated October 1602, and it served the whole correspondence to 1610. Bare two-digit figures are letters, up to four homophones each; a comma after the figure sends it to a list of small words and syllables ( le, la, leur, que, qui, qu’il, pour, pro, pre, ma, me, mon, ne, ny, nous, on, où, sa, se, roy ), two dots above it to a second ( con, ca, car, don, da, di, do, de, en, eulx, faire, faict, point, elle, forces, troupes, guerre, cour impériale, diète de l’Empire ), an overbar to names and titles ( Bouillon, Comte, Conseil, Pape, Empereur, Roi d’Espagne, Roi d’Angleterre, l’Archiduc, Brandebourg, Brunswick, provinces unies, Protestant, Allemagne, Angleterre, argent, armée, alliés, ambassadeur, au, aux, afin ). A dozen drawn symbols stand for te, tion, tant, tous, tout, tre, grand, va, ville, votre, Hongrie ; one sign doubles the symbol before it, one cancels it, and a few flourishes are nulls. Rommel’s print of the key is right in every letter value, but its lists are set with fewer words than figures and its fourth row of homophones is misaligned, so the texts had to fix the rest: 70 is a fourth p missing from the table ( presse, perdra, principalement ); 85 is m and 83 is o ( maison, ensemble, favorisé ); 17, is la and 18, 19, le ; 24, lettre , 25, leur ; 65, pro ( profiter, prospèrent ), 66, pre ; 83, rompre ( cor-rompre ); 70 with dots is faict , 84 with dots forces ; 26 with overbar is Comte (Rommel’s own glossary: le comte de Solms ), which shifts the names one place so that 31 is Pape , 33 Empereur , 35 Roi d’Espagne and 37 Roi d’Angleterre , as the 24 January 1609 line “les ministres du Pape et du Roi d’Espagne” and the 1604 control both require. The group Rommel set under l’administrateur de Strasbourg as 59 is le Turc (“la paix avec [59]”, December 1605); the tall 4 is te or tion and the print does not separate them; the typesetter’s “9 +” is the doubling sign 94; and the ♀-, Ψ- and tt-like flourishes are nulls (“ayant ♀ tt sceu que le duc de Féria…”). Every one of these is recorded in key.py with the passage that fixed it. Controls. Rommel printed Groen van Prinsterer’s decipherment of the 3 April 1604 letter beside the key; the first lines of p. 171 decode here word for word to his text (“…ainsy demander la paix à leurs ennemis en leur pays, que la nécessité qui les presse est très grande…”). His footnotes to the Landgrave’s letter of 10 February 1603 gloss five groups ( diète de l’Empire, l’Archiduc, Protestants, Empereur, cour impériale ) and the key returns each; his 1840 glossary “Passages déchiffrés” agrees throughout. The main check is internal: every passage decrypts to continuous early-seventeenth-century French that joins the clear text it interrupts.
