As in the reading, the ciphered passages are **bold**; `…` marks where the quoted text breaks off in clear; `[word]` a word supplied where the print is faulty or a table entry is unlisted; `[?word]` a doubtful word; `[?]` and the bracketed notes (unresolved groups, clear passages summarised) are kept. The "controls" read alongside (the Landgrave's own letters and a letter deciphered in 1846) are not translated here. ## 1. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 22 November 1602 (Rommel p. 84) … So I delay the despatch no longer except to await the **advice which you have promised me to be on it, and especially on the matter of the diet, and to know whether it is to take place, what is to be treated there, what proposal I am to make there for the public and the particular interest of my allies and o[thers], [fol]lowing the discussions we [had] together; and also to know whether I should have my said ambassador go on into Saxony and Denmark, with your good counsel on the [19, overbar: ?memorandum] and instruction I am to give him.** For I have taken such assurance of and confidence in your friendship and prudence that I wish hereafter … ## 2. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 12 January 1603 (Rommel p. 99) … **[what] can [be done] without prejudice to our allies,** on which I shall then be awaiting your good advice with good devotion. Since the Emperor will not appear at the diet, I consider that nothing of importance will be treated there, **and principally not the election of a King of the Romans,** of which I expect you will inform me, as of what will happen in the assembly of the Estates of Poland. [Brandenburg and Prussia, in clear.] **But the duke [de Bouillon] has not written me a single word in his letter about the coming here of the Administrator [of Strasbourg], nor about the matter of the bishopric of Stras[bourg], so that I do not know how he will have taken this journey, nor in what way he embraces the cause of the said Administrator;** I pray you to let me know what you have learned of it. ## 3. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 27 December 1604 (Rommel pp. 211-214) … what you have been pleased to refer to me about it. **[The duke of … (98 with overbar, not in Rommel's table)] makes every show of bearing me affection. I assure you also that I hold their friendship in great esteem; my brother the Duke of Lorraine is the go-between in it.** [Sending an embassy to the German princes:] But two reasons have prevented me: one is **the bad understanding I have observed among the Protestant [?princes], which I feared would make the said visit unfruitful;** and the other **the discontent and distaste which some of them have given me by their actions,** principally since **they gave credit to the talk of the Duke of Bouillon and favoured his cause with less respect and consideration for my person than I hoped from them,** as I have sometimes written to you … The fire of the revolt of Upper Hungary was soon put out, but **its sequel and consequence will be great, and may spread with time to the neighbourhood.** The King of England is sending the Duke of Lennox to me, and his admiral to Spain, to maintain himself in good friendship on all sides: **a counsel which I have not heard that he finds [good]** with time, but **he must put it to the proof before he believes it.** I am informed that **the United Provinces have as much courage to defend themselves and continue the war as ever,** and I will believe, this being so, that **the means will not fail them, provided as they are; they are sending deputies to England; they hope they will be better received and favoured than the Spaniards have promised themselves, for the s[aid] King does not wish to lose their friendship,** as I have been told. **The said provinces** were lately visited **by a new [name, 9 groups unresolved]**, by whose good qualities they were much edified. And he is indeed virtuous. I hear **that he gave them some hope of arming in their favour next year.** In which I pray you **to encourage and assist him,** if you find the occasion. **I am with the Spaniards as usual, discovering daily some new intrigue forged on their part to my disadvantage; but** God will preserve me from it. I have brought to justice the Count of Auvergne, his father-in-law and his sister, who **are charged and accused of having dealt with them further than they ought,** and you shall be informed of what follows … ## 4. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 28 April 1605 (Rommel p. 230) The passage Rommel footnoted "It is to be regretted that these lines are not yet deciphered": … and although my actions towards those who profess it, inside and outside my kingdom, **and even the [?favours] and aid which the United Provinces and [the] city of Geneva continue to receive from me, sufficiently justify the truth of my conduct and will in such cases, and the care I take to maintain and uphold those of the said religion, for the notable interests I have in their preservation and in that of the public cause, nevertheless** … I reco[gnise] … ## 5. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Paris, 22 December 1605 (Rommel pp. 269-272) [After the Mérargues affair and the attempt on the King:] … and even on my part, **it must be considered that all these accidents befell me almost at the same time as the conspiracy in England. It seems too that they were forged on the same anvil.** The ambassador of Spain wanted to make me believe that I had done his master an injury in detaining his secretary, who had been caught in the weaving of his treason, **so accustomed are the ministers of that nation to se[d]uce and corrupt the subjects of the princes with whom [they] reside.** I am assured that the King of Great Britain, my good brother, has as much reason to complain of it as I, **yet he covers and dissimulates it better.** But I cannot believe that for this **his affairs prosper** the more; which it would be needful **that all who love him should point out to him,** as **I have done by an ambassador whom** I sent to him expressly for this purpose … likewise I have commended to him **the United Provinces in the extreme need they have** at present of being **assisted and reinforced by their allies, to restore** next year **the reputation of their arms.** But, my cousin, as you have **a notable interest in their preservation, together with the other princes of Germany,** I pray you to work so that they are likewise **succoured from your side, with both money and troops,** following the hope that some **of the said princes have given them,** and you will do a very good work, **very useful to the common cause, and which will be** very agreeable [to me]; praying you to let me know what I am to hope for from it. For my part, I have resolved **to continue to them next year the same assistance in money and troops that I have given them this year; it is very considerable and not less than two million livres; but if with that they are not succoured from elsewhere, it will be impossible for them to resist their enemies, for these are gathering money and forces from all sides to attack them more vigorously and powerfully than they have ever [done].** Be then **the author,** my cousin, **of having them receive the said succour, and let it be as promptly as can be done, so that they may take the field among the first in the spring, for he who can forestall his opponent in that will be greatly advantaged by it.** For the rest, **let me know what the Emperor intends to treat in the diet of the Empire which he has summoned, and what** you hope **from the negotiations for peace with [the Turk] and from the agreement of the Hungarians with the Emperor, as also from the continuation of the siege of the city of Brunswick, in which I regret to see [the Duke of Brunswick] engaged.** I pray God … Written at Paris, the 22nd day of December 1605. ## 6. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Fontainebleau, 20 May 1606 (Rommel pp. 307-314) … to share it with the princes of Germany of that condition, **[7 groups unresolved] that things are still in great confusion,** because **the Emperor does not change his conduct, and he is very badly assisted and [served] in his affairs, principally on the side of** Hungary, where neither peace nor war is made as it should be … [p. 308 in clear: the Turks, the Austrian nobility in arms, the archdukes at Vienna, the Imperial diet] … on all sides. **The Spaniards will do what they can to have a King of the Romans elected from the House of Austria who is entirely at their devotion, having** learned that the Duke of Feria … [in clear: Feria sent to the diet to promote the election, to propose the pacification of the Netherlands, and if the States refuse, to engage the Empire to make war on them] … **which are two proposals of great consequence, and in which all Christendom has no less interest [than] Germany itself. That is why I consider it necessary that all the kings and princes who must be jealous of the growth and prosperity of the Spanish power should advise in good time and take counsel together on what is fitting to do to prevent the said Spaniards from making the affairs and resolutions of the said diet square with their wishes. For my part, I shall always contribute to it very willingly what depends on me and is becoming for me to do, principally when I recognise that the others can do the like, and above all the princes of [Holland: ?Germany], being no less desirous than the kings my predecessors have been to favour and second the good intentions of the ancient allies and friends of this crown on similar occasions, as on all others that may arise, for [the] preservation of German liberty, without however expecting any other advantage from it than to advance the good of the common cause and the public security; for which I shall be very glad not only that you inform those whom you judge worthy of it, but also that you give me advice and counsel on what I can and must [do] now, both to assure them of my good will and to advance its effects.** I have been informed that the King of England is with good right very ill satisfied with the last refusal [of Owen and Baldwin, in clear] … **[a run of letters and signs the 1840 typesetter could not render] I have at least … I have not heard that the King of England breaks with the said Spaniards for this just offence, so much does he desire to live in neutrality and peace; besides which I know that the said Spaniards omit nothing to do towards him and towards his servants to compensate for and make him forget this discontent, having had several very specious offers and overtures made to him anew expressly for this purpose. Nevertheless, as he is prudent and well counselled, I hope also that he will take good care not to let himself be drawn by their inducements and persuasions, which have no other aim than to abuse and circumvent those [to whom] they address them, so as to be able to [do] their business the better in the Low Countries, where they intend to make a great effort this year, principally on the side of the Rhine and of Friesland, having for this purpose doubled their army and awaiting only** the return to Brussels of the Marquis Spinola … Which it will be very difficult for the said States of the United Provinces to resist, **for as they are much weaker than the others, they will also be forced to put themselves on the defensive,** which will be **a wretched condition for them, and one whose outcomes are too [?greatly] to be feared in a state composed of and governed by several heads,** as is **the republic of the said provinces,** than in another. That is why **all who are joined in interest with them must think well on it,** so as **to set their hand to it** before **their weakness and exhaustion** become greater; **otherwise the remedies will come too late. You have [?seen] what I** wrote to you before on this subject, praying you **to favour their affairs and suits with the princes of Germany,** of which I understand very little effect has come. But the affairs and enterprises of the gentlemen of the said States, both on the side of the East Indies and on the coast of Portugal, are prospering greatly, to the great prejudice of those of the said Spaniards; **yet I doubt that this good fortune will last for them if that on land [?fails] them** and **their peoples grow weary of bearing the burden of the war.** I shall write you nothing of the dispute between the Pope and the Venetians, except that **I know the Spaniards will do what they can to take advantage of it,** as **they have always done** on similar occasions. That is why, on my side, I shall do all I can to settle it as soon as possible … Written at Fontainebleau, the 20th day of May 1606. ## 7. Everything here is an unvalidated reading from a printed transcription of 1840; the originals in Marburg were not seen. ## 1. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 22 November 1602 (Rommel p. 84) … Aussi, je n'en diffère plus la dépesche que pour attendre le **advis que vous m'avez promis est[re] sur icelle, et spécialement sur le faict de la diette, et sçavoir si elle doibt avoir lieu, ce qui s'y doibt traicter, quelle proposition j'y doibs faire pour le public et le particulier de mes alliés et a[utres], [en]suivant les discours que nous avons [eu] ensemble, et pour sçavoir aussi si je ferois passer en Saxe et Danemarch mon dit ambassadeur, avec votre bon conseil sur le [19, overbar: mémoire?] et instruction que je luy doibs donner.** Car j'ay pris telle asseurance et confiance de votre amitié et prudence, que je veux cy après … ## 2. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 12 January 1603 (Rommel p. 99) … **[ce qui se] peut sans préjudicier à nos alliés,** sur quoy je seray donques attendant en bonne dévotion votre bon advis. Puisque l'Empereur ne comparoistra en la diette, j'estime qu'il ne s'y traitera chose d'importance **et principallement de l'élection d'un roy des Romains,** dont je m'attends que vous m'advertirez, comme de ce qui se passera en l'assemblée des Estats de Polongne. [Brandenburg and Prussia, in clear.] **Mais le duc [de Bouillon] ne m'a escript par sa lettre un seul mot de la venue par deçà de l'Administrateur [de Strasbourg], ny du faict de l'évesché de Stras[bourg], tellement que je ne sçay co[m]me il aura pris ce voyage, ny de quelque sorte il embrasse la cause du dit Administrateur;** je vous prie me faire sçavoir ce que vous en aurez apris. ## 3. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 27 December 1604 (Rommel pp. 211–214) … ce que vous avez voulu m'en déférer. **[Le duc de … (98 with overbar, not in Rommel's table)] fait toute démonstration de me porter de l'affection. Je vous assure aussy que je fais grande estime de leur amitié; mon frère le duc de Lorraine en est l'entremetteur.** [Sending an embassy to the German princes:] Mais deux raisons m'en ont empesché: l'une est **la mauvaise intelligence que j'ay recogneue entre les [princes?] protestants, laquelle j'ay eu crainte estre cause de rendre la dite visitation peu fructueuse;** et l'autre **le mescontentement et dégoust qu'aucuns d'eulx m'ont donné de leurs actions,** principallement depuis **qu'ils ont adjousté foy aux discours du duc de Bouillon et favorisé sa cause avec moins de respect et considération à ma personne que je n'espérois d'eulx,** comme je vous ay quelques fois escrit … Le feu de la révolte de la haulte Hongrie a esté bientost esteint, mais **la suite et conséquence en sera grande, et pourra s'estendre avec le temps au voisinage.** Le roy d'Angleterre envoye vers moy le duc de Lenox, et en Espagne son admiral, pour s'entretenir en bonne amitié de toutes parts: **conseil duquel je n'ay pas ouï qu'il se trouve [bien]** avec le temps, mais il fault **qu'il en face les preuves devant qu'il le croye.** Je suis adverty que **les Provinces Unies ont autant de courage de se deffendre et continuer la guerre que jamais,** et veulx croire, cela estant, que **les moyens ne leur en manqueront point, estans pourveus comme ils sont; ils envoyent des députés en Angleterre; ils espèrent qu'ils seront mieulx receus et favorisés que les Espagnols ne se sont promis, car le d[it] roy ne veult perdre leur amitié,** ainsy que l'on m'a mandé. **Les dites provinces** ont esté naguères visiter **d'un nouveau [name, 9 groups unresolved]**, des bonnes quallités duquel ils sont demeurés bien édifiés. Aussi est-il vertueux. J'entends **qu'il leur a donné quelque espérance d'armer en leur faveur l'année prochaine.** En quoy je vous prie **de le conforter et assister,** sy vous en rencontrez l'occasion. **Je suis avec les Espagnols comme de coustume, découvrant journellement quelque nouvelle menée forgée de leur part à mon désavantage; mais** Dieu m'en préservera. J'ay mis en justice le comte d'Auvergne, son beau-père et sa sœur, qui **sont chargés et accusés d'avoir traité avec eulx plus avant qu'ils ne devoyent,** et serez adverty de ce qui en succèdera … ## 4. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 28 April 1605 (Rommel p. 230) The passage Rommel footnoted "Il est à regretter que ces lignes ne soient pas encore déchiffrées": … et encores que mes actions envers ceux qui en font proffession dedans et dehors mon royaume, **et mesmes les [faveurs?] et aydes que continuent à recevoir de moy les Provinces Unies et [la] ville de Genève, justifient assez la vérité de ma conduite et volonté en tels cas, et le soin que j'ay de maintenir et soubstenir ceulx de la dite religion, pour les notables intérests que j'ay à leur conservation et de la cause publicque, toutesfois** … Je reco[gnois] … ## 5. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Paris, 22 December 1605 (Rommel pp. 269–272) [After the Mérargues affair and the attempt on the King:] … et mesmes de ma part, **il fault considérer que tous ces accidens me sont arrivés quasi au mesme temps de la conspiration d'Angleterre. Il semble aussy qu'ils ayent esté forgés sur mesme enclume.** L'ambassadeur d'Espagne vouloit me faire accroire que j'avois faict injure à son maître d'avoir retenu son secrétaire, ayant esté surpris sur la tissure de sa trahison, **tant les ministres de ceste nation ont accoustumé se[d]uire et corrompre les subjects des princes auprès desquels [ils] résident.** Je suis asseuré que le roy de la Grande Bretagne, mon bon frère, a autant d'argument de s'en plaindre que moy, **toutesfois il le couvre et dissimule mieulx.** Mais je ne puis croire que pour ce faict **ses affaires en prospèrent** davantage; ce qui seroit besoin **que tous ceulx qui l'ayment luy remonstrassent,** comme **j'ay fait par un ambassadeur que** j'ay envoyé vers luy exprès pour cest effect … pareillement je luy ay recommandé **les Provinces Unies au besoin extrême qu'elles ont** à présent d'estre **assistées et renforcées par leurs alliés pour relever** l'année prochaine **la réputation de leurs armes.** Mais, mon cousin, comme vous avez **notable intérest à leur conservation avec les autres princes d'Allemagne,** je vous prie vous emploier à ce qu'ils soient pareillement **secourus de votre costé tant d'argent que de troupes,** suivant l'espérance qu'aucuns **des dits princes leur ont donnée,** et vous ferez un très bon œuvre, **très utile à la cause commune et qui [me] sera** très agréable, vous priant me mander ce que j'en doibs espérer; pour mon regard j'ay délibéré **leur continuer l'année prochaine la mesme assistance d'argent et de troupes que je leur ay départie ceste-cy; elle est très notable et non moindre de deux millions de livres; mais si avec cela ils ne sont point secourus d'ailleurs, il leur sera impossible de résister à leurs ennemis, car ils font amas d'argent et de forces de toutes parts pour les assaillir plus vivement et puissamment qu'ils n'ont point [faict].** Soyez donc **autheur,** mon cousin, **de leur faire recevoir ledict secours, et que ce soit le plus promptement que faire se pourra, afin qu'ils puissent se mettre aux champs au printemps des premiers, car celuy qui pourra prévenir sa partie en cela en sera grandement avantagé.** Au demeurant, **mandez-moy ce que l'Empereur prétend traiter en la diète de l'Empire qu'il a intimée, et ce que** vous espérez **des négotiations de la paix avec [le Turc] et de l'accord des Hongrois avec l'Empereur, comme de la poursuite du siège de la ville de Brunswick, où j'ay regret de voir [le duc de Brunswick] engagé.** Je prie Dieu … Escript à Paris le xxiie jour de décembre 1605. ## 6. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Fontainebleau, 20 May 1606 (Rommel pp. 307–314) … d'en faire part aux princes de la Germanie de ceste condition là, **[7 groups unresolved] que les choses sont tousjours en grande confusion,** parce que **l'Empereur ne change point de conduite, et qu'il est très mal assisté et [servi] en ses affaires, principa[l]lement du costé de** Hongrie, où l'on ne fait la paix ny la guerre comme il convient … [p. 308 in clear: the Turks, the Austrian nobility in arms, the archdukes at Vienna, the Imperial diet] … de toutes parts. **Les Espagnols feront ce qu'ils pourront pour faire eslire un roy des Romains de la maison d'Austriche qui soit entièrement à leur dévotion, ayant** sceu que le duc de Féria … [in clear: Feria sent to the diet to promote the election, to propose the pacification of the Netherlands, and if the States refuse, to engage the Empire to make war on them] … **qui sont deux propositions de grande conséquence et auxquelles toute la chrestienté n'a moins d'intérest [que] l'Allemagne mesme. C'est pourquoy j'estime estre nécessaire que tous les roys et princes qui doivent avoir jalousie de l'agrandissement et prospérité de la puissance espagnole doibvent d'heure aviser et prendre conseil ensemble de ce qu'il convient faire pour empescher que les dicts Espagnols ne fassent cadrer les affaires et résolutions de la dite diète à leur souhait. Pour mon regard, j'y contribueray tousjours très volontiers ce qui dépendra de moy et me sera bienséant de faire, principalement quand je recognoistray que les autres pourront faire le semblable, et par dessus tous les princes de la [Hollande: Germanie?], n'estant moins désireux que ont esté les roys mes prédécesseurs de favoriser et seconder les bonnes intentions des anciens alliés et amis de ceste couronne en semblables occasions comme en toutes autres qui se présenteront pour [la] conservation de la liberté germanique, sans toutesfois en attendre autre advantage que d'advancer le bien de la cause commune et la seureté publique; dont j'auray bien agréable non seulement que vous advertissiez ceulx que vous en jugerez dignes, mais aussy que vous me donniez advis et conseil de ce que je puis et doibs [faire] maintenant, tant pour les asseurer de ma bonne volonté que pour en advancer les effects.** J'ay esté adverty que le roy d'Angleterre est à bon droit très mal satisfait du dernier refus [of Owen and Baldwin, in clear] … **[a run of letters and signs the 1840 typesetter could not render] j'ay au moins … je n'ay pas ouï que le Roi d'Angleterre pour ceste juste offence rompe avec les dits Espagnols, tant il désire vivre en neutralité et en paix; joint que je sçay que les dits Espagnols n'obmettent rien à faire en son endroit et envers ses serviteurs pour compenser et faire oublier ce mescontentement, luy ayant de nouveau fait faire plusieurs offres et ouvertures très spécieuses exprès pour cest effet. Toutesfois, comme il est prudent et bien conseillé, j'espère aussi qu'il se gardera bien de se laisser aller à leurs inductions et persuasions, qui n'ont autre but que d'abuser et circonvenir ceulx [auxquels] ils les adressent, pour pouvoir mieux [faire] leur affaire aux Pays-Bas, où ils prétendent faire un grand effort ceste année, principa[l]lement du costé du Rhin et de Frise, ayans pour cest effect redoublé leur armée et n'attendans que** le retour à Brusselles du marquis Spinola … A quoy il sera très difficile que les dits Estats des Provinces Unies résistent, **car comme ils sont foibles beaucoup plus que les autres, ils seront contraints aussy de se mettre sur la défensive,** qui sera une **misérable condition pour eulx, et les événements de laquelle sont trop [fort?] à craindre en un estat composé et gouverné par plusieurs testes,** comme est la **république des dites provinces,** qu'en un autre. C'est pourquoy **tous ceulx qui sont conjoints d'intérest avec eulx doivent bien y penser,** affin de **y porter la main** devant que **leur débilité et inanition** soyent plus grandes, **autrement les remèdes y seront trop tardifs. Vous m'avez [veu?] ce que je** vous ay ci devant escrit sur ce subject, en vous priant de **favoriser leurs affaires et poursuites envers les princes d'Allemagne,** de quoy j'entends estre réussy fort peu d'effect. Mais les affaires et entreprises par messieurs des dits Etats, tant du costé des Indes Orientalles, qu'en la coste du Portugal, vont prospérant grandement au grand préjudice de celles des dits Espagnols; **touttefois je doubte que ceste bonne fortune leur dure si celle de la terre leur [manque?]** et que **leurs peuples se lassent de soustenir le faix de la guerre.** Je ne vous escriray rien du différent, qui est entre le Pape et les Vénitiens, sinon que **je sçay que les Espagnols feront ce qu'ils pourront pour s'en advantager,** aussy que **ils ont tousjours faict** de semblables occasions. C'est pourquoy, de mon costé, je feray tout ce qu'il me sera possible pour le composer au plus tost … Escrit à Fontainebleau, le 20e jour de may 1606. ## 7. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 22 November 1602 (Rommel p. 84) … So I delay the despatch no longer except to await the **advice which you have promised me to be on it, and especially on the matter of the diet, and to know whether it is to take place, what is to be treated there, what proposal I am to make there for the public and the particular interest of my allies and o[thers], [fol]lowing the discussions we [had] together; and also to know whether I should have my said ambassador go on into Saxony and Denmark, with your good counsel on the [19, overbar: ?memorandum] and instruction I am to give him.** For I have taken such assurance of and confidence in your friendship and prudence that I wish hereafter … ## 2. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 12 January 1603 (Rommel p. 99) … **[what] can [be done] without prejudice to our allies,** on which I shall then be awaiting your good advice with good devotion. Since the Emperor will not appear at the diet, I consider that nothing of importance will be treated there, **and principally not the election of a King of the Romans,** of which I expect you will inform me, as of what will happen in the assembly of the Estates of Poland. Il semble aussy qu'ils ayent esté forgés sur mesme enclume.** L'ambassadeur d'Espagne vouloit me faire accroire que j'avois faict injure à son maître d'avoir retenu son secrétaire, ayant esté surpris sur la tissure de sa trahison, **tant les ministres de ceste nation ont accoustumé se[d]uire et corrompre les subjects des princes auprès desquels [ils] résident.** Je suis asseuré que le roy de la Grande Bretagne, mon bon frère, a autant d'argument de s'en plaindre que moy, **toutesfois il le couvre et dissimule mieulx.** Mais je ne puis croire que pour ce faict **ses affaires en prospèrent** davantage; ce qui seroit besoin **que tous ceulx qui l'ayment luy remonstrassent,** comme **j'ay fait par un ambassadeur que** j'ay envoyé vers luy exprès pour cest effect … pareillement je luy ay recommandé **les Provinces Unies au besoin extrême qu'elles ont** à présent d'estre **assistées et renforcées par leurs alliés pour relever** l'année prochaine **la réputation de leurs armes.** Mais, mon cousin, comme vous avez **notable intérest à leur conservation avec les autres princes d'Allemagne,** je vous prie vous emploier à ce qu'ils soient pareillement **secourus de votre costé tant d'argent que de troupes,** suivant l'espérance qu'aucuns **des dits princes leur ont donnée,** et vous ferez un très bon œuvre, **très utile à la cause commune et qui [me] sera** très agréable, vous priant me mander ce que j'en doibs espérer; pour mon regard j'ay délibéré **leur continuer l'année prochaine la mesme assistance d'argent et de troupes que je leur ay départie ceste-cy; elle est très notable et non moindre de deux millions de livres; mais si avec cela ils ne sont point secourus d'ailleurs, il leur sera impossible de résister à leurs ennemis, car ils font amas d'argent et de forces de toutes parts pour les assaillir plus vivement et puissamment qu'ils n'ont point [faict].** Soyez donc **autheur,** mon cousin, **de leur faire recevoir ledict secours, et que ce soit le plus promptement que faire se pourra, afin qu'ils puissent se mettre aux champs au printemps des premiers, car celuy qui pourra prévenir sa partie en cela en sera grandement avantagé.** Au demeurant, **mandez-moy ce que l'Empereur prétend traiter en la diète de l'Empire qu'il a intimée, et ce que** vous espérez **des négotiations de la paix avec [le Turc] et de l'accord des Hongrois avec l'Empereur, comme de la poursuite du siège de la ville de Brunswick, où j'ay regret de voir [le duc de Brunswick] engagé.** Je prie Dieu … Escript à Paris le xxiie jour de décembre 1605. ## 6. C'est pourquoy j'estime estre nécessaire que tous les roys et princes qui doivent avoir jalousie de l'agrandissement et prospérité de la puissance espagnole doibvent d'heure aviser et prendre conseil ensemble de ce qu'il convient faire pour empescher que les dicts Espagnols ne fassent cadrer les affaires et résolutions de la dite diète à leur souhait. Pour mon regard, j'y contribueray tousjours très volontiers ce qui dépendra de moy et me sera bienséant de faire, principalement quand je recognoistray que les autres pourront faire le semblable, et par dessus tous les princes de la [Hollande: Germanie?], n'estant moins désireux que ont esté les roys mes prédécesseurs de favoriser et seconder les bonnes intentions des anciens alliés et amis de ceste couronne en semblables occasions comme en toutes autres qui se présenteront pour [la] conservation de la liberté germanique, sans toutesfois en attendre autre advantage que d'advancer le bien de la cause commune et la seureté publique; dont j'auray bien agréable non seulement que vous advertissiez ceulx que vous en jugerez dignes, mais aussy que vous me donniez advis et conseil de ce que je puis et doibs [faire] maintenant, tant pour les asseurer de ma bonne volonté que pour en advancer les effects.** J'ay esté adverty que le roy d'Angleterre est à bon droit très mal satisfait du dernier refus [of Owen and Baldwin, in clear] … **[a run of letters and signs the 1840 typesetter could not render] j'ay au moins … je n'ay pas ouï que le Roi d'Angleterre pour ceste juste offence rompe avec les dits Espagnols, tant il désire vivre en neutralité et en paix; joint que je sçay que les dits Espagnols n'obmettent rien à faire en son endroit et envers ses serviteurs pour compenser et faire oublier ce mescontentement, luy ayant de nouveau fait faire plusieurs offres et ouvertures très spécieuses exprès pour cest effet. Toutesfois, comme il est prudent et bien conseillé, j'espère aussi qu'il se gardera bien de se laisser aller à leurs inductions et persuasions, qui n'ont autre but que d'abuser et circonvenir ceulx [auxquels] ils les adressent, pour pouvoir mieux [faire] leur affaire aux Pays-Bas, où ils prétendent faire un grand effort ceste année, principa[l]lement du costé du Rhin et de Frise, ayans pour cest effect redoublé leur armée et n'attendans que** le retour à Brusselles du marquis Spinola … A quoy il sera très difficile que les dits Estats des Provinces Unies résistent, **car comme ils sont foibles beaucoup plus que les autres, ils seront contraints aussy de se mettre sur la défensive,** qui sera une **misérable condition pour eulx, et les événements de laquelle sont trop [fort?] à craindre en un estat composé et gouverné par plusieurs testes,** comme est la **république des dites provinces,** qu'en un autre. C'est pourquoy **tous ceulx qui sont conjoints d'intérest avec eulx doivent bien y penser,** affin de **y porter la main** devant que **leur débilité et inanition** soyent plus grandes, **autrement les remèdes y seront trop tardifs. Vous m'avez [veu?] ce que je** vous ay ci devant escrit sur ce subject, en vous priant de **favoriser leurs affaires et poursuites envers les princes d'Allemagne,** de quoy j'entends estre réussy fort peu d'effect. Mais les affaires et entreprises par messieurs des dits Etats, tant du costé des Indes Orientalles, qu'en la coste du Portugal, vont prospérant grandement au grand préjudice de celles des dits Espagnols; **touttefois je doubte que ceste bonne fortune leur dure si celle de la terre leur [manque?]** et que **leurs peuples se lassent de soustenir le faix de la guerre.** Je ne vous escriray rien du différent, qui est entre le Pape et les Vénitiens, sinon que **je sçay que les Espagnols feront ce qu'ils pourront pour s'en advantager,** aussy que **ils ont tousjours faict** de semblables occasions. C'est pourquoy, de mon costé, je feray tout ce qu'il me sera possible pour le composer au plus tost … Escrit à Fontainebleau, le 20e jour de may 1606. ## 7. As in the reading, the ciphered passages are **bold**; `…` marks where the quoted text breaks off in clear; `[word]` a word supplied where the print is faulty or a table entry is unlisted; `[?word]` a doubtful word; `[?]` and the bracketed notes (unresolved groups, clear passages summarised) are kept. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 22 November 1602 (Rommel p. 84) … So I delay the despatch no longer except to await the **advice which you have promised me to be on it, and especially on the matter of the diet, and to know whether it is to take place, what is to be treated there, what proposal I am to make there for the public and the particular interest of my allies and o[thers], [fol]lowing the discussions we [had] together; and also to know whether I should have my said ambassador go on into Saxony and Denmark, with your good counsel on the [19, overbar: ?memorandum] and instruction I am to give him.** For I have taken such assurance of and confidence in your friendship and prudence that I wish hereafter … ## 2. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 12 January 1603 (Rommel p. 99) … **[what] can [be done] without prejudice to our allies,** on which I shall then be awaiting your good advice with good devotion. Since the Emperor will not appear at the diet, I consider that nothing of importance will be treated there, **and principally not the election of a King of the Romans,** of which I expect you will inform me, as of what will happen in the assembly of the Estates of Poland. [Brandenburg and Prussia, in clear.] **But the duke [de Bouillon] has not written me a single word in his letter about the coming here of the Administrator [of Strasbourg], nor about the matter of the bishopric of Stras[bourg], so that I do not know how he will have taken this journey, nor in what way he embraces the cause of the said Administrator;** I pray you to let me know what you have learned of it. ## 3. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 27 December 1604 (Rommel pp. 211-214) … what you have been pleased to refer to me about it. **[The duke of … (98 with overbar, not in Rommel's table)] makes every show of bearing me affection. I assure you also that I hold their friendship in great esteem; my brother the Duke of Lorraine is the go-between in it.** [Sending an embassy to the German princes:] But two reasons have prevented me: one is **the bad understanding I have observed among the Protestant [?princes], which I feared would make the said visit unfruitful;** and the other **the discontent and distaste which some of them have given me by their actions,** principally since **they gave credit to the talk of the Duke of Bouillon and favoured his cause with less respect and consideration for my person than I hoped from them,** as I have sometimes written to you … The fire of the revolt of Upper Hungary was soon put out, but **its sequel and consequence will be great, and may spread with time to the neighbourhood.** The King of England is sending the Duke of Lennox to me, and his admiral to Spain, to maintain himself in good friendship on all sides: **a counsel which I have not heard that he finds [good]** with time, but **he must put it to the proof before he believes it.** I am informed that **the United Provinces have as much courage to defend themselves and continue the war as ever,** and I will believe, this being so, that **the means will not fail them, provided as they are; they are sending deputies to England; they hope they will be better received and favoured than the Spaniards have promised themselves, for the s[aid] King does not wish to lose their friendship,** as I have been told. **The said provinces** were lately visited **by a new [name, 9 groups unresolved]**, by whose good qualities they were much edified. And he is indeed virtuous. I hear **that he gave them some hope of arming in their favour next year.** In which I pray you **to encourage and assist him,** if you find the occasion. **I am with the Spaniards as usual, discovering daily some new intrigue forged on their part to my disadvantage; but** God will preserve me from it. I have brought to justice the Count of Auvergne, his father-in-law and his sister, who **are charged and accused of having dealt with them further than they ought,** and you shall be informed of what follows … ## 4. Henri IV to the Landgrave, 28 April 1605 (Rommel p. 230) The passage Rommel footnoted "It is to be regretted that these lines are not yet deciphered": … and although my actions towards those who profess it, inside and outside my kingdom, **and even the [?favours] and aid which the United Provinces and [the] city of Geneva continue to receive from me, sufficiently justify the truth of my conduct and will in such cases, and the care I take to maintain and uphold those of the said religion, for the notable interests I have in their preservation and in that of the public cause, nevertheless** … I reco[gnise] … ## 5. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Paris, 22 December 1605 (Rommel pp. 269-272) [After the Mérargues affair and the attempt on the King:] … and even on my part, **it must be considered that all these accidents befell me almost at the same time as the conspiracy in England. It seems too that they were forged on the same anvil.** The ambassador of Spain wanted to make me believe that I had done his master an injury in detaining his secretary, who had been caught in the weaving of his treason, **so accustomed are the ministers of that nation to se[d]uce and corrupt the subjects of the princes with whom [they] reside.** I am assured that the King of Great Britain, my good brother, has as much reason to complain of it as I, **yet he covers and dissimulates it better.** But I cannot believe that for this **his affairs prosper** the more; which it would be needful **that all who love him should point out to him,** as **I have done by an ambassador whom** I sent to him expressly for this purpose … likewise I have commended to him **the United Provinces in the extreme need they have** at present of being **assisted and reinforced by their allies, to restore** next year **the reputation of their arms.** But, my cousin, as you have **a notable interest in their preservation, together with the other princes of Germany,** I pray you to work so that they are likewise **succoured from your side, with both money and troops,** following the hope that some **of the said princes have given them,** and you will do a very good work, **very useful to the common cause, and which will be** very agreeable [to me]; praying you to let me know what I am to hope for from it. For my part, I have resolved **to continue to them next year the same assistance in money and troops that I have given them this year; it is very considerable and not less than two million livres; but if with that they are not succoured from elsewhere, it will be impossible for them to resist their enemies, for these are gathering money and forces from all sides to attack them more vigorously and powerfully than they have ever [done].** Be then **the author,** my cousin, **of having them receive the said succour, and let it be as promptly as can be done, so that they may take the field among the first in the spring, for he who can forestall his opponent in that will be greatly advantaged by it.** For the rest, **let me know what the Emperor intends to treat in the diet of the Empire which he has summoned, and what** you hope **from the negotiations for peace with [the Turk] and from the agreement of the Hungarians with the Emperor, as also from the continuation of the siege of the city of Brunswick, in which I regret to see [the Duke of Brunswick] engaged.** I pray God … Written at Paris, the 22nd day of December 1605. ## 6. Henri IV to the Landgrave, Fontainebleau, 20 May 1606 (Rommel pp. 307-314) … to share it with the princes of Germany of that condition, **[7 groups unresolved] that things are still in great confusion,** because **the Emperor does not change his conduct, and he is very badly assisted and [served] in his affairs, principally on the side of** Hungary, where neither peace nor war is made as it should be … [p. 308 in clear: the Turks, the Austrian nobility in arms, the archdukes at Vienna, the Imperial diet] … on all sides. **The Spaniards will do what they can to have a King of the Romans elected from the House of Austria who is entirely at their devotion, having** learned that the Duke of Feria … [in clear: Feria sent to the diet to promote the election, to propose the pacification of the Netherlands, and if the States refuse, to engage the Empire to make war on them] … **which are two proposals of great consequence, and in which all Christendom has no less interest [than] Germany itself. That is why I consider it necessary that all the kings and princes who must be jealous of the growth and prosperity of the Spanish power should advise in good time and take counsel together on what is fitting to do to prevent the said Spaniards from making the affairs and resolutions of the said diet square with their wishes. For my part, I shall always contribute to it very willingly what depends on me and is becoming for me to do, principally when I recognise that the others can do the like, and above all the princes of [Holland: ?Germany], being no less desirous than the kings my predecessors have been to favour and second the good intentions of the ancient allies and friends of this crown on similar occasions, as on all others that may arise, for [the] preservation of German liberty, without however expecting any other advantage from it than to advance the good of the common cause and the public security; for which I shall be very glad not only that you inform those whom you judge worthy of it, but also that you give me advice and counsel on what I can and must [do] now, both to assure them of my good will and to advance its effects.** I have been informed that the King of England is with good right very ill satisfied with the last refusal [of Owen and Baldwin, in clear] … **[a run of letters and signs the 1840 typesetter could not render] I have at least … I have not heard that the King of England breaks with the said Spaniards for this just offence, so much does he desire to live in neutrality and peace; besides which I know that the said Spaniards omit nothing to do towards him and towards his servants to compensate for and make him forget this discontent, having had several very specious offers and overtures made to him anew expressly for this purpose. That is why **all who are joined in interest with them must think well on it,** so as **to set their hand to it** before **their weakness and exhaustion** become greater; **otherwise the remedies will come too late. You have [?seen] what I** wrote to you before on this subject, praying you **to favour their affairs and suits with the princes of Germany,** of which I understand very little effect has come. But the affairs and enterprises of the gentlemen of the said States, both on the side of the East Indies and on the coast of Portugal, are prospering greatly, to the great prejudice of those of the said Spaniards; **yet I doubt that this good fortune will last for them if that on land [?fails] them** and **their peoples grow weary of bearing the burden of the war.** I shall write you nothing of the dispute between the Pope and the Venetians, except that **I know the Spaniards will do what they can to take advantage of it,** as **they have always done** on similar occasions. Groups under 10000 are sent with four figures, and all 54 groups of the two telegrams lie between 1347 and 67398, so the book probably has fewer than about 70,000 entries. Read each group as a page (n ÷ 100) and a line (n mod 100), and reverse the order of the pages below a split while keeping the lines in order: with the split at page 375, 21 of the 24 values fall in alphabetical order (rho 0.957). The reversed lower half holds a – h , the upper half i – v ; Livorno sits in a high block (67398), perhaps for names. Shuffling the 24 words and giving chance the same choice of split reaches a median of 0.275 and a maximum of 0.746 in 2,000 runs, so the model is not a fit to noise. It was found after the fact on these 24 values, with a fitted split, and stays a hypothesis until more decoded traffic in this code tests it. The model supports the doubtful words of the decode: divorciado falls among the d-words, contestar among the c-words, Arroio among the a-words (so the encoder used the common noun arroio for the name). Two groups are out of order: the model would rather make 3707 = franceza and 49641 a word between ministro and presidente . The decode’s split is kept. No group is shared with King Carlos’s code of the same spring ( carlos1903 ), Sabugosa’s, Manuel II’s of 1910 or Venceslau de Lima’s of 1909 ( code.py , part 5).

Ferdinand I’s resident at the Porte, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, sent Vienna an enciphered Latin copy of three letters of Henry II to Suleiman, among them the credence for the sieur d’Huyson, with his own Italian notes (HHStA Türkei I 7-2-18). Brice Dudout deciphered it with Malvezzi’s alphabet from DECODE R367/R386, calibrated on a sibling copy against its decipherment of the time and tested blind on a letter of 1550: about 97.5% of some 1,550 word groups. Henry asks the Sultan to have the Swiss included in the truce with Charles V and Ferdinand, warns against the Crépy articles slipped into the Emperor’s ratification, and asks for the Ottoman fleet. π 8̊ e #o h 7 13 Γ f k · Ʒ 12 °P F # h P e ϙ F Serenissime Ottomanorum π = s · 8̊ = e · h = n · 13 = ss · Ʒ = o · 12 = tt Constantinople → Ferdinand I · homophonic cipher of graphic signs with nulls and code syllables · 1547 · external key matched Henry II to Suleiman, 1547: the letters Malvezzi copied in cipher from Henry II → to Suleiman the Magnificent Go to the full text ↓ Ferdinand’s resident at the Porte sent Vienna a Latin copy, in his own cipher, of Henry II’s letters to Suleiman; his alphabet on DECODE, checked on a sibling copy, deciphers about 97.5% of it. The letters are of autumn 1547; the copy went to Ferdinand as an enclosure to Malvezzi’s dispatch of 8 March 1548. Where Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Vienna, Staatenabteilungen Türkei I 7-2-18, fols. 143r–146r, 207 lines of cipher. The archive’s catalogue marks it “Inhalt nicht dechiffriert”. Catalogue entry 500 (the other Türkei I files stay open there). The cipher Malvezzi’s alphabet: two to four graphic signs for each letter, numbers for doubled letters, null syllables and null Latin words, and a few code syllables (Bi the King of France, Ras the Sultan, Ab the French). How it was deciphered Brice Dudout took Malvezzi’s alphabet from DECODE R367 and R386, calibrated it on another enciphered copy of the series whose decipherment of the time survives (Türkei I 7-3-20), froze it, tested it blind on an unglossed letter of 1550, and then transcribed and deciphered 7-2-18 line by line on the archive’s images. What it says Henry II accredits d’Huyson, asks the Sultan to have France’s allies, the Swiss first, included in the truce Charles V and Ferdinand have just made with the Porte, warns that the Emperor’s ratification smuggles in the lapsed promises of Crépy, and asks for the Ottoman fleet. Malvezzi adds that the French present their king’s letters in Turkish and undated, “per posser negare”. Still open 18 unresolved groups in the contributor’s count (27 places marked as open in the established text, some of them part of a word), and 86 readings given as probable; the captain’s name rests on one sign. Credit Transcription, decipherment, Latin and Italian text and English translation by Brice Dudout, with Claude Opus 5.5 agents, 27 October 2026; his write-up on Europe chiffrée . The key is Malvezzi’s alphabet as filed on DECODE (R367, R386); the calibration used the decipherment made at the time of Türkei I 7-3-20.
huyson1547.html#copy

In the autumn of 1547 Henry II, king for six months, sent his pantler, the sieur d’Huyson (the copy spells him Duson, Dusson and Dussun), to Constantinople with a letter of credence for Suleiman and instructions; the French ambassador at the Porte was Gabriel d’Aramon. Charles V and Ferdinand had just obtained a five-year truce from the Porte, signed at Adrianople in June 1547. Henry wanted his allies included in it and the Emperor’s good faith put in doubt. Ferdinand’s resident at the Porte, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, got hold of the texts and sent them to his master in cipher. The copy fills four leaves, fols. 143r–146r, 207 lines. It has six parts: a two-line Italian heading by Malvezzi; the letter of credence (143r ll. 3–17); a note by Malvezzi on how the French handle their king’s letters at the Porte (143r ll. 18–30); the long letter on the truce (143r l. 31 to 145v l. 15); a second short Italian heading; and the letter brought by a captain after d’Huyson (145v l. 18 to 146r l. 19). The archive’s catalogue dates the item about September 1547 and records that it came as an enclosure to Malvezzi’s letter to Ferdinand of 8 March 1548. Malvezzi says how he made the Latin. The French, he writes, do not present the king’s letters in the form the Most Christian King wrote them: they have them put into Turkish language and script, adding and removing what they please, and leave out the date and place, so as to be able to deny them. He renders them dal turchesche in latino de uerbo ad uerbum . The Latin is therefore a back-translation from the Turkish, which explains its wavering between “we” and “I” and between “Your Majesty” and the third person, and the formula et {loco suo} before the signature, probably the place of the seal or the royal monogram in the Turkish version. No image of the manuscript is reproduced on this page: the Austrian State Archives ask to be notified, and charge a fee, before reproductions of their holdings are published. The signs on this page are typed from the transcription.
huyson1547.html#cipher

The cipher is Malvezzi’s own, the one that also carries Ferdinand’s letter to him of 23 January 1548, which has its own page: Ferdinand I to Malvezzi, 1548 . Each letter has two to four graphic signs: planetary and alchemical signs, Greek letters, and Latin letters used with other values (e for r, f for m, h for n, a for s). Doubled letters are numbers (12 tt, 13 ss, 16 nn). Nulls are of three kinds: syllables written as separate groups (Dam, Dim, Dem, Dom, Dum, Dar, Der, about 64 times in this copy), loose letters (b, d, n, z), and whole Latin words (cum, etiam, idcirco, atque, porro). The last make the reading treacherous, because cum and etiam also occur as real words, spelt in signs or not. A short repertory of code syllables covers the principals: Bi for the King of France, Ras for the Sultan, Ab for the French and Mes, probably for His Majesty, Malvezzi’s master. The key is the alphabet filed on DECODE with Ferdinand’s letter (R367, Hadtörténelmi Levéltár 1548/3) and its second copy (R386, Széchényi Library, Quart. Lat. 2254). Brice Dudout calibrated it on another enciphered copy in the same Vienna series, Türkei I 7-3-20 f. 44, whose decipherment made at the time is on f. 45, and froze the result as K-C01 before opening 7-2-18 ( key_KC01.json , with its SHA-256 fingerprint). Several sign shapes run close together, and a few signs carry two values that the Latin settles (n or o, g or s, e or u); the family of 8-like signs is told apart by its foot. Values added during the reading are justified in the reading notes; K-C01 itself was not changed.

Serenissime princeps et frater carissime, significamus qualiter istum nobilem et nobis sincere dilectum {credencerium} nomine Duson ipsum misimus cum literis nostris ad curiam ‹…›, {ut} {quam} primum accedat ad eius curiam simul cum oratore nostro Gabriele de Ramon ‹…› circa negotia magna que ore dicenda sunt; indubitatam fidem {prestare} debeat tanquam praesentialiter affuissem. Most serene and most invincible Emperor of the Ottomans, lord, lord Sultan Suleiman, my dearest brother, greeting, the feeling of affection, all good fortune and continual increase of felicity. Most serene prince and dearest brother, we let you know that this nobleman, sincerely dear to us, our pantler named Duson, we have sent with our letters to [your] court ‹…›, that he may go as soon as possible to his court with our ambassador Gabriel de Ramon ‹…› on great matters that must be told by word of mouth; [Your Highness] is to give him undoubted faith, as if I were present in person. Ribier printed the French credence in 1666. It opens “Très-Haut, Très-Excellent … Soltan Soliman Sach” and names the bearer as the king’s beloved and loyal ordinary pantler, the sieur d’Huyson. The Latin opens “Serenissime Ottomanorum Imperator … mi frater carissime”: it does not translate that French, and comes back from the Turkish text actually delivered at the Porte.
huyson1547.html#truce

The long letter, 143r l. 31 to 145v l. 15, about 1,100 words of Latin, is the case Henry II makes against the Habsburg truce. Its argument, in the order of the text: The two truces. Francis I had obtained a one-year truce for Charles V and Ferdinand. Then, without his knowledge, their envoys came back and made a five-year peace; they came, the King says, to deceive the Sultan. When the Emperor sent envoys to ratify it, he wrote Henry literas lusorias et ridicolas , and the French ambassador at the Emperor’s court obtained a copy of the letters of the peace ab ipsis cancellariis regis Ispanie , which d’Huyson now carries to the Porte. No oath, and Crépy at the end. The Emperor did not swear, as emperors and kings do. At the end of the ratification he slipped in the articles of the peace of Crépy (1544): the marriage of Henry’s brother Charles of Orléans to a daughter or niece of the Emperor with Milan as dowry, and France’s restitution of places taken in the wars. Charles of Orléans died in 1545 and Francis I in March 1547, so these promises have lapsed; the Emperor counted on the Porte having no interpreters able to explain them. The Sultan should not let them into the ratification. The proper form. Had the Emperor meant the peace, he would have sent princes and great lords to confirm it, as he did when he made peace with the King of England. The allies. The ratification should say that Henry, with his friends and confederates, stays in the peace, each keeping what he holds. The Swiss above all, michi iam multis annis confederati , raise armies for him; if the Emperor subdued them, France would be greatly weakened. If he will not confirm the article, the Sultan should not hold the peace as firm. Hungary. The Emperor’s envoys promised thirty thousand florins for some castles and places of the kingdom of Hungary; had the Sultan held them and asked a hundred thousand, they would have paid it, since with those places they can recover the whole kingdom. Enemies are to be kept weak on every side. The French instructions that Ribier prints ask for the inclusion of “the thirteen cantons of the Swiss leagues and the two of the Grey League”. The Latin develops the Swiss argument and does not name the Grey League; the group between populi and Suiceri is unresolved. The oath, the Crépy articles at the end of the ratification, the comparison with the English peace and the thirty thousand florins are not in the printed French.
huyson1547.html#captain

Malvezzi’s second heading introduces lo spaccio quale ha portato un certo capitano {Bar[t]olamio} doppo Dussun , the dispatch carried by a Captain Bartolomeo after d’Huyson. In it Henry II tells the Sultan that the King of Spain is uir multa sciens, attamen deceptor ; that he, his brother and the princes of Germany have held a great council in ciuitate Augusta , the Diet of Augsburg (September 1547 to June 1548), and are ready day and night for war. He asks the Sultan to keep his fleet ready at sea and to send it to his help if needed, promises the French fleet if the Spaniards raid Barbary, and confirms dominus de Ramon , Gabriel d’Aramon, as his ambassador. This third letter is not printed by Ribier as a letter to the Sultan. The signs of the captain’s name give b-a-r-e-o l-a-m-i-o. Reading the fourth sign, very close in shape, as t (its value elsewhere on the page) gives Bartolamio , a Venetian form of Bartolomeo. A Captain Bartholomeo reached Venice with d’Huyson in March 1548, according to the ambassador Morvilliers in the letters printed by Charrière, and d’Aramon was expecting a “capitaine Barthélemy” at the Sultan’s camp.
huyson1547.html#method

Starting key. Malvezzi’s alphabet from DECODE R367/R386, as used on this site for Ferdinand’s letter of 23 January 1548. Calibration. Fitted on the first lines of Türkei I 7-3-20 f. 44, another enciphered copy in the series, against its decipherment of the time on f. 45 (for instance an 8 stacked on a stem for e, and υ for l), then frozen as K-C01 before any reading of 7-2-18. Held-out test. On an unglossed copy of an enciphered letter of 1550 (Türkei I 8-3-8), the decoding was frozen before its contemporary decipherment was opened: 92.5% of letters agree with it (84.3% mechanically from the key alone), against 20% on average and 31% at most for permuted keys. Hand. An atlas of the copyist’s letter forms was drawn up; the show-through on 145v was subtracted digitally for reading. Transcription and reading. All 207 lines were transcribed sign by sign on the archive’s native images in four passes, with no known text, and every group was counted as sure, probable or unresolved. Review. Brice Dudout looked again, without the decryption, at 20 doubtful signs shown as shapes: 19 confirmed, one re-examined. Ribier and Charrière were used to identify the people and check the sense, never to fix a value. By section, Brice Dudout’s counts: 143r ll. 1–17, 94%; 143r l. 18 to 143v l. 16, about 94%; 143v ll. 17–32, 97.5%; 144r, 98.8%; 144v, 98.6%; 145r, 99.6%; 145v ll. 1–27, 97.4%; 145v ll. 28–30 and 146r, about 95–97% (the last four estimated line by line, the others counted group by group). The 1,146 groups of the final two passes read at 98.1%; the whole copy, about 1,550 groups, at about 97.5%. Read as sentences against the translation on this site, the Latin and the Italian hold together throughout: the holes are scattered, the longest run of them three groups after ne deceptione (143v l. 30).
huyson1547.html#prior

The archive’s catalogue records the item as not deciphered, and no earlier decipherment of this Latin text was found. The content of the letter of credence and of d’Huyson’s instructions has been known in French since 1666: Guillaume Ribier, Lettres et mémoires d’estat , prints the credence and the instruction, and Charrière’s Négociations de la France dans le Levant , vol. II, summarises them and prints the letters on d’Huyson’s journey. What the cipher adds is the Latin delivered at the Porte, Malvezzi’s notes and the third letter. Malvezzi’s correspondence is edited in Austro-Turcica 1541–1552 (Munich 1995), which was not consulted.

Henry II to Suleiman (credence for d'Huyson and two other letters), Malvezzi's enciphered copy, HHStA Türkei I 7-2-18 In the autumn of 1547 Henry II, king for six months, sent his pantler, the sieur d’Huyson, to Constantinople with a letter of credence for Suleiman and instructions: join the truce that Charles V and Ferdinand had just made with the Porte, but have the king’s allies — the Swiss first — included in it, and expose imperial bad faith. Ferdinand’s resident in Constantinople, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, got hold of the text, translated it back “from Turkish into Latin, word for word” and sent it to Vienna in cipher, together with a second, longer letter and a third, carried by a captain, about the Diet of Augsburg and asking for the Ottoman fleet. No earlier decipherment of the cipher is known; the archive's catalogue marks it not deciphered. Most serene prince and dearest brother, we let you know that this nobleman, sincerely dear to us, our pantler named Duson, we have sent with our letters to [your] court ‹…›, that he may go as soon as possible to his court with our ambassador Gabriel de Ramon ‹…› on great matters that must be told by word of mouth; [Your Highness] is to give him undoubted faith, as if I were present in person. These matters, Most Serene, will also profit us greatly afterwards; take care to fare well and to live long and happily; and, {in its place}, Henry, King of France. ## h3 (143r l. 18–30) Your Majesty must be warned that these Frenchmen do not present the king’s letters to the Porte in the form in which the Most Christian writes them, but have them translated into the Turkish language and script, adding and removing whatever they like, and moreover without putting the date, neither where nor when; and they do this as a precaution, so as to be able to deny it: these are diabolical expedients ‹…› for the future. So I render these writings from Turkish into Latin, word for word, like the one above and the ones below. The first below is his dispatch; Dusson carried it, namely: ## h4 (143r l. 31 – 145v l. 15) First we let you know that the most serene king my father, deceased, long ago sent his ambassador [to your court] together with the ambassador of the King of Spain and of King Ferdinand his brother, and asked, for the sake of the ancient friendship, [that] a quiet peace [be made] with those princes; and at his prayers a truce was made for one year; and he did so because of the singular friendship long kept with the most serene king my deceased father. Last year the same King of Spain, with Ferdinand his brother, again sent ambassadors to conclude a peace of some years, without the knowledge of my late father: let [Your Highness] know that they did not come sincerely to make peace but rather to deceive [Your] imperial Majesty; that is why they would not inform my father of what was being negotiated [with the Porte]; and I have learnt that these ambassadors made a peace of five years, and not ‹…›, after which they went back to the court of the King of Spain and of Ferdinand with letters of confirmation of this peace or truce made with [Your] imperial [Majesty] — a matter negotiated at the time of the death of the King of France my father. And when the Emperor again sent ambassadors to ratify the peace, he then wrote me deceitful and ridiculous letters; and {now} my ambassador at the court of the King of Spain has acted so cautiously that he has obtained a copy of the letters of the peace concluded, in which I clearly saw that they {mean} to deceive. Therefore I have sent our pantler with the copies of the letters of the confirmed peace, so that [Your Highness] may know the truth; I sent him for this, and faith is to be given him as if I were present in person, lest by the deceit ‹…› [Your Highness] remain deceived; for in them I have seen fraud and guile, to the great harm and prejudice of your {empire} and of my kingdom. From this I saw the fraud: in these letters he did not swear, as is the custom of emperors and kings. Moreover, all that was negotiated with my father I shall also observe in these pacts ‹…›, in this promise and covenant to be kept; but what my father promised I cannot ‹…›, for my father is dead and his promise has lapsed. We therefore let you know that the promise made to my deceased brother [was] to marry [the Emperor’s] daughter, with the State of Milan and some other places as dowry; and conversely the king my father promised the King of Spain to restore certain provinces long occupied by the French, taken by them in the wars; but then my brother died, and afterwards my father exchanged life for death; and so what had been promised has vanished. That is why he wrote these articles at the end of the confirmation of his letters, thinking that [the Porte] would have no interpreters able to explain them; and then the King of Spain, as soon as he has received the letters of confirmation of the peace made {by his ambassadors}, intends to take those [French] provinces on the strength of the promise made. Another point: had the King of Spain wished to remain amicably in this peace, he ought to have sent princes and noblemen to confirm it, as he did when he made peace with the King of England; let [Your Highness] know that, by custom, the King of Spain and Ferdinand his brother ought to have sent men great and capable enough to promise and ‹…› ‹…› until the term of the promise was fulfilled. I also inform you that my ambassador at the court of the King of Spain then, with remarkable diligence and skill, obtained a copy of those letters from the very chanceries of the King of Spain, and sent them to me at once; from them I saw that the King of Spain, with his brother Ferdinand, means to deceive. As soon as these copies reached my hands I sent them in all haste to [your] court by my pantler Dusson, so that [Your Highness] may know their wickedness and how they wish to deceive [Her], together with Her friends and confederates; and I hope [Your Highness] will not let Herself be deceived once She has understood their schemes, laid for Her ruin. And if [Your Highness] will accept these letters of the promise made, and if he will again give such letters of confirmation of the peace upon them, I ask that [Your Highness] should not accept the article promised by my father, since my father is dead; but an article of this kind must be written into the letters of confirmation: that King Henry, our faithful friend, with his friends and confederates, remain in this peace already concluded with Our Majesty, on the ‹…› condition that each remain firm and peacefully possess what is at present in his hands; and that the King of Spain and his brother must likewise be told that if they wish to remain at peace until the promised term, without fraud, he must accept me, King of France, as friend and confederate, with my friends and confederates. I let you know that there are certain provinces in Germany, of the people ‹…› of the Swiss, who have been my confederates for many years; they have many men fit for war, and whenever I need it I quickly raise an army from them; they give me the greatest help. If he does not have the King of Spain confirm [the inclusion of] these with my confederates and friends, the King of Spain will make war on these Swiss, my confederates; and let [Your Highness] know that if that king should happen to defeat and subjugate those Swiss peoples, I should afterwards be greatly weakened by their oppression. I therefore ask Her to have this article confirmed, namely that of the confederates and friends of the King of France; and if the King of Spain will not confirm it, that She not consent to hold this peace as firm, ratified or agreeable. Likewise, that the King of Spain neither dare nor presume to ask me to restore what my father acquired in war, wherever it may be. Again I inform you that when [Your Highness] had in hand the ambassadors of the King of Spain and of Ferdinand, they promised thirty thousand florins for some castles or places of the kingdom of Hungary, and asked Your Majesty’s court for letters of confirmation of the peace; had She then not accepted this deceitful bargain of thirty thousand and asked for a hundred thousand florins, not letting the ambassadors leave, they would then have promised and paid a hundred thousand, for with those places they can {recover} the whole kingdom of Hungary. Let Her know also that there is no need to give such enemies help or favour; on the contrary ‹…› with ‹…›; it must always be ensured that they remain weak on all sides; if She makes peace and gives them part of the kingdom of Hungary, they will grow stronger every day and their enemies {will become} weak. I have informed you of everything, and I shall always let you know what news I have, because of the singular friendship long kept with my father, which I hope to keep perpetual. Again and again I ask you to see to it that the King of Spain observe the peace {according to} the articles written, for they do not keep their word; it must be well considered. ‹…› ## h5 (145v l. 16–18) What follows is the dispatch carried by a certain Captain {Bartolomeo}, after Dusson, from the ‹…›, namely: ## h6 (145v l. 18 – 146r l. 19) Most serene Emperor of the Ottomans, lord Sultan Suleiman, my dearest brother, greeting, the feeling of affection, all good fortune and increase of felicity. ilten1697.html#the-catalogue

The project’s scan of 23 September 2026 listed six items in the Ilten papers at the GWLB as “not deciphered”. The Kalliope records say the opposite. The four letters of 1697–1706 (this one, and three of 1705–06 in another code) are each noted Dechiffrierter Brief , a deciphered letter, and the two of 1743 Teilweise dechiffrierter Brief . The scan also said the images were not online. They are: the GWLB’s Kitodo library has the Receuil de Lettres a Jobst Hermann d’Ilten , parts I–IV, VII and VIII, in public-domain colour scans. Its search form has to be submitted as a POST with the page’s own token, and a plain search URL returns nothing, which is probably why the scan missed them. The two 1743 letters, to Johann Georg von Ilten, turned out to be something else: one of them carries no decipherment, and none was found elsewhere in the papers. They have their own write-up .

Code A (1697, groups up to about 505): a small syllabary. Examples are 445.71 ses , 124.73 affaires , 331.107.484 mettre , 75.256.505 Barfus and 500.505 vous . It has homophones ( et is 237 or 238) and a null, 62, which opens la discorde and de l’un des and closes aisée . Code B (1705–06, groups up to 1010), used by Heusch, Hattorf and the Elector for the later letters, is a different code: Letters to Ilten, 1705–1706 (a different cipher, with its own page).

French. No holes. ## Translation Hanover, this 7th of Nov. 1697. Monsieur, His Electoral Highness, in signing the despatch which will be delivered to you by this post, told me that a thought had come to him of which I was to inform you, namely that it would be advantageous to his affairs if discord could be sown between Colbe and Barfus, and the friendship of one of the two won. His Electoral Highness is willing to believe that you could do this by means of the wife of the former, with whom he has been told you stand extremely well. The project’s scan of 23 September 2026 listed the Ilten letters at the GWLB as “not deciphered”. Kalliope notes each of them Dechiffrierter Brief , a deciphered letter, and the images are in the GWLB’s Kitodo library ( Receuil de Lettres a Jobst Hermann d’Ilten , part VII); how they were found is told on the page of the 1697 letter. That letter, Hattorf to Ilten of 7 November 1697, is in an earlier and smaller code: Hattorf to Ilten, 1697 (a different cipher, with its own page). The two letters of 1743 to Johann Georg von Ilten are in a later code, on their own page . Kalliope gives “Herzog Georg Wilhelm” as the sender of the letter of 25 May 1706. The letter is signed Georg Ludwig Churfürst and countersigned by Hattorf, and Kalliope’s own creator field names Georg I.

The same group keeps its meaning across languages: 977 is Roy de Prusse and König in Preußen , 988 Gr. Chambellan and Ober-Cammerherr , and 609 Princesse and Princessin . 665 is Roy or König , 476 mariage and 224 de , and 405.709.543 spells in-si-nu- in insinuer , n’insinuiés and insinuationes . Heusch to Ilten, Berlin, 10 October 1705 The chamberlain Count Wartensleben, back from Hanover, had Heusch told, par Monsr. de Berlips “pour mieux cacher nostre commerce ”, that he had set out the Elector’s good intentions to the King. He had also spoken well of Madame la Princesse, fille de S.A.El. , without touching on le point de Mariage . He had raised it with the Grand Chamberlain instead, ce Ministre , who was committed de parole to another match but might be won over. Neither Madame de Bulow nor Mademoiselle de Pelnitz must appear to have a hand in it, and it can succeed only par le Canal du Gr. Chambellan . Hattorf to Ilten, Hanover, 31 January 1706 Ilten’s two letters reached the Elector en ses mains propres , seen by no one but Hattorf. When the mariage is raised with him again in Berlin, Ilten is to let it be understood que vous n’en estes pas instruit , since it is not la coutume d’offrir aussi bientost les Princesses de cette maison . There is a clear postscript on Goertz’s rheumatism, Eltz’s mission to Mainz and Trier, the Lübeck see, and the fear that Charles XII might march out of Poland. The Elector to Ilten, Hanover, 25 May 1706 Georg Ludwig to Ilten, 25 May 1706, f. 329r: code B carrying German, glossed in Kurrent. The first code line reads “der König in Preußen würde sich selbst persöhnlich”. Image: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek Hannover, Ms XXIII 1245:7 f. 329r, via the GWLB digital library (public domain). …daß ihr Ursache zu glauben zu haben vermeinet, der König in Preußen würde sich selbst persöhnlich umb die Princessin unsere Tochter für den Cron Printzen in Preußen ansprechen wollen, in maßen der Ober-Cammerherr euch zu erkennen gegeben … Wann ihr nun mit guter maniere abwenden könnet, daß solche persöhnliche anwerbung unterbliebe, so wird es Uns sehr lieb seyn… The Elector expects the King to come in person to ask for his daughter’s hand. Ilten is to prevent the visit discreetly, “bloss als für euch”, by insinuations to the Ober-Cammerherr alone. Sophia Dorothea married the Crown Prince Frederick William on 28 November 1706.

French. Same hole: `[?]` a run left without a gloss. ## Translation Monsieur. The 10th of October 1705. The Chamberlain, Monsieur the Count of Wartensleben, cannot praise enough the courtesies and honours he received at Hanover; he is confused by the fine present that was added there, and which he did not expect. He has had it intimated to me by Monsieur de Berlips, the better to hide our dealings, that, having had occasion to make known to the King the uprightness of His Electoral Highness's sentiments, he had put His Majesty into rather favourable dispositions; that he had also done justice to [?] Madame the Princess, daughter of His Electoral Highness, speaking very advantageously of her, without however touching on the point of marriage; but that he had nevertheless spoken of it to the Grand Chamberlain, making him understand the particular interest he had in favouring the marriage of the Crown Prince with the said Princess; that, although this Minister was pledged by his word to another quarter, he hoped nevertheless to win him over in such a way that the aforesaid affair could in time be put on the table with hope of success, and that then your expedient could be sent here to work on it; that it was still necessary to temporise a little and to show the King of Prussia every possible complaisance, and above all to avoid its appearing that either Madame de Bülow or Mademoiselle de Pöllnitz have a hand in the affair. I gave assurance that people were much mistaken to believe that these ladies were employed in an affair of such consequence, since one was only too persuaded that it could succeed only through the channel of the Grand Chamberlain. The said Count will continue to have me warned secretly of what passes on the subject in question, so that measures can be taken accordingly. Your Excellency will be pleased to give an account of this, judging yourself how necessary it is that everything be carefully handled. For the rest I refer to my report, and am always, with the same zeal and respect, Monsieur, Your Excellency's very humble and very obedient servant, Heusch. Berlin, this 10th of October 1705. Monsieur, the two letters you wrote to His Electoral Highness for his own hands were duly delivered to him without anyone having seen them except me. I have been charged to ask in this regard that, when you are spoken to again of the marriage where you are, you will do well, Monsieur, to give it to be understood that you are not instructed about it, and that, as far as you can [?] judge, it was not the custom to offer the Princesses of this house so soon. His Electoral Highness does not doubt, Monsieur, that you will intimate this with good grace, and in such a manner that no one [?] is shocked by it [?]. Besides, one [?] greatly wishes here for a happy success of this affair, of which in that case you will have very great merit. Since the rheumatism of Monsieur the Baron von Goertz has not yet ceased, Monsieur the Baron von Eltz has orders to go in his place to the courts of Mainz and Trier, intending to leave as soon as Monsieur the Count of Schönborn, Grand Huntsman of the Elector of Mainz, has arrived here; he is expected at any moment. The reunion of the House is concluded and ratified. The affair of the bishopric of Lübeck seems to be growing sour. If the King of Sweden comes out of Poland to come to the help of the Administrator of Holstein, the circles of Saxony and all Germany will be set ablaze. Which God forbid. I am, with all imaginable zeal, Monsieur, your very humble and very obedient servant, Hattorf. Our gracious greeting first, noble, steadfast councillor, and dear faithful subject! We have learned from your report in your own hand of the 22nd of this month that you think you have reason to believe that the King in Prussia would himself in person ask for the Princess our daughter for the Crown Prince in Prussia, inasmuch as the Grand Chamberlain gave you to understand that the King desired to see you. Now, if you can with good manner avert it, so that such a personal suit does not take place, it will be very welcome to Us, and you would also try your best in it, yet merely as on your own account, and perhaps through intimations to the Grand Chamberlain, inasmuch as you [are] towards no one else, or [?with] him either, to let anything of it be noticed. We remain graciously disposed towards you. Hanover, the 25th of May in the year 1706. Georg Ludwig, Elector. J. Hattorf

Eleven cipher lines in a despatch of Jean de Langeac, bishop of Avranches, ambassador at Venice, to Anne de Montmorency (BnF fr. 3083 no. 8). George Lasry recovered the key, “Avranches’ cipher 1”, in 2023 and deciphered the letter then, unpublished; his table was applied here and refined. All but about six signs are deciphered: Saint-Pol wants leave to quit the army in Lombardy, and the Signoria refuses.
