A clear despatch with an eleven-line cipher block. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3083 no. 8, ff. 20–21 (Gallica btv1b90601328, views 35–36). One of the four letters of catalogue item 6. The cipher Lasry’s “Avranches’ cipher 1”: a simple substitution on graphic signs with a few homophones and signs for LL, SS and LE. How it was deciphered Lasry’s 2023 table, which Tomokiyo had partly reconstructed from the sibling fr. 3005 f. 107, applied to the leaf by eye from line strips, with four refinements. What it says Saint-Pol asked Langeac to obtain his leave from the Signoria; Venice refused and protested it would be “la totalle ruine des emprinses”. Still open A group of three or four signs and one of two signs. Credit George Lasry recovered the key and deciphered the letter in 2023; his decipherment was not published.
langeac1529.html#documents

The catalogue grouped this letter with three others to Montmorency (catalogue item 6). Each of the four is in its own key, and since 14 October 2026 each key has its own page: Gramont at Rome in 1529 ( Gramont’s cipher, 1529 ), Gramont again in 1530 ( Gramont’s cipher, 1530 ) and the cardinal de Mâcon in 1537, with his other letters in Mascon’s cipher . Each is a different cipher, with its own page. The key here is George Lasry’s “Avranches’ cipher 1”, one of his tables dated 5 November 2023 on Satoshi Tomokiyo’s cryptiana; Tomokiyo had a partial table of the same key from the sibling letter fr. 3005 f. 107. Lasry also deciphered this letter in 2023 (personal communication, 21 September 2026), but neither site gives any plaintext. The leaf refines the table: a y-shaped sign with a zigzag descender is C; a 9 with a long curved tail is A in raison and V in secourir ; a ɓ-shaped sign serves for P and for I; ₠ is LL and a crossed C is SS; 8∞ is LE, distinct from 8o = P; and a macron over ∞ stands for n ( argēt ).

Fr. 3083 f. 21r. Above the cipher, in clear, is the news that Aquila has been taken “par le conte de Montore et Camille Pardo”. The block opens with two nulls and MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3083 f. 21r, via Gallica btv1b90601328 view 36. Cipher in capitals, clear in lower case, spelling of the leaf kept MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL M’A CONMANDE RECHER[CHER] SON CONGE A CESTE SEIGNEVRIE, CE QV’ELLE N’A VOLV CONSENTIR, AINS A PROTESTE QVE S’IL SE DEPARTOIT QVE CE SEROIT LA TOTALLE RVINE DES EMPRINSES. ET ME SEMBLE QV’IL N’I A RAISON, VEV L’EMPRINSE DE MILLAN, LA VENVE DES ESPAIGNOLS AVEC ARGĒT POVR ICELLE SECOVRIR, ET LA PRIMEVERE APROCHER. IE CROY QV’IL NE DEPARTIRA SI LE FAICT […] sans LE CONSENTEMENT DE TOVS LES CONFEDERES, ET SI APORTEROIT […] VNG PREIVDICE IREPARABLE. Je luy ay escript AV MIEVLX QV’IL M’A ESTE POSSIBLE pour LE DIVERTIR DE CESTE OPINION, QVI EST PAR TROP DANGEREVSE. In modern terms: Saint-Pol has told Langeac to ask the Signoria for his leave. Venice would not consent, and protested that if he left it would be the ruin of the enterprises. Langeac sees no reason for it, with the Milan enterprise in hand, Spanish money coming to relieve Milan and spring approaching, and has written to him as well as he could to turn him from an opinion “par trop dangereuse”. The comte de Saint-Pol commanded the French army in Lombardy from the autumn of 1528 until his defeat at Landriano on 21 June 1529. So five months before Landriano the commander wanted to leave. Venice, the league’s paymaster in the north, refused his leave on the ground that the Milan enterprise was in hand. The year is not on the leaf, but it is fixed by Saint-Pol’s command and by the clear news that Aquila had been retaken for the French by the count of Montorio and Camillo Pardo Orsini in the Abruzzi campaign of winter 1528–29.

BnF fr. 3083 no. 8, ff. 20-21, Venice, 14 Jan [1529] Langeac, bishop of Avranches and ambassador at Venice, reports that Saint-Pol, commanding the French army in Lombardy, asked leave of the Seigneurie, which refused and protested it would be the total ruin of the enterprises; Langeac sees no reason for him to go, given the Milan enterprise, the Spaniards coming with money and the approach of spring, and has written to dissuade him (January 1529, before Landriano). Decryption fr3083_no8_langeac.md # BnF fr. 3083 no. 8, f. 20-21 — Jean de Langeac, bishop of Avranches, Venice, to Montmorency, 14 January [1529] Image: Gallica btv1b90601328, canvas 36 (= f. 21r). The cipher block is 11 lines after the clear news of the taking of Aquila "par le conte de Montore et Camille Pardo" and the request for help "pour suyvre la victoire". Key: "Avranches' cipher 1" (Lasry, table dated 05/11/2023, cryptiana GL.htm; Tomokiyo's partial table `img/francisAvranches1.png` from fr. 3005 f. 107). Simple substitution with a few homophones. Readings here refine the table: * y-shaped sign with a zigzag descender = C (Lasry's C); ɤ (loop-bottomed gamma) = S, as in Lasry's second S. * 9-shaped sign with a long curved tail = A (Lasry's second A) in RAISON, DEPARTIRA; = V in SECOVRIR, VENVE (Lasry's second V). The two are very close on this leaf; context decides. * ɓ-shaped sign = P (APROCHER, APORTEROIT, OPINION), I (MILLAN, IREPARABLE), N? (CONSENTEMENT). Lasry lists it under I and P. * ₠ = LL (ALLER, MILLAN, ICELLE, QV'ELLE); crossed C = SS (POSSIBLE). * 8∞ = LE (L + E), distinct from 8o = P. * Macron over ∞ = en (ARGĒT). ## Reading (cipher in capitals; clear text in lower case) [clear] … et pour suyvre la victoire. MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL M'A CONMANDE RECHER[CHER] SON CONGE A CESTE SEIGNEVRIE, CE QV'ELLE N'A VOLV CONSENTIR, AINS A PROTESTE QVE S'IL SE DEPARTOIT QVE CE SEROIT LA TOTALLE RVIN[E] DES [EN]EMPRINSES. ET ME SEMBLE QV'IL N'I A RAISON, VEV L'EMPRINSE DE MILLAN, LA VENVE DES ESPAIGNOLS AVEC ARGĒT POVR ICELLE SECOVRIR, ET LA PRIMEVERE APROCHER. IE CROY QV'IL NE DEPARTIRA SI LE FAICT [3-4 signs unread] sans LE CONSENTEMENT DE TOVS LES CONFEDERES, ET SI APORTEROIT [E + crossed sign] VNG PREIVDICE IREPARABLE. [clear] Je luy ay [dict et?] escript AV MIEVLX QV'IL M'A ESTE POSSIBLE pour LE DIVERTIR DE CESTE OPINION, QVI EST PAR TROP DANGEREVSE. [clear] Monseigneur, il vous plaira m'avoir en vostre bonne grace et souvenance, a laquelle tres humblement me recommande. Escript [à Venise] le xiiii^me de janvier. ## In modern French Monseigneur de Saint-Pol m'a chargé de demander pour lui congé à la Seigneurie [de Venise]. Elle n'a pas voulu y consentir, et a protesté que s'il se retirait ce serait la ruine totale des entreprises. Il me semble qu'il n'y a pas de raison [de partir], vu l'entreprise de Milan, la venue des Espagnols avec de l'argent pour secourir [Milan] et l'approche du printemps. Je crois qu'il ne partira pas si la chose [ne se fait] pas sans le consentement de tous les confédérés, et cela porterait un préjudice irréparable. Je lui ai écrit du mieux que j'ai pu pour le détourner de cette opinion, qui est par trop dangereuse. ## Date and context No year on the leaf. Saint-Pol commanded the French army in Lombardy from autumn 1528 to his defeat at Landriano (21 June 1529); Aquila was retaken for the French by the Count of Montorio and Camillo Pardo Orsini in the Abruzzi campaign of winter 1528-29; Langeac (bishop of Avranches) was ambassador at Venice. So **14 January 1529**. The cipher shows Saint-Pol already wanting to leave Italy in January, and Venice (and Langeac) holding him there for the Milan enterprise that ended at Landriano. Unread: a group of 3-4 signs before "sans" in line 7, and 2 signs before VNG in line 9. loeschnen1816.html#the-document

The eleven openings contain one continuous memorandum in a single clerical hand. After the heading, each paragraph cites a place in the instruction it amends: "Seite 2, Spalte 2, Zeile 3 von Unten", "Seite 9, Spalte 2, Zeile 5", "Seite 10, Spalte 2", "Seite 23, nach der Zahl 1918", "Seite 32", "Seite 33, Linie 2 von Unten". It closes with an appendix, Beilage: Ueber den Gebrauch der Doppel- (Supplementar-) Zahlen . The last page carries the date and the signature, W. Loeschner . DECODE's "Loeschnen?" misreads the final letter. Among the topics: the misleading name "Ziffernkabinett", which the author wants dropped from an instruction meant for Austria's diplomats; entering new words in the Déchiffrant (the deciphering half of the key) as well as the Chiffrant. The author cites a despatch of Prince Kaunitz that added supplements 16–17 to a key; the range of numbers from 3 to 6000, and the supplementary figures ( Ergänzungszahlen ); how to cipher proper names, the envelope of a ciphered despatch, and the Parenthesis and Claudatur signs.
loeschnen1816.html#why-there-is-nothing-to-decipher

The figures occur only inside examples. On opening 9 the plaintext le Roi d'Espagne vient de nommer (Parenthesis) M. le Duc de San Carlos (Claudatur) son Amb.r &c is written directly above its code groups, 388 1949 600 477 2395 1800 983 1440 692 1369 267 2506 1801 1949 335 1954 709 1212 958 477 1211 307 2415, with ⊖ marks for the word divisions. Opening 5 has a short table of the same kind (A, B and syllables against four-digit numbers). Opening 3 shows syllable splits such as "Com-pa-ra-tion". Every one of these examples comes with its plaintext. The memorandum describes a key but does not contain one, and it hides no message.
loeschnen1816.html#what-stays-open

Nothing on the cipher side. The memorandum was not transcribed in full. It is a useful source for Austrian cipher-office practice around 1816, and the numeric examples could be checked against the Staatskanzlei keys of that period on DECODE. For DECODE, the queued correction asks for the author to be changed to W. Loeschner, the record to be described as an instruction memorandum, and its decryption status to be set to not applicable.

Michael Brackx corrected Tomokiyo’s key against the margin decipherment of f. 163r (97.6% on its first stretch): that stretch reads in part, f. 162r and the second stretch are decoded, not read, and four pages are still to come. consiste en la creance du porteur · 0 = e · 7 = a · no = que · th = de Niort → Henri III · homophonic letter cipher with word signs · 21 April 1586 · read with known key, partial Malicorne to Henri III, Niort, 21 April 1586 to Henri III Go to the full text ↓ The governor of Poitou reports failed plots on Lusignan and a raid on two Protestant companies; one margin-confirmed sentence reads, and the rest of the decode is still being built. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 · updated 27 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (4% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Michael Brackx (solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (4% of the cipher) The letter Jean de Chourses, sieur de Malicorne, governor of Poitou, to Henri III, “A Nyort ce xxie avril 1586”, signed Malycorne: six pages mostly in cipher. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15572 ff. 162–164 (Gallica views 169–173). Not in DECODE or the catalogue. The cipher Invented signs and digits, several for each letter, with signs for de, la, le, que, sur, nous, et and for doubled letters, and nulls. Thirteen look-alike signs still carry two values. How it was deciphered Michael Brackx applied Tomokiyo's key table, corrected it, and checked the decode against the decipherment written in the margin of f. 163r at the time. What it says The rest “consiste en la creance du porteur et lesdicts articles”; two plots on Lusignan were discovered; Villeluisant's men cut two companies to pieces near Sanxay. Still open f. 162r, the second stretch of f. 163r and the four later pages give phrases between gaps; no other letter in this key has a decipherment to check them against. Credit Transcription, corrected key and decode: Michael Brackx ( @brackxm ) with Claude Code, 22–23 October 2026 ( issue #92 ). Key table: Satoshi Tomokiyo, Cryptiana. The same volume holds Camus de Pontcarré's letters to Villeroy in another cipher ( Camus 1586 ) and Matignon's and Mayenne's despatches ( Mayenne–Forget ), each with its own page.

The decode builds phrases, not sentences (62% of words read as sense, 65 holes): the failed enterprises against Lusignan, “le sieur de Uilleluisant et ceulx que ie … enuoies”, an attack in the bourg of Sanxay a league from Lusignan on two companies, “les taill[e]rent en piesses, prinrent les … capitaines … et l[e]urs enseignes … les amenerent ici”, with no loss but “l'enseigne du capit[a]ine Cossart et trois [?soldats]”. Most holes are letter strings that are not French, which points to look-alike signs still merged under one label rather than to a wrong key.
malicorne1586.html#later

Brackx then sent aligned decodes and readings of the other four pages, with a legend tying each sign label to its shape. Measured on his readings: f. 162v 63% of words read as sense, view 171 67%, view 172 left 57%, view 172 right 79%. Fewer than 1% of the letters rest on a hand-chosen value. None of these pages has a decipherment in the margin, and sentences build only between holes: on f. 162v, [?Laval] a pris ung tel deplaisir et ennui de ce que ses deulx freres furent tues a Sainctes, et l'en est demeure mallade … et en est mort de samedi dernier ; on view 172 right, soldiers with intelligences with the enemy and the companies still to come; on view 171, ladders de [?bois] et de corde to surprise a town on an intelligence. He also checked the labels that seemed to merge two signs, on tiles cut from the full-size images after straightening each block. The barred £ is always m , but the looped ℒ stands for both b and m . The barred £ for m and n , the f with a bar, the hooked y and the crossed p ( h or s ) each turn out to be one sign with two values, so none of these can be settled by shape.

Key. Tomokiyo's table, corrected: the hooked y is s (14 of 14 tokens; his table's t is probably a slip), the curly y p, the looped ꝺ n, 10 i, ρ p and h, and new word signs for nous and et . Three per-page keys were merged and pruned one value at a time, from 43 to 13 two-valued signs. Against the margin. Stretch A 97.6% of the margin's letters matched in order, against 22–27% for shuffled keys; B lines 1–3 83.3%. For B lines 4–14 the first posted figure (72.8%) could not be reproduced; restated on the legible margin words against cipher rows 4–8 it is 79.3%, against 15–24%. Departures from the raw decode. Six readings were chosen by hand on two-valued signs ( Lusignan, ceulx, ici, Cossart, tramee, ce : 7 letters, under 1% of each page's letters) and three words of f. 163r B are taken from the margin where the decode is a letter or more off ( i'auois, charbonnieres, descouuertes ). manuel1910.html

Three telegrams King Manuel II sent his mother from Bussaco to the Pena palace on 2 and 8 August 1910, two months before the revolution: clear greetings (“Querida mãe … Tudo bem tempo lindo”) around 93 five-figure code items. The telegrams share four groups and an opening run after the same clear words, so they are one code with a stock phrase. Count Sabugosa’s code does not fit, and no decode or codebook has been found. Tudo bem tempo lindo · 36508 50178 37708 97183 39644 05 36508 06 Tudo bem Tempo lindo veio Sabugosa hoje · 4965 37708 89864 97183 39644 06 93608 Bussaco → Pena (Sintra) · five-figure code groups in a clear telegram · 2 and 8 August 1910 King Manuel II to Queen Amélie: three code telegrams from Bussaco, August 1910 from Manuel II of Portugal → to Amélie of Orléans Two months before the revolution the young King cabled his mother in code from Bussaco; the three telegrams are transcribed and share one code and an opening phrase, but no decode or codebook has been found. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription, identification) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The telegrams King Manuel II to his mother, Queen Amélie, at the Pena palace in Sintra: two telegrams of 2 August 1910 and one of 8 August, sent from Bussaco. Each opens and closes in clear (“Querida mãe … Tudo bem … Beijo mão Manuel”) with code groups between. Where Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Documentos de D. Carlos, D. Amélia e D. Manuel II , maço 13 (PT/TT/CAM/M13), images m0015–m0022, via DigitArq. Catalogue entry 408, which gave “1908–1910” and an unknown place. The cipher A code of five-figure groups, with short items “05” and “06” between them. The two long telegrams share four groups and open with a parallel run after the same clear words, so they use one code. How it was tried All three telegrams transcribed from the receiving forms and the item counts checked against the word count on each form. Repeats and shared groups listed, with a chance control. Count Sabugosa’s code of 1903–1910 was tested and does not fit. Why it resists No decode of these telegrams is in M13 and no codebook was found, so no group has a value to start from. Still open All 93 items. One decoded telegram in this code, perhaps in another CAM unit of Manuel II’s papers, would make the shared opening a crib. Credit Transcription, dating and the group analysis by WAINUT (contributed 27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents; the transcriptions were made with a vision-capable language model from the DigitArq images, and the first sheet of m0021 was transcribed a second time by another agent.
manuel1910.html#unit

Maço 13 of the papers of King Carlos, Queen Amélie and King Manuel II at the Torre do Tombo has 22 images on DigitArq. Only the three telegrams are in code: the letters and cards (m0001–m0014) are in clear. One of them, m0001–m0002, is a pencil text in telegram style signed Manuel (“Confidencialíssimo. Realisou-se hoje jantar no Paço offerecido Rainha Viuva …”), which may be the decode of a London telegram of May 1910. Its coded form is not in M13, and it does not match these three telegrams.
manuel1910.html#telegrams

All three are receiving forms (Modelo 72) of the telegraph office of the Real Paço da Pena, stamped 2 AGO 10 and 8 AGO 10, with the groups written out by hand by the receiving clerk. The telegram of 8 August 1910, sheet 1: “Querida Mãe. Recebi sua carta Tudo bem tempo lindo”, then 36508 50178 37708 97183 / 39644 05 36508 06 … . The receiver dashed each group. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M13, image m0015, via DigitArq. images route and date items clear words m0019 Bussaco → Pena, 2 Aug 1910, no. 62 3 groups “Resposta A 22/2” (reading uncertain) m0021 + m0022 Bussaco → Pena, 2 Aug 1910, no. 55, “urgente” 54 (49 groups, five “06”) “Querida mãe Tudo bem Tempo lindo veio Sabugosa hoje” … “Beijo mão Manoel” m0015 + m0017 Bussaco → Pena (Cintra), 8 Aug 1910 36 (31 groups, one “05”, four “06”) “Querida Mãe. Recebi sua carta Tudo bem tempo lindo” … “Beijo mão Manuel” In English the clear words say “Dear Mother, all well, lovely weather, Sabugosa came today … I kiss your hand, Manuel” and “Dear Mother, I received your letter, all well, lovely weather … I kiss your hand, Manuel”. On both long telegrams the word count on the form (72 and 54) equals the code items plus the clear and address words, which checks the number of items. The telegram no. 55 of 2 August 1910, sheet 1: “Querida mãe Tudo bem Tempo lindo veio Sabugosa hoje”, then 4965 37708 89864 / 47183 39644 06 93608 … . At Pena the receiver struck each group through its third figure and wrote a small 9 over the 4 of 47183 , correcting it to 97183 . Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, PT/TT/CAM/M13, image m0021, via DigitArq. A first pass listed 15 groups of m0021 starting at 37708 . The sheet has two more groups before it, the group read 37644 is 39644 (as in m0015 and m0022), and the telegram goes on for 37 items on m0022, marked as sheet 2.
manuel1910.html#groups

One code. m0021–22 and m0015 share 37708 , 39644 , 93608 and 97183 . Two random telegrams of 36 and 54 groups drawn from 00000–99999 share two groups in about 1 trial in 10,000. A stock phrase. After the same clear words “Tudo bem tempo lindo” both open with a parallel run: 36508 50178 37708 97183 39644 05 36508 06 on 8 August, and 4965 37708 89864 97183 39644 06 93608 on 2 August (after “veio Sabugosa hoje”). Repeats. Within m0015: 36508 , 97183 and 93843 twice each. Within m0021–22: 39644 , 41877 and 71394 twice each. The short telegram. m0019 consists of the three groups of m0022 that are underlined in brown ( 57710 29134 70790 ). It is probably a service repetition of doubtful groups; that is an inference. Short items. “05” and “06” stand between groups, as “03” does in King Carlos’s telegrams of 1903.
manuel1910.html#tried

Known keys. Count Sabugosa’s alphabetical code of 1903–1910 (52 values known) does not fit: no group matches, as written or with the struck third figure dropped, and 7 of 79 groups would then fall beyond its last known value (veio, 9019 ). King Carlos’s 1903 code has no values to test. Clear pages. The clear openings and closings are transcribed; the letters of M13 hold no decode of these telegrams. Print. One web search found no printed decipherment. The days fit the King’s stay at Bussaco in August 1910, which was not checked against the literature. Key rebuilding. Not possible without one decoded telegram in the code.
manuel1910.html#uncertain

All 93 items of the three telegrams have no value: m0021–22, 54 items; m0015–17, 36 items; m0019, 3 groups. Doubtful figures, mostly under the receiver’s stroke: 4965 (read as four figures), 89864 , 47183 (corrected to 97183 by the receiver), 29773 , 09774 , 07124 , 65554 , 61538 , 20078 in no. 55, and 11784 in the telegram of 8 August. Telegrams m0015–17 and m0022 have had one reading only. The clear line of m0019, “Resposta A 22/2”, is an uncertain reading. What the receiver’s strokes through the third figure (m0021–22) and his dashes (m0015) mean is not known. What would finish it: a decode of any telegram in this code. The pencil text on m0001–m0002 and the telegram behind Sabugosa’s decode of 22 May 1910 may have coded forms in another CAM unit; either would be a crib.

Forty-two cipher signs in three runs sit inside the clear Catalan. Both printed Aragonese keys of the decade were obtained and tested, the queen’s and the king’s registers for 1421–39 were swept page by page on PARES, and a solver with a Catalan language model was run on the signs. No plaintext was obtained. The text is too short on its own, and none of the online sources that could hold more of this cipher contains any. Folio 59r (“LVIIII”) of reg. 3225 carries three items, all dated Valencia, 5 August 1435: a letter to the queen’s procurator at the Roman curia, one to the vice-chancellor and ambassador Jacme Pelegrí, and one to the king. Only the last contains cipher. By the numbering of the series, reg. 3225 is Secretorum locumtenentiae reginae Mariae 4, the queen’s secret register for late 1423 to early 1437. PARES has neither a description nor images of it; DECODE holds this one page, uploaded in February 2026. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r, the letter to the king: three runs of signs in the first four lines of the text, then the clear close, Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435 , and the subscription Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília . Image: Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r, via DECODE R10171. Working transcription of the clear text, with the runs in brackets: Molt alt e molt excellent Senyor. Apres humil recomendacio, a [gran?] instancia dels [run 1] los daquest Regne, veents la gran necessitat, he treballat que [run 2] es continuada daci a tots sants. E [run 3] / stat exseguit e complit tot quant per vostra senyoria es stat manat, segons per mossen Matheu Pujades … daco e dels altres fets ha avisada vostra excellencia, la qual me mane lo que li sia plasent, e la qual nostre Senyor exalte longament. Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435. — Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília, qui humilment se recomana en vostra gracia e merce. La Reyna. “Most high and excellent lord. After humble recommendation: at the [great] instance of [run 1] and those of this kingdom, seeing the great need, I have worked so that [run 2] is continued from now until All Saints. And [run 3] has been carried out and fulfilled, everything your lordship ordered, as mossèn Mateu Pujades has informed your excellency of this and the other matters.”
maria1435.html#signs

Transcribed sign by sign from 5× to 7× crops. The runs mix digit-like forms (2, 3, 6, 8, 9), letter-like forms (a, d, n, v, M, ȝ, a doubled f with a bar) and figures: a triangle, a square hook, a b in a bracket, a circle with a dot, a cross on a curved foot, two E-shapes. Three of them (the hook, the bracketed b and the dotted circle) are flanked by dots, the usual mark of a nomenclator word. The 8 comes in three forms: plain, with a stroke at the top right, and with a tail at the lower left, and the tailed form follows every 6. 1437, Montcada and Amat. The key of the embassy of Guillem Ramon de Montcada and Antoni Amat to Charles VII, dated 18 March 1437 (ACA, Cartas Reales Alfonso IV, Varios 69; Aragó, Cuadernos de Arqueología e Historia de la Ciudad 12, 1968; DECODE R10183, public; PARES 3205682). Its alphabet is dots, strokes and small hooks, one sign per letter; its nomenclator of about ninety entries uses a triangle for treva and a circle for naus . The alphabet shares nothing with the letter. 1429, the Castile war. The key published by Josepa Cortès Escrivà and Vicent Pons Alós, “Una clau criptogràfica d’Alfons el Magnànim per a la guerra amb Castella (1429)”, Saitabi 36 (1986), pp. 25–36: Biblioteca-Arxiu Històric Maiansià (Col·legi del Corpus Christi, València), ms. 677 f. 435v, headed cum baiulo generali Valencie , the king’s key with his batle general Joan Mercader. It has seventeen consonant signs, three signs for each vowel, nine nulls ( nichil importantes ), and a nomenclator of persons, places and terms of war drawn for the conflict with Castile. Alphabet: no fit. A few shapes recur (a crossed triple stroke for f, 8-like forms among the homophones of a and u, a 2-shaped q, a 3-shaped y), but a decryption built on them gives no Catalan. Nomenclator: a plausible fit. The letter’s triangle matches the key’s regne d’Aragó (a triangle on a base); its dotted square hook, the key’s Catalunya (a barred hook); its dotted bracketed b, the key’s rei de Castella (a looped b set between dots); its 6 with a top stroke, the key’s curl for Navarra or naus ; and a plain 3 is one of the key’s nulls. On that reading run 1 would say, roughly, “at the instance of […] Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, the king of Castile […] and those of this kingdom”, with the plain 8 as e , “and”. That suits a letter about extending a truce among Aragon, Navarre and Castile. It rests on four or five sign matches, and the alphabet signs between the word signs stay unassigned, so it is recorded here as a hypothesis. The article also notes a second alphabet in the same volume, “aliud abecedarium in libro intitulato Segon d’estols e armades, cartes CLX–CLXI”, which has not been published.
maria1435.html#siblings

Forty-two signs cannot fix a homophonic alphabet, so the plan was to find more text in the same key. Reg. 3225 is not on PARES (only 460 of the 866 registers of Alfonso IV are described there), so four neighbours were fetched in full and examined page by page: Register Series Span Images Cipher 3226 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 5 Mar 1437 – Apr 1438 264 none 3224 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 3 Aug 1421 – Nov 1423 286 none 3113 Comune Sigilli Secreti loc. 6 June 1432 – 21 June 1435 472 none 2693 Secretorum 3 (the king) 1431 – July 1435 392 none The queen’s letters to the king in these registers, and her instructions to envoys in Castile, are all in clear. Reg. 3113 stops on 21 June 1435, before the truce expired. The Cartas Reales of Alfonso IV on PARES (3,055 items with images) hold thirteen pieces of 1435, none from the king to the queen and none in cipher. The king’s register explains the silence. His chancery copied ciphered despatches in clear and marked them fuit expedita in cifra : to his envoys at Rome in 1434, to the bishop of Lleida, to his almoner at Basel, to the archbishop of Zaragoza on 26 July 1435 (“the peace with Castile is signed and to be kept secret”), and to the queen herself on 27 July 1435. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 2693 f. 187r: Alfonso to the queen, Reyna molt cara e molt amada muller , from the siege of Gaeta, 27 July 1435, registered in clear and marked In ciffra at the foot. The letter itself explains: les vies d’aqui no son prou segures, conve scriure ab ciffra , “the roads from here are not safe enough; one must write in cipher”. The ciphered original, received in Valencia, has not been found. Image: Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 2693 f. 187r, via PARES (image 374). So a king–queen cipher was in use in the very week before her letter. The queen’s secretary copied cipher into the register; the king’s did not. The only place more of her side can survive is reg. 3225 itself, and the only place his ciphered originals can survive is among the letters she received, which on PARES do not include them.
maria1435.html#method

A Catalan letter-quadgram model was built from about three million characters of Catalan text, and a simulated annealer searched one-sign-one-letter keys over the three runs, each scored with its clear context on both sides and the dotted signs treated as word boundaries. Without cribs it returns fluent-looking nonsense, as 42 signs must. Every crib is penalised heavily: la treua at the head of run 2 costs 63 log-units against the free optimum, treua at any offset 35 to 90, tregua 61 or more, castella anywhere in run 3 between 50 and 128, and most other offsets are impossible because a repeated sign would have to stand for two letters. With the 1429 nomenclator applied the result is the same. A plain substitution does not carry the expected words, which points to homophones, nulls and word signs, and those cannot be recovered from this little text.

Gallica’s catalogue was queried for diplomatic manuscripts of 1575–1620 absent from Tomokiyo’s pages, and the hits in range checked against his coverage of the League volumes and the reigns of Henri III and IV. Of the residue, fr. 16127 (original letters of French agents in the Low Countries, 1571–94) was fetched entire (from the Gallica PDF after the IIIF service throttled) and examined on contact sheets. Roughly twenty of Mondoucet’s despatches carry cipher, and almost every ciphered leaf is followed, on the next folio or in the margin, by a contemporary decipherment in the Court’s hand. One stands out: 13 July 1572, ff. 60–61 , has no decipherment anywhere in the volume. Its date places it four days before the Huguenot relief column under Genlis was destroyed at Saint-Ghislain outside Mons, and six weeks before the massacre of St Bartholomew. Mondoucet’s office was the covert French contact with William of Orange’s revolt that these weeks turned on; the absence of a Court decipherment, in a volume where every other ciphered despatch has one, is why the leaf was chosen.

Three transcriptions had been made (one by hand at glyph level, two by automatic segmentation and k -means clustering of glyph shapes), and four aligners built and validated on synthetic controls of the same size and shape: hard-EM Viterbi, a consistency beam, a soft-EM banded HMM, and the same with word-signs consuming several letters. The controls recovered 44 of 44 and 56 of 58 symbols. Against the two decipherments that can be checked (the 29 August letter deciphered at f. 9, the 16 July block deciphered at f. 64), every method scored at the shuffled-plaintext baseline. The clue was a number. On the 16 July pair, which is verbatim where the gloss lets one check it, the automatic segmentation counted 1.3–1.4 connected glyph components per plaintext letter. That was taken at the time as a property of the cipher (heavy nulls, or letters written with more than one separable stroke), and it was what defeated the aligners, since a solver that assumes one glyph maps to one letter cannot align a stream with 35 % too many symbols. But the ratio was measured on the output of the segmentation , the one component never validated against a hand count. Hand transcription of the glossed words settles it: under the f. 62r gloss leur délivrance , the number of pen-lifted glyphs equals the number of letters, and the same holds under pouvez and au 30 and across the 16 July block wherever the f. 64 decipherment fixes the letters. The excess was an artefact: the segmentation split looped d , the long- s with crossbar, and the barred o and q into two components each, and attached dots and bars as separate glyphs. One glyph is one letter. The error was in the first stage of the processing.

The volume contains its own crib. The 16 July 1572 pair (ff. 62–64) is enciphered in the same system and glossed : on f. 62r the Court decipherer wrote several plaintext words above the cipher ( pouvez , leur délivrance , la bruslation , nous maintenant , au 30 ), and f. 64 (“16 juillet 1572, déchiffré de la précédente”) gives the whole block in clear, 17 lines and 863 letters. Placing the glossed words fixes about twenty letters at once. Carried into a HMM alignment of the hand transcription — forward–backward and Viterbi, banded around the glossed words, with a per-glyph null rate, they give a table of homophone counts per glyph and a small null set { * , C , mq , j } . The cipher is homophonic with a 24-letter early-modern alphabet ( i = j , u = v ), a few digraph symbols (the symbol transcribed 23 = qu , crossed-phi = ll ), and those four nulls. Decryption is then a decoding problem: a decoder (keeping the best 300 partial texts, width 300) combines, per glyph, the probability of each letter from the aligned counts with the transition probability from a 5-gram model of sixteenth-century French, and emits a null marker where even the best letter is improbable. The control is internal. Decoding the 16 July block with the recovered key (its clear text is known from f. 64) reproduces the decipherer’s own gloss. The line under which f. 62r has leur délivrance decodes to “… leur delivrance des espagnols a ce moyen …” and the surrounding lines decode continuously with it (“… penser que le roi lui a prester ses affaires …”, “… envoyer afin … clement adverti du premier … de son armée assemblée de laquelle aura …”, “… prelate teste en flandres …”). The gloss match shows the key is partly right; the re-check in §04 puts it at about 60 % of letters on this block, the one it was fitted on.

f. 60r, the head of the 13 July 1572 despatch: the docket 13 juillet 1572, Bruxelles, du sr de Mondoucet au Roy , the clear opening Sire, encores que je vous aye faict une depesche de l’unziesme de ce moys … , then the first of its 22 cipher lines on this page, which still read only as scattered words. Clear-text bands carry the connective narrative and the whole close, and the cipher is reserved for the sensitive matter, as usual for a resident who trusted the courier with the rest. The clear bands need no key. On f. 60v, a Spanish informant’s report: J’ay esté asseuré par Espaignol mesme qui cy vient qu’il n’y a pas troys mil hommes de pied & cinq cens chevaux cy tout. Toutesfois ilz demourent encores là arrestez. Et dit on que du costé de Mastricq se marche quelques regymens d’allemans nouvellement leuez… f. 61r closes in clear: Sire je supplie le Createur qu’il vous donne … très longue vie. De Bruxelles ce [Ve] jour de Juillet 1572 , signed de Mondoucet , over vostre treshumble tresobeyssant et tresaffectionné serviteur et subiect . The ciphered lines (22 on f. 60r, one on f. 60v, six on f. 61r) decode in stretches with the same key. They speak of religieuse , Espaigne , the saint père and the pape , Escosse , Angleterre , troupes de terre , catholique , ministres , liberté , garnison ; f. 61r gives … le prince … service du roi , … parenté entre les autres cour[s] , … avaient esté capitulé … réduit . Re-checked 21 September 2026: these words overstate the decryption. Re-marking the open alpha (= r ) on the 13 July strips and decoding again with the 1572 key, the 1573 key and a merged key gives no real gain. On the 16 July control block the 1572 key scores only about 60 % of letters, and that block is the one it was fitted on. Counted strictly, word-divided output that reads as French sense covers about 1 % of the 1,082 cipher glyphs of 13 July, and about 8 % counted leniently. The words above are the language model's fill as much as the cipher's. The despatch is not deciphered: the leaves are legible, and what is missing is a better 1572 key, for which the single 863-letter crib is too short.

The catalogue listed two 1573 letters from Antwerp and Amsterdam as having no full reading. On the leaves, the 9 September 1573 letter (Amsterdam; cipher ff. 135r–137v) has a complete Court decipherment on ff. 139r–141r (“deschiffré”), and it is verbatim: a hard-EM alignment of 4,735 hand-transcribed glyphs against it runs line for line with a glyph-to-letter ratio of 0.91, the shortfall being word signs such as dict , faict , monsieur . The alignment gives the 1573 key, about 55 signs, the 1572 system with the same homophones. The 4 January 1573 letter (Antwerp; cipher f. 126v, 4 lines, f. 127r, 31 lines, f. 127v, 4 lines) has no decipherment anywhere in the volume, only four interlinear glosses on f. 127r ( hambourg , Lan… , and two unsure). It was decrypted with the 9 September key and the French 5-gram decoder. The control: a key rebuilt without block 1 of 9 September decodes that block blind at 77.5 % of letters. Re-transcribing every 4 January line on the strips corrected 20 glyphs, and splitting the round a from the open alpha with a crossing tail, which the first transcription had merged, showed that the alpha is always r and the round a never is (l, y, i); the control rose to 79.0 %. The gloss hambourg decoded in place, and about 55–60 % of the 4 January letters gave sense, among them “seize ou dix huict”, “soubz ombre de chercher parti”, “desavantaige … qu’il fera”, “l’Angleterre avoit … tenir cent …”, “[H]ambourg, où on croit debvoir servir pareil”. The text was then found in print. Mondoucet kept a register of his despatches from September 1572 (Bibliothèque de Reims), and L. Didier printed it in 1891: the letter of 4 January 1573 is on pp. 141–142 of volume 1, in clear, ending “D’Anvers, ce IIIIe jour de janvier 1573”. The ciphered part is: … il se donnoit fort secrètement wartgueld des costez de Collongne, Francfort, Spire et autres villes, sans qu’il se puisse savoir de quelle part; et aultres encores, ne voullans estre descouvertz, prenent aultre voye, donnans argent aux collonnelz pour entretenir leurs reistres-mestres et gentilzhommes, et lesdictz reistres-mestres entretenans leurs soldatz particulliers. Aussi, que les villes de [Hesse?], Strasbourg et aultres faisoient levées de gens; outre plus, qu’il estoit depuis naguières arrivé à Collongne seize ou dix huict cappitaines venans de Suède et Dannemarch … De tout ce qui se passera j’espère en donner toute lumyère à V. Ma té par le rapport que m’en fera ung cappitaine allemand … qui m’a semblé estre plus propre que aultre, par ce que, soubz umbre de chercher party, il descouvrira tout ce qui se fait … J’ay seu que Mons r le duc d’Alve avoit pris ceste forme de wartgueld avec le duc de Brunsvick … et croy qu’il aura fait le semblable à l’endroit du duc de Lauembourg de Saxe … Davantaige, Sire, je ne veulx oublier de vous advertir comme j’ay [apprins] que la royne d’Angleterre avoit fait tenir cent mil escuz à Hambourg, que l’on croyt debvoir servir pour pareil effect. Estant en ceste ville, j’ay descouvert qu’il y avoit quelque temps qu’un certain évesque de Hirlande y séjournoit, quy y est entretenu par ledict sieur duc, avec lequel il conduit la pratique dudict pays de Hirlande … (Didier 1891, i, 141–142; spelling normalised from the OCR where it was garbled.) Every stretch the decoder had given stands in the printed text, and the lines it had not decrypted are now filled: Louis of Nassau’s secret wartgeld retainers, captains from Sweden and Denmark at Cologne, a German captain sent as a spy, Alba’s own wartgeld with Brunswick and Saxe-Lauenburg (the gloss Lan… ), English money at Hamburg, and an Irish bishop kept at Antwerp by Alba for a design on Ireland (the decoder’s “de l’Irlande” in l. 31). The edition was in the page’s sources from the start but was not opened until after the ciphertext-only passes, so those passes are an independent partial decryption; the text of 4 January is the edition’s. The 13 July 1572 despatch is not in Didier: the register begins on 6 September 1572, and Didier’s own inventory of fr. 16127 calls that letter “chiffrée et en grande partie sans déchiffrement”.

A ciphered despatch that four validated aligners could not align is an ordinary homophonic substitution; what defeated the solvers was an unvalidated automatic segmentation that produced a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio and broke the one-to-one mapping. The lesson: check a glyph-per-letter ratio taken from an automatic segmentation against a hand count on a passage of known plaintext before relying on it. What remains is a clean retranscription of the ciphered lines to a fixed glyph accuracy and the collation of the clear bands with the other fr. 16127 letters. A second lesson came from 1573: open the edition before decoding. Didier printed the 4 January letter in clear, and the page’s sources had cited it all along.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Amsterdam, 9 Sept 1573, ff. 135-137 (Court decipherment ff. 139-141) Mondoucet reports to Charles IX on Alba's siege of Alkmaar (it can be assaulted from one place only), Alba's recall by the King of Spain, Medinaceli, the King of Poland's passage and Danzig, and a letter from France predicting things greater than St Bartholomew's Day. The Court's verbatim decipherment on ff. 139-141 was typed and aligned against the cipher; the tail (f. 137v against f. 141r) was compared by length only and is not transcribed. The published partial decipherment supplies many cribs, including repeated IST , DIE and the phrase about a round sphere. The opening gives no sense if the nested angles are confused with the semicircular D, or if the first curled staff is taken for F. Three nested angles give M in PRIMA , MATERIA and VOM . Two give N in EINE , RUNDE and OFFEN . The semicircle is D. The first curled staff has an upper curl as well as a lower one: P. The B of HALB has only the lower curl. The cross supplies F consistently in GEFAE and the two adjacent F positions of OFFEN . A solid dot above a line is I, whereas an open ring above a line is O. The three signs after GALLE are therefore V-O-M. The result means “gall of the ram”; it does not enumerate “gall and ram.” The 19 attested sign classes. IDs refer to the reproducible transcription. The book is catalogued 1618; the cipher itself carries no date or signature. ## Literal substitution ```text PRIMA MATERIA IST DIE GALLE UOM WIDDER DAS GEFAE IST EINE HALB RUNDE KUGEL DER OFFEN IST DIE WAGE ``` U and V share one sign: UOM is read VOM. Commas are visible after GALLE, WIDDER, KUGEL and at the end; they are not cipher tokens. The first one need not be modern syntactic punctuation. Spaces above are editorial word divisions consistent with the broad manuscript spacing. ## Conservative reading Prima materia ist die Galle vom Widder. Das Gefae [wohl: Gefäß] ist eine halb runde Kugel. Der Offen ist die Wage. ## Normalized German (one explicit emendation) Die Prima Materia ist die Galle vom Widder. Das Gefä[ß] ist eine halbrunde Kugel. Der Ofen ist die Waage. The final ß of Gefäß is an editorial replacement of the E actually obtained from the cipher, not a recovered sign. The f is an inferred key value, supported again by both crosses in OFFEN. ## English The prime matter is the gall of the ram. The vessel [emended] is a half-round sphere. The furnace is the balance [or Libra]. These are the words, not a demonstrated chemical recipe. Whether ram and balance carry zodiacal or other alchemical meanings remains undetermined. ## Confidence and coverage All 79 signs in 19 classes receive values. Of them, 78/79 (98.73%) read without a conjectural textual correction; line 3 sign 8 is clearly the E sign, but GEFAE does not make a satisfactory word in context. GEFAS / Gefäß is the likely intended word, graded M. The remaining reconstructed mappings are I under this repository's provenance grades (inferred from repeated words and context, not read from an archival key). This is a reading assisted by prior partial work, not an independent ciphertext-only break. ## Prior work and the changes Anne-Simone Rous's partial reading is printed by Uwe Maximilian Korn (2023), p. 178 n. 41. It was found before this attempt and used. The main corrections are PRIMA MATERIA (distinguish the two forms of curled staff and the triple angles), VOM (ring rather than dot; triple rather than double angles), F for the crosses, and N for the double angles ending OFFEN. The anomalous final E of GEFAE is retained as a source discrepancy. No full earlier decipherment was found in the searches recorded in NOTES.md. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) At a glance Existing decipherment · partial (100% of the cipher) The letter Ferenc Rákóczi II to an unnamed envoy on his way to Holland, Lwów, 27 June 1711, six pages signed in autograph “Franciscus Princeps”. Where Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár, P237 Festetics 10. d. 2. 42–44; DECODE R483, dated there 7 June. It was catalogued with three French letters to Rákóczi (catalogue 44). The cipher A numerical Latin syllabary with homophones: several numbers for each common letter, codes for open syllables, a few for words and names. Cipher and clear alternate within the lines. How it was deciphered A clerk wrote the decipherment above every ciphered stretch. It was transcribed with the cipher, and an alignment of the two rebuilt 224 codes of the key, which reproduce 70% of the clerk’s letters. What it says Rákóczi rejects the Peace of Szatmár and a king proclaimed outside a free diet, asks the Tsar and Poland to mediate, and reports Pálffy’s guns before Munkács. Still open Five words of the clear opening on page 1, and about a dozen doubtful words on groups seen once or not at all in the rebuilt key. With them the running text builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.9% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. This letter was filed with three French reports sent to Rákóczi, which use the Bonac–Groffey key DECODE R639. It is in a different cipher; those letters have their own page: three letters to Rákóczi, 1706–1707 .
rakoczi1711.html#the-letter

The letter is signed in autograph “Franciscus Princeps” and dated in clear “Leopoli die 27. Junii Anno 1711”; DECODE’s 7 June is a misreading. It is addressed to “Fidelis nobis sincere dilecte”, an envoy on his way to Holland, who is in poor health and handles money and the mathematical instruments ordered from Mangold. A clear postscript deals with those instruments. Thaly’s Archivum Rákóczianum I/3 (the letter-books of 1710–1712) does not print the letter, but its no. 44, an order to Mihály Klement about the Hegyi wines, makes Klement the likely addressee (searched 23 October 2026). The six pages carry 2,531 cipher groups in 180 lines, transcribed here from the images; cipher and clear alternate within the lines.
rakoczi1711.html#content

Rákóczi sends a copy of the “Tractatus sic dictae Pacis Carolianae”, the Peace of Szatmár, which he calls a fraud worked out in Vienna, and reports that Archduke Charles was proclaimed king in every Hungarian county, contrary to the 1687 article of the Pozsony diet. He will not recognise a king proclaimed outside a free diet: nos Regem extra dietam promulgatum, non deposito praevio modo juramento suo, agnoscere non posse sine [?totali] ruina libertatum nostrarum He appeals to the Tsar and the Polish Republic to mediate. He offers to come to a free diet in person or by plenipotentiaries and to recognise a lawfully crowned king, provided the confederates recover their estates. He says the Allies looked only to a “diversionem armorum domus Austriacae” once Hungary was quieted, not to Hungarian liberties, and asks for the war to go on. Page 4 reports Pálffy’s artillery before “arcem nostram Munkatsiensem” and the restitution of Transylvanian liberty. Page 5 turns to the general confederation in Poland, letters to go “per Saxoniam”, the Muscovite advance, a warning to trust only news sent directly from Rákóczi, and a complaint about the “Indiscretum procedendi modum Magni Cancellarii Regii Raday”, the Grand Chancellor Pál Ráday. Page 6 concerns receipts left with a Jew and a member of the Economic Council who took treasury money for his own use.
rakoczi1711.html#the-key

The clerk wrote the decipherment above every ciphered stretch. Of the 2,531 groups, 2,524 lie on a line with an interlinear; the other seven continue words written on the neighbouring line (a one-group ending, a catchword repeated at the head of the next page, and three groups whose words stand on the line above). The key is not preserved. Each cipher line was aligned with the Latin above it by an alignment algorithm (hard expectation-maximisation), with each code taking up to four letters. The result is a syllabic cipher with homophones. Single letters have several values (190 and 430 s; 140 and 380 n; 60 and 300 e; 20 and 260 a; 130 and 370 m), open syllables have their own codes (257 re, 428 ti, 68 se, 362 de, 96 no, 457 ri, 148 si, 92 ce, 152 co, 59 tu, 378 ta), and a few words and names are coded whole. Of 224 codes, 156 occur at least twice. Decoding the letter with this key reproduces 3,180 of the clerk’s 4,547 letters (69.9%). The mismatches are rare codes, homophones seen once and the clerk’s own abbreviations. Where the clerk’s handwriting is doubtful, the cipher often settles the word, as in the sentence quoted above and in “ne fors etiam”. The running text (23 October 2026). The reading audit of 22 October 2026 had set the letter back to decoded, not read: the clerk’s interlinear merged with the clear passages line by line stood out of reading order, with doubts or alternatives on most lines. It is now written out as one running Latin text ( R483_reading.md , English R483_en.md ): the interlinear stretches and the clear passages interleaved as they stand in each line, every clear word and every doubtful interlinear word re-read on the six DECODE images, and the clerk’s doubts settled group by group with the rebuilt key. 72 changes are listed in R483_corrections.tsv : ab inimicitiis for the clerk’s ab Armistitiis , inimicitias suas for amicitiis fidis , tranquillos reddat animos for his letter-by-letter Transi- l w s re d da , domino Jablonski for Fablanski ; juramento suo , which the clerk skipped, is restored from the figures. No word is supplied without figures under it. Counted by words, with the open and doubtful words as holes, the running text reads at 94.9%: just under the 95% a complete reading needs. The Bonac–Groffey table R639, which deciphers the French letters once filed with this one, gives nonsense on it.

Five words of the clear opening on page 1 (“Supponimus redditas jam […] …”): fast cursive not settled on the DECODE images; a higher-resolution scan from the archive is the way on. About a dozen doubtful words where the clerk and the key disagree and the group occurs once or not at all in the rebuilt key ([?concludendam], [?remediationis], [?possidere], [?commisso], domino Jablonski […] ). 68 of the 224 rebuilt codes occur only once (C). The recipient is not named; probably Mihály Klement (above).

Fideli nobis sincere dilecte. Supponimus redditas jam […] Vobis fuisse Responsorias Literas nostras ad […] […] Vestras transmissas, et quid [?contineant], et annexis [?earundem] abunde […] […]nistris, in quonam cardine vertentur negotia nostra. Nec nos fefellit opinio, quid enim minister quidam scribat [?Viennae] hisce [?audivimus], et ex his omnibus alliatas quoque Potentias agnituras speramus justas et aequas rationes nostras, ob quas ad [?concludendam] illam mente Imperatoris subjecta fraudulosam negotiationem ultimam manum admovere renuimus. Verum prout Vobis in memoratis Literis nostris [?…] Literas ante [?Capitulationem] [?armistitii] [?Generali] Palffio missas transmisimus, ita nunc quoque [?postreme] scriptas copiam communicamus, quae ipsi in proprias quidem manus traditae fuere, sed Tabellarius denegato responso reversus est. Interea vero certum est Palatinum in omnibus Hungariae Comitatibus Carolum archiducem pro Rege promulgasse, contra manifesta Jura et Libertates Regni, quae similem Promulgationem pacatis [?prius] animis in universali Dieta Regni fieri debere praescribunt. Et ipsemet articulus Dietae Posoniensis anni millesimi sexcentesimi octogesimi septimi, hic copialiter annexus, quidnam praescribat fieri debere ante Promulgationem et agnitionem Regis abunde videre poterunt. Agnoscent, speramus, si qui sine praejudicio sana conscientia de rebus nostris judicare voluerint, nos Regem extra dietam promulgatum, non deposito praevio modo juramento suo, agnoscere non posse sine [?totali] ruina libertatum nostrarum, quae profecto per haereditariae successionis praetensionem, et ne fors etiam futura [?in] [?agnitionem], in tantum non laederentur aut annihilarentur quam per actum hunc, per quem juri suo Regibus Conditiones praescribendi et illos super eas adjurandi cederet natio. Ac proinde Czaro Moscoviae et Rege Poloniarum hic existentibus, Reipublicae Poloniae in Senatus consultum convocatae suo modo institimus, ut ope [?remediationis] reassumpta Declarationem nostram pro justa agnoscere velint, qua mediante nos ab inimicitiis desistere velle affidavimus ad id usque Tempus, donec Libertates et Leges nostras de novo [?latis] publicis actibus compertum non fuerit. Appromisimus praeterea nos in promulganda libera dieta, habita sufficiente securitate, vel personaliter vel per plenipotentiarios nostros comparere velle et eum pro Rege agnituros, qui legaliter agnitus et coronatus fuerit, eique juramentum praestituros. Petimus proinde ut hacce declaratione nostra facta omnes in confoederatione nostra perseverantes restituantur in integrum et bona nostra, interea quoque pro securitate personarum nostrarum in Polonia degentes [?possidere] valeamus. Institimus prout dictum ut Potentiae supra memoratae haec effectuare velint, quae et operanda suis ministris quoque commiserunt, et Securitatem nostram pacisque conciliationem Respublica expresso Senatusconsulti statuto sanxit. Ex adjuncta Literis Vestris Copia Literas generalium ordinum viduae Imperatrici regnanti scriptas profecto sat dolenter videmus praecipitatam agnitionem Archiducis pro Rege Hungariae, ubi potius sperassemus praefatos omnes per acta Mediationis negotiationum [?Tirnavii] [?ex] […] abunde [?informatos] esse debuisse […] Regem in Hungaria sine observantia praemissorum promulgatum pro aequanimitate mediationis suae agnoscere non potuisse. Interim praeterea Nos suspicari posse credimus non satis sinceras fuisse toties repetitas assecurationes alliatorum de restituendis et solidandis libertatibus nostris, sed tantum modo in id intendisse, ut pacatis quoquo modo rebus Hungaricis diversionem armorum domus Austriacae [?ferrent]. Necessarium igitur judicamus, ut iis abunde [?demonstretis] facile illos in opinione sua falli posse, qui nobis media non superexistere [?credunt]. Et profecto hoc tempore reassument animum vindicandae libertatis, nisi ea ita assecurata fuerit, ut et nostros et eorum tranquillos reddat animos. Patefacta sunt magna ex parte aulae Viennensis consilia per continuationem inimicitiae Comitis Palfi contra arcem nostram Munkatsiensem facta. We suppose that our letters in answer to […] […] your letters, already […], have been delivered to you, and what they [?contain], and from the annexes [?of them] […] fully […] in what hinge our affairs will turn. To these we therefore add what was lacking then, namely a copy of the treaty of the so-called Peace of Charles [Szatmár], which the Viennese court now calls Points of [?Submission], together with [?remarks] which will be able to show you and the allies the [?hidden] poison, because of which we did not consider it consistent with our obligation to our country to accept them. Nor were we mistaken in our opinion: for what a certain minister writes [?in Vienna] we [?have heard] by these, and from all this we hope that the allied Powers too will recognise the just and fair reasons for which we refused to put the last hand to [?concluding] that fraudulent negotiation, subject to the mind of the Emperor. And just as in our said letters we sent you [?…] the letters sent to [?General] Pálffy before the [?capitulation] of the [?armistice], so now we also communicate a copy of those written [?last], which were indeed handed to him into his own hands; but the courier came back with an answer refused. Meanwhile it is certain that the Palatine has proclaimed Archduke Charles king in all the counties of Hungary, against the manifest rights and liberties of the Kingdom, which prescribe that such a proclamation must be made, minds [?first] being pacified, in a general Diet of the Kingdom. And the very article of the Diet of Pozsony of the year 1687, annexed here in copy, will show them fully what it prescribes must be done before the proclamation and recognition of a King. Those who will judge our affairs without prejudice and with a sound conscience will recognise, we hope, that we cannot recognise a King proclaimed outside a diet, who has not first taken his oath in the due manner, without the [?total] ruin of our liberties; which indeed would not be harmed or annihilated so much by the claim of hereditary succession, and lest perhaps even future ones [?in] [?recognition], as by this act, by which the nation would yield its right of prescribing conditions to its kings and of binding them by oath to them. And therefore, the Tsar of Muscovy and the King of Poland being here, we have pressed the Polish Republic, assembled in a Senate council in its own way, to recognise our declaration as just, its [?mediation] being resumed; by means of which [declaration] we affirmed that we are willing to desist from hostilities until such time as it is established by public acts that our liberties and laws have been [?restored] anew. We promised moreover that, given sufficient security, we would appear at the proclamation of a free diet either in person or through our plenipotentiaries, and would recognise as King him who has been lawfully recognised and crowned, and would swear the oath to him. We therefore ask that, this declaration of ours being made, all who persevere in our confederation be restored in full, and our goods, and that meanwhile for the security of our persons we, living in Poland, may [?hold (them)]. We have pressed, as was said, that the Powers mentioned above will bring this about, which they have also entrusted to their ministers to work on; and the Republic has sanctioned our security and the reconciliation of peace by an express statute of the Senate council. From the copy, added to your letters, of the letter of the general estates written to the widowed reigning Empress, we see indeed with great sorrow the precipitate recognition of the Archduke as King of Hungary, where we would rather have hoped that all the aforesaid, from the acts of the mediation of the negotiations [?at Nagyszombat] […], ought to have been fully [?informed] that […] they could not, for the even-handedness of their mediation, recognise a King proclaimed in Hungary without observing the premises. For we hoped [?that by this] […] [?they] [?were bound] to the restoration of our liberties, in which they often promised they wished to maintain us, and that no stronger means could be found to help us than the delay of this recognition until the execution of those things which they acknowledged ought justly to be done for the common good and for the much-desired security of the religions in Hungary. Meanwhile, moreover, we believe we may suspect that the so often repeated assurances of the allies about restoring and consolidating our liberties were not sincere enough, but that they only aimed at this: that, Hungarian affairs being pacified in any way, they would [?bring] a diversion of the arms of the House of Austria. We therefore judge it necessary that you show them fully that those who believe we have no means left can easily be wrong in their opinion. But [as to] the continuation of the war [?which will follow] in case of the oppression of the nation, and those who imagine that the nation is so estranged from us that […] of thousands of faithless men could thus better be wished for, had we not with our consent soothed them, who [?believe] they have now been deceived. And indeed at this time they will take up again the spirit of claiming their liberty, unless it is so secured that it makes both our minds and theirs tranquil. The designs of the Viennese court have been largely revealed by the continuation of Count Pálffy's hostility against our castle of Munkács. Our declaration, and the one made by our order to the garrison, which we add to the present, being disregarded, notwithstanding which he continued his hostilities below the castle, brought cannon against it and, forcing it to surrender against all laws, occupied that castle by force from us. Let the allies therefore not wonder that in all things we [?have judged] fit for preserving our liberties [we] wish to proceed securely, and they would keep us in [our] state […] also maintain, [?we can], unless they have supplied us as soon as possible with the means of securing them through a firm and stable security, [?than] which a better can hardly be supplied than through the restoration of the liberty of Transylvania, which in the present conjuncture the Archduke ought not to make difficulties over, so that, the minds of the Hungarians being won and bound entirely, he could apply his army according to the necessity and exigency of his affairs. [?If] [?therefore] you yourself, because of your state of health, could not continue your journey to Holland, you are to communicate this without delay, as the need of our interest requires, to those who are well disposed and to whom it shall be necessary. You are to send [?the same] views to the King of Poland's Commissary General, a man named Spiegel, who is here in Poland, and to write them out as soon as possible in [?letters] directed through Saxony, so that we can adapt the present conjuncture, whether tending to peace (if a suitable one can be made) or to war, to our affairs and the interest of our country. Further we announce what [?happier] news our correspondents have brought of the progress of the Muscovite arms, from which it can firmly be hoped that that war will be finished with easy labour, as the Tsar desires. As for your expenses, we believe it is fully clear to you what we have so far disapproved; [you are] to adapt yourself in future too to the state of affairs and of the times, whose straits restrict us as well. Trust least of all [?letters] and information from private persons, unless they come directly from us; for in the present circumstances it can hardly be decided whom one should trust. Ráday ought long ago, by our order, to have [?written] to Lord Jabłonowski […] about the indiscreet way of proceeding of the Royal Grand Chancellor, assuming that you had continued your journey to Holland; but at the same time we received letters of the said Grand Chancellor written from Dukla, in which he notifies that he does not want to keep the wines once [?accepted] still at vintage time, the original receipts having been issued about them and being held by us, but to leave them in the care of a certain Jew, to be handed over to our deputed man when he comes. But since we believe that we have satisfied [the matter] entirely by [the decision] of our Economic Council issued on it […], the wines having been consigned to the custody of his own man from the time the receipts were issued, carried at our expense to the appointed place and left in his custody, if any damage has befallen the royal cellar through the carelessness of the keepers, we do not consider ourselves answerable for it. For the wines, the money advanced to Hegyi of the [?Council] of the Realm's Economy [is to be claimed] from him to whom he can claim [it] as owed beyond our orders; for he, [?having committed] a breach of faith with the others, has turned the money to his own uses, and is not at all subject to our authority. For the rest we remain benignly inclined to you with our princely favour. Lwów, 27 June, year 1711. Francis, Prince. We are astonished that no mention is made in your letters of the mathematical instruments and other things ordered from Mangold, for whose payment your assignation too has been dispatched; we wish to enjoin you seriously that all those things which we ordered to be made there be carried out without delay and sent here. Two royalist cipher letters that Cryptiana lists with no decipherment, Prince Maurice to Rupert (Worcester, 7 July 1645) and the intercepts of May 1646 in BL Add MS 72438 ff. 9–10, were transcribed and tried against all 73 keys taken in Lord Digby’s coach (index f. 25r).
